docs.title: 8.1 The Application: The Acceleration of the Saturn V & Werner Romberg's Extrapolation
docs.text:
In university calculus, students spend semesters memorizing symbolic anti-derivative techniques: integration by parts, trigonometric substitutions, and partial fractions. Every textbook problem is an artificial puzzle engineered to yield a tidy closed-form formula like \(x^3/3\) or \(-\cos x\).

Then you step into an aerospace telemetry center or a nuclear fluid dynamics laboratory. In the real physical universe, almost NO engineering function has a closed-form anti-derivative!

docs.title: 8.1.1 The Saturn V Burnout Problem: Integrating Telemetry Under G-Forces
docs.text:
When the five massive Rocketdyne F-1 engines ignite beneath the Apollo Saturn V lunar launch vehicle, they consume fifteen metric tons of kerosene and liquid oxygen every second. As propellants drain from the colossal tanks, the vehicle's thrust-to-weight ratio surges dramatically, pinning the astronauts into their custom contour couches under four and a half times the acceleration of gravity.

Vehicle acceleration \(a(t)\) does not follow a sterile, textbook polynomial. It is shaped by supersonic atmospheric compressibility shocks, non-linear atmospheric density gradients, aerodynamic buffet, and propellant sloshing. Real vehicle acceleration is captured not as an equation, but as an empirical stream of high-frequency telemetry data.

How fast is the spacecraft travelling when the S-IC first stage burns out at \(T = 160\text{ seconds}\)? Under the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, velocity is the definite integral of acceleration:

\[v(T) = v_0 + \int_0^T a(t)\,dt\]

If the flight guidance calculator cannot evaluate that integral with certified numerical precision, engine cut-off will occur fractions of a second too early or too late. A \(0.1\%\) velocity shortfall means missing translunar injection entirely and tumbling into the void of deep space.

docs.title: The Trapezoidal Trap: Why Brute Force Fails
docs.text: Approximating an integral using elementary trapezoidal sums reduces error at a painfully slow pace—proportional to \(O(h^2)\), cutting error by a factor of four when slice width is halved. To extract ten decimal digits of precision from a complex curve, a brute-force calculator would need to sample hundreds of thousands of evaluation points, draining battery cells for twenty minutes of continuous calculation.

docs.title: Werner Romberg (1955): Algebraic Error Cancellation
docs.text:
In 1955, Norwegian mathematician Werner Romberg made an extraordinary mathematical breakthrough (Romberg, 1955). By examining the Euler-Maclaurin summation formula, Romberg proved that the truncation error in a composite trapezoidal approximation is not random noise—it is a structured, analytic power series in even powers of the step size:

\[\int_a^b f(t)\,dt = T(h) + c_1 h^2 + c_2 h^4 + c_3 h^6 + \dots\]

Romberg asked a revolutionary question: Why evaluate millions of microscopic slices when we can take two coarse approximations at step \(h\) and step \(h/2\), and algebraically combine them to annihilate the dominant \(h^2\) error term entirely?

This is Richardson extrapolation. By assembling successive halving approximations into a lower-triangular Romberg Tableau, Romberg turned a sluggish \(O(h^2)\) crawl into an \(O(h^{2k})\) rocket of convergence. Four Romberg step-halvings achieve greater precision than 500,000 brute-force trapezoids.

On the StackCalc SC-32, pressing [↱] [∫] executes Romberg's tableau directly on your operational stack, evaluating non-integrable reality with breathtaking elegance.

Transflective LCD dot-matrix integration status line and 4-stack preservation. 3. Abstract Level(Analytical Theorems & Asymptotic Expansions) • Fundamental Theorem of Calculus: \(\frac{d}{dx} \left[\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\right] = f(x)\)• Euler-Maclaurin asymptotic expansion of numerical quadrature errors: \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = T(h) + c_1 h^2 + c_2 h^4 + c_3 h^6 + \dots\)• Richardson extrapolation: Analytical elimination of dominant truncation powers without requiring infinitesimal step sizes. docs.title: 8.3 Adaptive Romberg Numerical Quadrature ([↱] [∫])
docs.text:
The Feynman Intuition: The Coastline of Britain & The Richardson Leap

Suppose you set out to measure the perimeter of a rugged, rocky island. You walk along the shore with a 10-meter chain, recording a total distance of 1,000 meters. Next, you re-measure the same coastline with a 5-meter rod. Because the shorter rod fits into small bays and rocky inlets, your measurement increases to 1,200 meters!

Traditional brute-force intuition insists: To find the true, exact value, we must measure with a 1-centimeter ruler, then a 1-millimeter gauge, taking forever.

In 1910, English polymath Lewis Fry Richardson discovered a profound mathematical shortcut: You do not need an infinite number of microscopic rulers! If you understand mathematically how measurement error scales with the size of your ruler (for instance, error proportional to $h^2, h^4, h^6$), you can algebraically combine your 10-meter and 5-meter measurements to cancel the error completely!

That is Richardson Extrapolation—the analytical engine inside Werner Romberg's 1955 quadrature algorithm. It evaluates a few coarse trapezoids and then uses the geometry of error to vault directly to $10^{-12}$ precision with over $95\%$ fewer function evaluations.

Figure 8.2: The bilateral Prime Studio slide rule comparator stage physically illustrates logarithmic scaling and proportional interval halving corresponding to Richardson extrapolation steps.

Definite integrals calculate accumulated physical quantities across continuous domains: total distance traversed under non-constant velocity, mechanical work performed under variable forces, electrical charge accumulated from transient current pulses, and fluid pressure forces exerted across curved dams.

The StackCalc SC-32 evaluates definite integrals using Adaptive Romberg Numerical Quadrature ([↱] [∫]):

\[I = \int_a^b f(x) \, dx\]

Romberg Quadrature & Richardson Error Extrapolation

  1. Successive Step-Size Halving (Trapezoidal Base): $$h_0 = b - a, \quad h_1 = \frac{h_0}{2}, \quad h_2 = \frac{h_1}{2}, \quad \dots, \quad h_k = \frac{b - a}{2^k}$$
  2. Richardson Extrapolation Tableau: Base column: $R(k, 0) = \text{Extended Trapezoidal sum at step } h_k$ Recursive update: $$R(k, j) = R(k, j-1) + \frac{R(k, j-1) - R(k-1, j-1)}{4^j - 1}$$
| Column Index | Classical Quadrature Rule Equivalent | Error Order | Convergence Characteristics | | :---: | :--- | :---: | :--- | | **$j = 0$** | Extended Composite Trapezoidal Rule | $\mathcal{O}(h^2)$ | Coarse baseline; samples function boundaries and midpoints. | | **$j = 1$** | Simpson's $1/3$ Parabolic Rule | $\mathcal{O}(h^4)$ | Cancels leading $h^2$ error term via 4:1 weighting. | | **$j = 2$** | Boole's 5-Point Rule | $\mathcal{O}(h^6)$ | Cancels $h^4$ curvature artifact; achieves 6 digits. | | **$j = 3$** | High-Order Analytical Extrapolation | $\mathcal{O}(h^8)$ | Sub-ppm precision on smooth transcendentals. | | **$j = 4$** | Machine Epsilon Extrapolation Limit | $\mathcal{O}(h^{10}) < 10^{-12}$ | Terminates when $|R(k, k) - R(k-1, k-1)| < 10^{-11}$. |

docs.title: 8.3.1 The Lower-Triangular Romberg Tableau
docs.text:
As step size \(h_k = (b - a)/2^k\) is halved at each row \(k\), the algorithm populates the lower-triangular Romberg matrix \(R(k, j)\) from left to right. Within 4 to 6 step halvings, the diagonal entry \(R(k, k)\) achieves \(10^{-12}\) precision with over 95% fewer function evaluations than standard composite quadrature:

Step Index \(k\) Intervals (\(2^k\)) Step Size \(h_k\) Column \(j=0\) (Trapezoid) Column \(j=1\) (Simpson) Column \(j=2\) (Boole) Column \(j=3\) (Extrapolated) \(k = 0\) 1 \(b - a\) \(R(0, 0)\) [Trapezoid] — — — \(k = 1\) 2 \((b - a)/2\) \(R(1, 0)\) \(\longrightarrow R(1, 1)\) [Simpson] — — \(k = 2\) 4 \((b - a)/4\) \(R(2, 0)\) \(\longrightarrow R(2, 1)\) \(\longrightarrow R(2, 2)\) [Boole] — \(k = 3\) 8 \((b - a)/8\) \(R(3, 0)\) \(\longrightarrow R(3, 1)\) \(\longrightarrow R(3, 2)\) \(\longrightarrow R(3, 3)\)

docs.title: 8.3.2 Avoidance of Runge's Phenomenon
docs.text:
When engineers attempt high-accuracy quadrature by fitting a high-degree polynomial across equally spaced points (as in high-order Newton-Cotes formulas like Weddle's Rule or 10-point formulas), they encounter Runge's Phenomenon: wild polynomial oscillations near the boundaries of the interval that cause numerical error to explode exponentially.

Romberg Quadrature completely eliminates Runge's phenomenon: 1. Low-Order Local Panels: It evaluates only stable, piecewise linear trapezoids on local sub-intervals \(h_k\). 2. Global Richardson Convergence: High-order accuracy is achieved not by increasing polynomial degree across the whole interval, but by extrapolating step sizes \(h \to 0\) in the frequency domain. 3. Monotonic Error Decay: Each diagonal entry \(R(k, k)\) provides a strictly contracting upper error bound without spurious boundary ringing.

docs.title: 8.4 Grounded Case 1: Rocket Motor Burnout Velocity Integration
docs.text:
During the boost phase of a solid-propellant model rocket, combustion chamber pressure and progressive propellant grain geometry produce a non-linear acceleration curve over burn duration \(t \in [0, 6]\text{ seconds}\):

\[a(t) = 4 t^2 - 0.5 t^3 \quad (\text{m/s}^2)\]

Determine the rocket's burnout velocity \(v_{\text{burn}}\) at \(t = 6\text{ seconds}\) by integrating acceleration from \(t = 0\) to \(t = 6\):

\[v_{\text{burn}} = \int_0^6 \left(4 t^2 - 0.5 t^3\right) \, dt\]

docs.title: 8.6 Numerical Differentiation: Central Differences & Adaptive Steps
docs.text:
In addition to integration, the SC-32 provides central-difference numerical differentiation via [d/dx]:

\[f'(x) \approx \frac{f(x + h) - f(x - h)}{2 h}$$ $$f''(x) \approx \frac{f(x + h) - 2 f(x) + f(x - h)}{h^2}\]

Central Difference Numerical Differentiation Mechanics

  1. First Derivative (Central Difference, $\mathcal{O}(h^2)$): $$f'(x) \approx \frac{f(x + h) - f(x - h)}{2h}$$
  2. Optimal Step-Size Selection: $$h = \sqrt{\varepsilon_{\text{mach}}} \cdot \max(1, |x|) \approx 1.49 \times 10^{-8} \cdot \max(1, |x|)$$ Balances truncation error $\mathcal{O}(h^2)$ against floating-point cancellation.
  3. Higher-Order Richardson Derivative ($\mathcal{O}(h^4)$): $$f'(x) \approx \frac{4 D(h/2) - D(h)}{3}$$

docs.title: 8.7 Singularity Handling & Non-Integrable Boundary Detection
docs.text:
When an integrand possesses an essential singularity, pole, or vertical asymptote within the integration interval \([a, b]\), classical numerical quadrature can diverge to infinity.

Consider integrating \(f(x) = 1/x\) from \(a = 0\) to \(b = 1\): $\(\int_0^1 \frac{1}{x} \, dx = [\ln x]_0^1 = 0 - (-\infty) = +\infty\)$

docs.title: 8.7.1 Firmware Singularity Trap
docs.text: When the Romberg engine evaluates the integrand at \(x = 0\), the SC-32 hardware detects division by zero: 1. Halts the trapezoidal accumulation loop immediately. 2. Displays Error 02: DIVIDE BY 0 on the status line. 3. Sets Register \(X = 0.0\) and leaves stack registers intact for recovery.

docs.title: 8.8.1 Richardson Extrapolation & Algorithmic Efficiency
docs.text: In introductory calculus, students learn Riemann sums with left, right, and trapezoidal endpoints. Achieving even four digits of precision with uniform trapezoids requires millions of sub-intervals. Romberg quadrature demonstrates how mathematical insight surpasses brute-force computation: by combining two coarse approximations evaluated at step sizes \(h\) and \(h/2\), Richardson extrapolation cancels the leading \(O(h^2)\) truncation error term algebraically. On the SC-32, students observe that extracting rocket motor burnout velocities (\(126.0\text{ m/s}\)) converges within a fraction of a second to an error bound of \(10^{-11}\).

docs.title: 8.8.2 Numerical Quadrature in Real-World STEM Modeling
docs.text: While textbook calculus emphasizes symbolic integration of idealized elementary functions, practical engineering problems routinely involve empirical data, non-linear rate equations, or non-integrable forms. When calculating total impulse or burnout velocity for a solid-fuel motor, published thrust profiles are higher-order polynomials or piecewise spline fits. Similarly, evaluating cumulative normal probabilities requires integrating the Gaussian bell curve over arbitrary bounds. Entering the integrand into the SC-32 and executing Romberg quadrature grounds abstract calculus in direct numerical reality.

docs.title: 8.8.3 Dual-Register Return & Heritage of the HP-34C
docs.text: In 1979, the Hewlett-Packard HP-34C became the world's first handheld calculator with numerical integration, engineered under the guidance of Turing Award laureate Prof. William Kahan (Kahan, 1979). StackCalc SC-32 advances this lineage with 64-bit IEEE-754 arithmetic and a dynamic Romberg tableau driving truncation error below \(10^{-12}\). Crucially, the SC-32 delivers both the definite integral in Register \(X\) and the certified uncertainty bound \(\pm\epsilon\) in Register \(Y\). Inspecting Register \(Y\) after execution provides immediate confirmation of numerical convergence without requiring secondary verification runs.

docs.title: 8.9 Diagnostic Checkpoints & Singularity Handling
docs.text:
[!CHECKPOINT] Diagnostic Checkpoint 8.1: Limit Ordering Convention Remember the fundamental identity \(\int_b^a f(x) dx = -\int_a^b f(x) dx\). * Lower limit \(a\) must be in Register \(Y\). * Upper limit \(b\) must be in Register \(X\). * If you enter the upper limit first, the result will have the opposite sign!

[!CHECKPOINT] Diagnostic Checkpoint 8.2: Angular Mode Discipline in Trig Integrals All calculus operations involving trigonometric functions (SIN, COS, TAN) mathematically require Radians mode ([RAD]). Because \(d/dx[\sin x] = \cos x\) is only valid when \(x\) is measured in radians (in degrees, a scaling factor of \(\pi/180\) appears), running numerical integration on trig equations in [DEG] produces erroneous results scaled by \((180/\pi)\).

[!CHECKPOINT] Diagnostic Checkpoint 8.3: Inspection of Error Estimate (\(\pm\epsilon\)) After every integration, press [x⇄y] to inspect Register \(Y\). If Register \(Y\) shows a value like \(1.4 \times 10^{-11}\), the integral converged to full precision. If Register \(Y\) shows a large value (e.g. \(0.05\)), the integrand may be highly oscillatory or near a singularity, requiring interval subdivision.

docs.title: 8.10 Engineering Design Briefing: Saturn V Rocket Motor Thrust Integration (Problems 8.1 through 8.40)
docs.text:
Inside-Out Stack Architecture: Algebraic Trap vs. RPN Shortcut — Definite Numerical Integration & Richardson Extrapolation

The Algebraic Parenthesis Trap: Numerical integration of non-linear rate equations (e.g., rocket motor variable thrust $F(t) = k_1 t + k_2 t^3$ or aerodynamic drag) on algebraic calculators requires entering lengthy formula strings into an opaque integration prompt:

fnInt( 2500 * X + 40000 * X ^ 3, X, 0, 0.15 )

If an engineer omits a multiplication symbol or groups an exponent ambiguously, the evaluation either runs indefinitely, drains the battery, or returns an undocumented convergence error without indicating which interval failed *([Brent, 1973](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-brent1973))*.

The RPN Stack Shortcut: The SC-32 executes Adaptive Romberg Quadrature ([↱] [∫]) by combining deterministic postfix equation execution with automated Richardson extrapolation *([Romberg, 1955](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-romberg1955))*. The user defines the integrand directly in RPN, sets the limits $a$ and $b$ onto the stack, and presses [↱] [∫]. The dual-core engine evaluates step sizes dynamically, eliminates low-order truncation error via $O(h^4) \to O(h^6) \to O(h^8)$ tableau refinement, and returns the certified integral into Register $X$ while depositing the estimated absolute error directly into Register $Y$ for instant stack inspection.

docs.title: 8.10.9 Problem 8.9: Center of Mass of Non-Uniform Density Rod
docs.text:

docs.title: 8.10.11 Problem 8.11: RMS Value of Clipped Sinusoidal Voltage Waveform
docs.text:
Power Electronics Context: A \(60\text{ Hz}\) AC line voltage \(v(t) = V_p \sin(\theta)\) with peak \(V_p = 170.0\text{ V}\) is clipped by a metal-oxide varistor (MOV) clamp at \(V_c = 0.80 V_p = 136.0\text{ V}\). The clipping threshold angle occurs at \(\sin \theta_c = 0.80 \implies \theta_c = \arcsin(0.80) \approx 0.927295\text{ rad}\). By quarter-wave symmetry, the mean square value over \([0, \pi/2]\) is: $\(\langle v^2 \rangle = \frac{2}{\pi} \left[ \int_0^{\theta_c} (170 \sin \theta)^2 d\theta + \int_{\theta_c}^{\pi/2} 136^2 d\theta \right]\)$ $\(\int_0^{0.927295} 28,900 \sin^2 \theta \, d\theta = 28,900 \left[ \frac{\theta}{2} - \frac{\sin 2\theta}{4} \right]_0^{0.927295} = 28,900 [0.463648 - 0.240000] = 6,463.42\text{ V}^2\cdot\text{rad}\)$ $\(\int_{0.927295}^{\pi/2} 136^2 \, d\theta = 18,496 \left(\frac{\pi}{2} - 0.927295\right) = 18,496(0.643501) = 11,902.19\text{ V}^2\cdot\text{rad}\)$ $\(\langle v^2 \rangle = \frac{2}{\pi}(6,463.42 + 11,902.19) = \frac{2}{\pi}(18,365.61) = 11,691.88\text{ V}^2\)$ $\(V_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{11,691.88} = \mathbf{108.1290\text{ Volts}}\)$

docs.title: 8.10.12 Problem 8.12: Polytropic Gas Expansion Work: \(P V^{1.4} = C\)
docs.text:
Thermodynamics Context: An ideal diatomic gas expands reversibly in an insulated cylinder from \(V_1 = 0.02\text{ m}^3\) to \(V_2 = 0.08\text{ m}^3\). State constant \(C = P_1 V_1^{1.4} = 600,000 \times (0.02)^{1.4} \approx 2,492.357\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{m}^{4.2}\). Heat Transfer Context: High-temperature furnace wall of thickness \(L = 0.20\text{ m}\) and cross-sectional area \(A = 10.0\text{ m}^2\). docs.title: 8.10.22 Problem 8.22: Sound Exposure Level (SEL) from Transient Flyover Noise
docs.text:
Acoustics Context: An aircraft flyover noise pulse at an airfield boundary is modeled by acoustic pressure \(p(t) = p_0 e^{-t^2 / 20}\text{ Pa}\) with peak pressure \(p_0 = 2.00\text{ Pa}\) over \(t \in [-15, +15]\text{ s}\). Reference acoustic pressure \(p_{\text{ref}} = 20\,\mu\text{Pa} = 2.0 \times 10^{-5}\text{ Pa}\), reference time \(t_0 = 1.0\text{ s}\). docs.title: 8.11 Summary & Looking Ahead

docs.title: 9.1 The Celestial Drama: How 24-Year-Old Carl Friedrich Gauss Rediscovered Ceres (1801)
docs.text:
On the clear, cold evening of January 1, 1801, Italian astronomer Giuseppe Piazzi peered through his Ramsden circle telescope at the Palermo Observatory in Sicily and spotted a faint, uncataloged eighth-magnitude star moving against the starry backdrop of Taurus. Tracking the mysterious object across forty-one nights, Piazzi realized he had discovered a new wandering celestial body—a dwarf planet orbiting between Mars and Jupiter, which he christened Ceres Ferdinandea.

Then catastrophe struck.

By mid-February, Ceres drifted behind the blinding solar glare of the Sun. Astronomers across Europe desperately attempted to predict where the object would re-emerge in late autumn. But eighteenth-century celestial mechanics required months of continuous observations to calculate an elliptical orbit. Piazzi had captured only three degrees of orbital arc—barely one percent of its total trajectory across the heavens. Using traditional orbital approximations, Europe's foremost mathematicians computed orbits that pointed telescopes into empty sky. Ceres appeared irrevocably lost in the void.

Enter twenty-four-year-old Carl Friedrich Gauss in Göttingen.

Refusing to treat Piazzi's sparse observations as sterile, isolated geometric points, Gauss attacked the problem from a radically new perspective: observational uncertainty. Every telescope reading contained minute human, optical, and atmospheric errors. Rather than searching for a single hypothetical curve that passed exactly through flawed points, Gauss sought the unique elliptical orbit that minimized the sum of the squared deviations between prediction and observation.

In a whirlwind of superhuman arithmetic over three months in the autumn of 1801, Gauss invented the Method of Least Squares entirely in his head, along with what we now recognize as the Gaussian Normal Distribution of measurement errors (Gauss, 1809). When German astronomer Franz Xaver von Zach pointed his telescope into the constellation Virgo on the night of December 31, 1801—guided exclusively by Gauss's least-squares predictions—Ceres was rediscovered within half a degree of Gauss's coordinates.

Gauss had demonstrated that statistical aggregation does not blur truth—it reveals the signal buried beneath the noise.

Figure 9.1: Physical probability mapping and discrete outcome distributions. The random fluctuations of physical trials converge systematically to smooth statistical distributions.

Figure 9.2: Precision CNC-machined dice spinner mechanism, demonstrating physical symmetry and mechanical tolerance analysis required for unbiased stochastic generation.

Today, an engineer does not need weeks of manual quill-and-ink calculations to perform Gauss's least-squares synthesis. On the StackCalc SC-32, the dual-variable statistical accumulation engine ([Σ+]) automates Gauss's discovery directly on the RPN stack. Every time you enter a coordinate pair \((x, y)\) and tap [Σ+], six dedicated hardware accumulators update instantaneously in continuous CMOS memory, calculating means, sample variances, covariance, and the least-squares regression line with certified 64-bit precision.

docs.title: 9.2 The Philosophy of Data in the Stack
docs.text:
In conventional algebraic calculators, statistical analysis is treated as an external, table-bound spreadsheet mode. The user enters a separate data grid, loses sight of the calculation stack, and must memorize cryptic sub-menu codes to retrieve basic parameters.

On the StackCalc SC-32, statistics is a first-class, dynamic extension of the Reverse Polish Notation operational stack. Data coordinates \((x, y)\) are entered directly into Registers \(X\) and \(Y\), transformed in real time using the full power of transcendental operators (LN, 1/x, x², √x), and committed into hardware accumulators with a single tap of [Σ+].

docs.title: 9.2.1 The SC-32 Statistical Pipeline
docs.text:
The statistical processing pipeline operates seamlessly between the operational stack and hardware accumulators:

  1. Input Coordinates: The dependent value \(y\) rests in Register \(Y\); the independent value \(x\) rests in Register \(X\).
  2. Commit via [Σ+]: Pressing [Σ+] updates all six internal statistical registers simultaneously without clearing the display.
  3. Hardware Storage: Six dedicated 64-bit accumulators maintain the running sums: \(\Sigma x\), \(\Sigma y\), \(\Sigma x^2\), \(\Sigma y^2\), \(\Sigma xy\), and sample count \(n\).
  4. Instant Synthesis: Dynamic softkey menus provide instantaneous access to means (\(\bar{x}, \bar{y}, \bar{x}_w\)), standard deviations (\(s_x, s_y, \sigma_x, \sigma_y\)), and linear regression parameters (slope \(m\), intercept \(b\), correlation \(r\), and predictive estimates \(\hat{y}, \hat{x}\)).

docs.title: 9.3.1 Data Entry Protocol: [Σ+]
docs.text:
Data pairs \((x_k, y_k)\) are entered according to the classic RPN convention: 1. Key in \(y_k\) and press [ENTER] to push into Register \(Y\). 2. Key in \(x_k\) into Register \(X\). 3. Press [Σ+] (Row 1, Column 6).

Upon pressing [Σ+]: $\(\Sigma x \leftarrow \Sigma x + x_k\)$ $\(\Sigma y \leftarrow \Sigma y + y_k\)$ $\(\Sigma x^2 \leftarrow \Sigma x^2 + x_k^2\)$ $\(\Sigma y^2 \leftarrow \Sigma y^2 + y_k^2\)$ $\(\Sigma xy \leftarrow \Sigma xy + (x_k \times y_k)\)$ $\(n \leftarrow n + 1\)$

Register \(X\) displays the current integer sample count \(n\). Stack lift is disabled so that the next data pair can be typed immediately without clearing the display.

docs.title: 9.3.2 Correcting Data Entry Errors: [↰] [Σ-]
docs.text: If you mistype a data pair, re-enter the exact incorrect pair (\(y \text{ in } Y, x \text{ in } X\)) and press Left Shift [↰] followed by [↰] [Σ-]. The accumulators subtract the erroneous values and decrement \(n\), restoring statistical integrity without restarting the dataset: $\(\Sigma x \leftarrow \Sigma x - x_k, \quad \Sigma y \leftarrow \Sigma y - y_k, \quad n \leftarrow n - 1\)$

docs.title: Sample Means (\(\bar{x}, \bar{y}\))
docs.text: \[\bar{x} = \frac{\Sigma x}{n}, \quad \bar{y} = \frac{\Sigma y}{n}\]

docs.title: Weighted Mean (\(\bar{x}_w\))
docs.text: When \(y_k\) represents the weighting factor (e.g., credit hours, mass, probability) and \(x_k\) is the measurement: $\(\bar{x}_w = \frac{\Sigma xy}{\Sigma y}\)$

docs.title: Sample Standard Deviations (\(s_x, s_y\))
docs.text: Unbiased estimator using Bessel's correction with \(n - 1\) degrees of freedom: $\(s_x = \sqrt{\frac{\Sigma x^2 - \frac{(\Sigma x)^2}{n}}{n - 1}} = \sqrt{\frac{n \Sigma x^2 - (\Sigma x)^2}{n(n - 1)}}\)$ $\(s_y = \sqrt{\frac{\Sigma y^2 - \frac{(\Sigma y)^2}{n}}{n - 1}} = \sqrt{\frac{n \Sigma y^2 - (\Sigma y)^2}{n(n - 1)}}\)$

docs.title: Population Standard Deviations (\(\sigma_x, \sigma_y\))
docs.text: Assumes the data set constitutes the entirety of the target population with \(n\) degrees of freedom: $\(\sigma_x = \sqrt{\frac{\Sigma x^2 - \frac{(\Sigma x)^2}{n}}{n}}, \quad \sigma_y = \sqrt{\frac{\Sigma y^2 - \frac{(\Sigma y)^2}{n}}{n}}\)$

docs.title: Relationship Between Sample and Population Metrics
docs.text: \[s = \sigma \sqrt{\frac{n}{n - 1}}\]

docs.title: 9.5 Bivariate Linear Regression & Pearson Correlation (\(r\))
docs.text:
Bivariate linear regression fits the best-fit line \(y = m x + b\) using ordinary least squares (OLS) minimization of vertical squared residuals:

\[\text{Slope } m = \frac{\Sigma xy - \frac{\Sigma x \Sigma y}{n}}{\Sigma x^2 - \frac{(\Sigma x)^2}{n}} = \frac{n \Sigma xy - \Sigma x \Sigma y}{n \Sigma x^2 - (\Sigma x)^2}\] \[\text{Intercept } b = \bar{y} - m \bar{x} = \frac{\Sigma y - m \Sigma x}{n}\] \[\text{Pearson Correlation } r = \frac{n \Sigma xy - \Sigma x \Sigma y}{\sqrt{\left[ n \Sigma x^2 - (\Sigma x)^2 \right] \left[ n \Sigma y^2 - (\Sigma y)^2 \right]}}\]

The coefficient of determination \(r^2\) represents the proportion of variance in \(y\) predictable from \(x\).

docs.title: 9.5.1 Prediction Operators (\(\hat{y}\) and \(\hat{x}\))
docs.text:
• Predicting \(y\) from a given \(x\) (\(\hat{y}\)): Key in known \(x\) and press [↱] [L.R.] [ŷ]: $\(\hat{y} = m x + b\)$ In the SC-32 engine, [ŷ] returns the predicted \(\hat{y}\) in Register \(X\) and places the correlation coefficient \(r\) in Register \(Y\)! This allows instant assessment of prediction quality without additional keystrokes.
  • Predicting \(x\) from a given \(y\) (\(\hat{x}\)): Key in known \(y\) and press [↱] [L.R.] [x̂]: $\(\hat{x} = \frac{y - b}{m}\)$

docs.title: 9.6 The Gaussian Normal Distribution & Probability Density Function (PDF)
docs.text:
The Galton Board Quincunx: Why Chaos Gives Birth to the Bell Curve

In 1873, Victorian polymath Francis Galton built a vertical wooden board packed with rows of alternating brass pins—the Quincunx.

He dropped thousands of small steel ball bearings from a single funnel at the top. At each pin, an individual ball has a purely random 50/50 choice: bounce left or bounce right. Down through 12 rows of pins, every single trajectory is wildly unpredictable chaos.

Yet, when the 10,000 balls settle into the vertical glass slots at the bottom, something magical happens: they never form a flat line. They never form a jagged heap. Invariably, with breathtaking geometric precision, they sculpt the smooth, silky bell curve of Carl Friedrich Gauss!

Why? Because to land at the extreme left, a ball must bounce left 12 times in a row (probability 1 in 4,096). But to land in the center, there are 924 different intertwined paths of lefts and rights!

This is the Central Limit Theorem: when millions of tiny, independent, random disturbances push against a physical measurement (air molecules, thermal noise, lathe blade vibrations), their sum always converges to the Gaussian Normal PDF.

The continuous Gaussian Normal probability density function models stochastic error, dimensional tolerances, sensor noise, and natural phenomena:

\[f(x; \mu, \sigma) = \frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\left( -\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2} \right)\]

where: * \(\mu\) is the distribution mean (center of symmetry). * \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation (scale parameter). * \(Z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\) is the dimensionless standard score (Z-score).

The normalized standard normal distribution with \(\mu = 0\) and \(\sigma = 1\) is: $\(\phi(z) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-z^2 / 2}\)$

docs.text:

Step 1: Compute (x - μ)²: x [ENTER] μ [-] [x²] Step 2: Compute 2σ²: σ [x²] 2 [×] Step 3: Exponent argument: [÷] [+/-] [eˣ] Step 4: Denominator σ√(2π): σ [ENTER] 2 [ENTER] [π] [×] [√x] [×] Step 5: Final PDF quotient: [÷]

docs.text:
The cumulative probability \(\Phi(z) = P(Z \le z)\) represents the area under the Gaussian curve: $\(\Phi(z) = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_0^z e^{-t^2 / 2} \, dt\)$

The SC-32's adaptive Romberg numerical quadrature solver [↱] [∫] evaluates this integral directly to 10 decimal places, reproducing the classic Empirical Rule (\(68.27\% - 95.45\% - 99.73\%\)).

docs.title: 9.8 Engineering Design Briefing: The Astronomical Observatory & Semiconductor Quality Fab (Problems 9.1 through 9.43)

Switching between spreadsheet data entry, calculation screens, and regression output disrupts cognitive flow, and verifying outliers requires navigating multi-tiered setup menus *([Gauss, 1809](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-gauss1809))*.

The RPN Stack Shortcut: The SC-32 utilizes six dedicated hardware accumulators ($\Sigma x, \Sigma y, \Sigma x^2, \Sigma y^2, \Sigma xy, n$) updated instantaneously via the physical coordinate key [Σ+] *([HP, 1982](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-hp15c1982); [HP, 1991](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-hp32sii1991))*. The engineer keys coordinate pairs directly into Registers $Y$ and $X$ and taps [Σ+]. docs.title: 9.8.5 Problem 9.5: Cumulative Normal Probability via Romberg Quadrature (\(Z = 1.0\))

docs.title: 9.8.36 Problem 9.36: Residual Analysis and Standard Error of the Estimate (\(s_e\))
docs.text:
In linear regression \(y = m x + b\), the standard error of the estimate measures the dispersion of observed values around the regression line: $\(s_e = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{n - 2}} = \sqrt{\frac{\Sigma y^2 - b \Sigma y - m \Sigma xy}{n - 2}}\)$

For the pressure sensor dataset from Problem 9.1: * \(n = 4\), degrees of freedom \(n - 2 = 2\) * \(\Sigma y = 12.45\), \(\Sigma y^2 = 46.5075\), \(\Sigma xy = 373.5\) * \(m = 0.1245\), \(b = 0.0000\)

Compute residual sum of squares: $\(\text{SS}_{\text{res}} = 46.5075 - 0.0000(12.45) - 0.1245(373.5) = 46.5075 - 46.50075 = 0.00675\text{ V}^2\)$ $\(s_e = \sqrt{\frac{0.00675}{2}} = \sqrt{0.003375} \approx 0.05809\text{ V}\)$

docs.title: Keystrokes:
docs.text:
46.5075 [ENTER] .1245 [ENTER] 373.5 [×] [-] 2 [÷] [√x] \(\rightarrow\) 0.0580947502

Named RPN Stack Idiom: The Inside-Out Radical & Standard Error Pipeline — Stream bivariate sums through residual variance formula \(\frac{\Sigma y^2 - b\Sigma y - m\Sigma xy}{n-2}\) and extract square root in place (HP, 1982).

docs.title: 9.8.37 Problem 9.37: Two-Sample Pooled Variance and Student's \(t\)-Test
docs.text:
Compare the mean tensile strengths of two alloy formulations: * Alloy A: \(n_1 = 8\), mean \(\bar{x}_1 = 450.0\text{ MPa}\), standard deviation \(s_1 = 12.5\text{ MPa}\) * Alloy B: \(n_2 = 10\), mean \(\bar{x}_2 = 468.0\text{ MPa}\), standard deviation \(s_2 = 14.0\text{ MPa}\)

Pooled variance: $\(s_p^2 = \frac{(n_1 - 1)s_1^2 + (n_2 - 1)s_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2}\)$ Student's \(t\)-statistic for difference in means: $\(t = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{s_p \sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}}\)$

docs.title: Step 2: Compute \(t\)-Statistic:
docs.text:
• Standard error: \(s_p \times \sqrt{1/8 + 1/10} = 13.36448 \times \sqrt{0.125 + 0.10} = 13.36448 \times \sqrt{0.225} = 13.36448 \times 0.4743416 = 6.33933\text{ MPa}\)
  • \(t = (450.0 - 468.0) / 6.33933 = -18.0 / 6.33933 = \mathbf{-2.8394}\)

At \(\alpha = 0.05\) with \(df = 16\), critical \(t_{0.025} = 2.120\). Since \(|-2.8394| > 2.120\), the difference in alloy strengths is statistically significant!

docs.title: 9.8.38 Problem 9.38: Confidence Band for Mean Response at Specific \(x_0\)
docs.text:
In linear regression, the 95% confidence interval for the true mean response \(E(y \mid x_0)\) is: $\(\hat{y}_0 \pm t_{\alpha/2, n-2} \cdot s_e \sqrt{\frac{1}{n} + \frac{(x_0 - \bar{x})^2}{\Sigma x^2 - \frac{(\Sigma x)^2}{n}}}\)$

For the sensor in Problem 9.1 at \(x_0 = 25\text{ kPa}\): * \(n = 4, \bar{x} = 25.0, s_e = 0.058095\text{ V}\) * Notice that at \(x_0 = \bar{x} = 25.0\), the distance term \((x_0 - \bar{x})^2 = 0\)! * Margin of error reduces to: \(t_{0.025, 2} \cdot s_e \sqrt{1/4} = 4.303 \times 0.058095 \times 0.5 = \mathbf{0.1250\text{ V}}\). * Mean prediction: \(\hat{y} = 3.1125\text{ V}\). * 95% Confidence Interval: \([3.1125 - 0.1250, 3.1125 + 0.1250] = \mathbf{[2.9875\text{ V}, 3.2375\text{ V}]}\).

Step-by-Step RPN Reasoning & Stack Logic: 1. Accumulate Bivariate Pairs via [Σ+]: After [CLΣ], enter each \((y_i, x_i)\) pair as \(y_i\) [ENTER] \(x_i\) [Σ+] to update all six statistical sums (\(\Sigma x, \Sigma y, \Sigma x^2, \Sigma y^2, \Sigma xy, n\)). 2. Evaluate Regression / Confidence Metric: Query the linear regression estimator ([↱] [L.R.]) or combine the sample standard deviation \(s_x, s_y\) on \((Y, X)\) with the \(t\)-distribution multiplier to obtain the final interval in Register \(X\).

docs.title: 9.8.40 Problem 9.40: Spearman Rank Correlation via Monotonic Ranking
docs.text: When two variables have a non-linear but monotonic relationship, evaluate Spearman rank correlation \(r_s\): $\(r_s = 1 - \frac{6 \Sigma d_i^2}{n(n^2 - 1)}\)$ Given rank differences \(d_i\) across 5 items: \(d = [1, -1, 2, -1, -1]\): * Squared differences: \(1^2 + (-1)^2 + 2^2 + (-1)^2 + (-1)^2 = 1 + 1 + 4 + 1 + 1 = 8.0\) * \(n = 5 \implies n(n^2 - 1) = 5(24) = 120\) * \(6 \times 8 / 120 = 48 / 120 = 0.40\) * \(r_s = 1 - 0.40 = \mathbf{0.6000}\).

Named RPN Stack Idiom: The LASTX Dual-Branch Trick & Monotonic Rank Correlation — Scale squared rank differences by 6, divide by \(n(n^2 - 1)\), and subtract from unity via [x⇄y] without scratch registers (Ellenberg, 2014; HP, 1982).

docs.title: 9.8.45 Problem 9.45: Log-Normal Aerosol Droplet Size Distribution
docs.text: In medical nebulizer sprays, aerosol droplet diameters \(D\) follow a log-normal distribution with geometric mean \(\mu_{\ln} = \ln(4.5\text{ }\mu\text{m}) = 1.504077\) and geometric standard deviation \(\sigma_{\ln} = 0.35\). Calculate the probability density for a droplet of diameter \(D = 5.0\text{ }\mu\text{m}\): $\(f(D) = \frac{1}{D \sigma_{\ln} \sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\left( -\frac{(\ln D - \mu_{\ln})^2}{2\sigma_{\ln}^2} \right)\)$

docs.title: 9.9 Diagnostic Checkpoints & Singularity Handling
docs.text:
[!CHECKPOINT] Diagnostic Checkpoint 9.1: Zero Variance Singularity (STAT ERROR) If all entered \(x\)-values are identical (e.g., \((10, 2), (10, 5), (10, 9)\)), attempting to solve for linear regression slope [m] triggers STAT ERROR. Cause: The denominator \(n \Sigma x^2 - (\Sigma x)^2 = 0\), representing an infinite vertical slope. Remedy: Press [C] to dismiss the error message. Ensure \(x\)-coordinates span a non-zero domain.

[!CHECKPOINT] Diagnostic Checkpoint 9.2: Single-Point Standard Deviation (STAT ERROR) Attempting to compute sample standard deviations [sx] or [sy] with only \(n = 1\) point triggers STAT ERROR. Cause: Division by degrees of freedom \(n - 1 = 0\). Remedy: Accumulate at least two distinct data points before querying sample metrics.

[!CHECKPOINT] Diagnostic Checkpoint 9.3: Coordinate Orientation Diagnostic Verification If the linear regression slope on a sensor calibration displays as an inverse value (e.g. \(8.0321\) instead of \(m = 0.1245\)), the \((x, y)\) coordinate entry order was inverted. In the standard RPN convention, key the dependent variable \(y\) first, press [ENTER], key the independent variable \(x\), and tap [Σ+].

docs.title: 9.10.1 Least-Squares Geometry & Data Hygiene via [↰] [Σ-]
docs.text: In secondary and university statistics, linear regression is frequently treated as a routine calculation: entering data, pressing compute, and recording \(m\), \(b\), and \(r\). At its core, least-squares regression balances variance across bivariate distributions by minimizing the sum of squared vertical residuals \(\sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\). Demonstrating this with collinear data (\(r = 1.0000\)) and observing the effect of a single outlier point illustrates outlier sensitivity directly. Furthermore, data hygiene is maintained through [↰] [Σ-]: re-entering an errant point and pressing [↰] [Σ-] performs exact inverse subtraction across all six accumulators, restoring pristine statistics without navigating multi-tiered spreadsheet menus.

docs.title: 9.10.2 Sensor Calibration & Coordinate Orientation Discipline
docs.text: Practical empirical science relies on sensor calibration. By logging transducer voltage against known physical reference states (such as temperature baths or hydrostatic pressures) and keying points with \(y\) [ENTER] \(x\) [Σ+], the linear calibration slope \(m\) and intercept \(b\) are determined via [↱] [L.R.]. The estimation keys [ŷ] and [x̂] then translate raw voltages directly into physical quantities. The standard RPN coordinate convention positions the dependent variable \(y\) in Register \(Y\) and the independent variable \(x\) in Register \(X\). If a user inadvertently keys \(x\) first, the resulting slope is inverted (\(1/m\)), which is diagnosed immediately and corrected with [x⇄y].

docs.title: 9.10.3 Dedicated Hardware Accumulators & LASTX Preservation
docs.text: On vintage RPN calculators (such as the HP-32SII and HP-15C), statistical summation overwrote user storage registers \(R_0\) through \(R_5\), erasing user-stored matrix coefficients or intermediate constants. The SC-32 resolves this limitation by isolating its six 64-bit statistical accumulators (\(\Sigma x, \Sigma y, \Sigma x^2, \Sigma y^2, \Sigma xy, n\)) from general user storage registers (\(R_{00} \dots R_{29}\)). Furthermore, tapping [Σ+] or [↰] [Σ-] automatically saves the entered \(x\)-coordinate to [↰] [LASTX], allowing instant recall and verification of data points without disturbing the operational stack.

docs.title: 9.11 Summary & Looking Ahead
docs.text:
Chapter 9 established rigorous data reduction, regression analysis, and empirical modeling on the SC-32. You harnessed the six dedicated hardware statistical accumulators (\(\Sigma x, \Sigma y, \Sigma x^2, \Sigma y^2, \Sigma xy, n\)) to compute bivariate means, sample standard deviations, covariance, and least-squares regression lines without disturbing user storage registers. Through [↰] [Σ-], you maintained pristine data hygiene, while [ŷ] and [x̂] converted transducer voltages into physical measurements. You then extended statistical theory into probability distributions, evaluating Gaussian normal PDFs, Poisson arrival rates, and Weibull reliability life cycles in place.

Continuous distributions and decimal floating-point arithmetic form only half of computational science. Beneath modern instrumentation lies the discrete digital architecture of binary bits, logic words, and memory addresses. In Chapter 10: Computer Science, Bases & 36-Bit Integers, you will explore the SC-32's authentic 36-bit two's complement integer architecture. You will navigate hexadecimal, decimal, octal, and binary bases while preserving stack integrity, execute modular integer division via [↱] [÷R] returning quotient in \(Y\) and remainder in \(X\), harness word length clipping and mathematical bit-packing without dedicated Boolean keys, calculate IPv4 CIDR subnet masks and packed RGB color channels, and master discrete combinatorics.

docs.title: 10.1 Claude Shannon's 1937 Switchboard Epiphany & Why Classic Mainframes Used 36-Bit Words
docs.text:
In the summer of 1936, a twenty-one-year-old graduate student named Claude Elwood Shannon was working in the basement of MIT's electrical engineering building. His task was operating Vannevar Bush's Differential Analyzer—a colossal mechanical analog computer composed of spinning steel discs, brass gears, and motorized lead screws that solved differential equations through physical rotation.

To reset the machine for each differential run, Shannon had to rewire complex arrays of electromechanical telephone relays.

As Shannon manipulated the clicking relays, he recalled an obscure 1854 treatise by British mathematician George Boole, An Investigation of the Laws of Thought, which he had studied in an undergraduate philosophy course at the University of Michigan. Boole had formulated an abstract algebraic system where variables took only two truth values: \(1\) (True) or \(0\) (False).

In a sudden flash of insight, Shannon realized: a telephone relay is not merely an electrical switch—it is a physical instantiation of binary arithmetic and two-state logic!

In his 1937 MIT master's thesis—published in 1938 (Shannon, 1938) and subsequently hailed by computer scientist Howard Gardner as "possibly the most important, and also the most famous, master's thesis of the century"—Shannon proved that any mathematical or logical expression can be evaluated by an arrangement of physical binary switches. Every microprocessor, FPGA, and memory cell built in the past nine decades traces its intellectual lineage directly to Shannon's switchboard epiphany.

docs.title: 10.1.1 The Architectural Drama: The 36-Bit Word vs. The 8-Bit Byte
docs.text:
When scientific mainframe pioneers at IBM, MIT, and Digital Equipment Corporation engineered the legendary machines of the 1950s and 1960s—the IBM 704, IBM 7094, and DEC PDP-10—they converged on a word length that seems curious to modern programmers accustomed to 32-bit and 64-bit boundaries: the 36-bit word.

Why 36 bits?

In that era, computers processed floating-point scientific calculations and alphabetic text concurrently. Thirty-six bits was mathematical perfection: 1. Ten Decimal Digits of Scientific Precision: \(2^{36} \approx 6.87 \times 10^{10}\), granting ten certified decimal digits of integer and mantissa precision. 2. Six 6-Bit Characters: Standard alphanumeric teleprinters encoded text in 6-bit BCD (Fieldata/ASCII-6). A 36-bit word packed exactly six characters with zero wasted silicon. 3. Dual 18-Bit Pointers: The PDP-10 split its 36-bit words into two symmetric 18-bit halves, allowing instructions to hold both a left register address and a right memory pointer simultaneously.

When IBM introduced the System/360 in 1964, Gene Amdahl and Fred Brooks shifted commercial computing to 8-bit bytes and 32-bit words to streamline commercial billing and byte-stream peripherals. Yet in aerospace telemetry, radar processing, and scientific research, the 36-bit word remained legendary for its graceful handling of precision and unsigned headroom.

The StackCalc SC-32 honors this golden architectural heritage. Rather than confining programmers to signed 32-bit limits that choke on unsigned 0xFFFFFFFF network masks, the SC-32 provides an authentic 36-bit two's complement integer architecture.

Figure 10.1: Prime factorization and set intersection modeling. Discrete number-theoretic operations map directly to modular division and radix partitioning.

Figure 10.2: Concrete physical unit packaging representing modular grouping and discrete word-length partitioning across physical registers.

CHAPTER BASELINE MODE: [DEC] (Decimal integer base default; 36-Bit Two's Complement Integer Architecture; Full precision [ALL]). Switching dynamically between [HEX], [DEC], [OCT], and [BIN] preserves all four stack registers ($X, Y, Z, T$) with zero data corruption.

docs.title: 10.2 The 36-Bit Two's Complement Integer Architecture
docs.text:
In digital electronics, systems programming, firmware development, and network engineering, calculations operate directly upon discrete binary registers rather than continuous floating-point approximations.

The StackCalc SC-32 incorporates an authentic hardware-modeled 36-Bit Two's Complement Integer Architecture:

Bit Position Field Designation Meaning in 36-Bit Two's Complement Bit 35 MSB / Sign Bit 0 = Positive integer; 1 = Negative integer (Two's complement) Bits 34–32 Upper Headroom Provides 4 full bits of positive headroom above standard 32-bit unsigned words Bits 31–0 Standard 32-Bit Word Holds full 32-bit unsigned addresses, IPv4 netmasks, and GPIO bitfields
  • Word Size (\(W\)): Exactly 36 bits (\(0\) to \(35\)).
  • Maximum Value (\(+2^{35} - 1\)): \(+34,359,738,367\) (0x7FFFFFFFF).
  • Minimum Value (\(-2^{35}\)): \(-34,359,738,368\) (0x800000000).
  • \(-1\) Representation: 0xFFFFFFFFF (all 36 bits set to 1).
  • Overflow Handling: Values exceeding 36 bits trigger the non-destructive status annunciator TOO BIG.

docs.title: 10.2.1 Why 36 Bits?
docs.text: The 36-bit word length honors legendary scientific mainframe computing heritage (such as the DEC PDP-10, IBM 7090, and MIT Project MAC architectures) while providing crucial engineering utility in modern embedded digital design: 1. Full 32-Bit Unsigned Headroom: Traditional 32-bit signed calculators overflow when representing unsigned 32-bit addresses and masks (such as IPv4 broadcast 0xFFFFFFFF or 4 GiB memory bounds). A 36-bit architecture represents any 32-bit unsigned integer up to 0xFFFFFFFF (\(4,294,967,295\)) with 4 full bits of positive headroom before the sign bit is reached. 2. Parity & Status Bit Packing: It provides 4 dedicated upper bits for hardware error detection, cyclic redundancy codes, and register bank tags without stealing bits from 32-bit payloads. 3. Exact Integer Arithmetic: Integers in HEX, OCT, and BIN modes are maintained as exact 36-bit two's complement words internally, guaranteeing that integer division, remainder extraction, and radix conversions never suffer floating-point roundoff errors.

docs.text: Switching between base modes never destroys, alters, or shifts the values in the operational stack (\(X, Y, Z, T\)). * If Register \(X\) holds 255 in Decimal mode, pressing [↰] [BASE] [HEX] instantly renders FFh. * Pressing [↰] [BASE] [OCT] immediately renders 377o. * Pressing [↰] [BASE] [BIN] immediately renders 11111111b. * The underlying 36-bit integer representation in CPU registers remains identical.

docs.title: 10.3.2 Direct Hexadecimal Digit Input (A through F)
docs.text:
When Hexadecimal mode ([HEX]) is active, the top row of primary scientific keys (Row 1, Columns 0 through 5) maps directly to the printed alpha legends \(A\) through \(F\): * [√x] \(\to \mathbf{A}\) (\(10_{10}\)) * [eˣ] \(\to \mathbf{B}\) (\(11_{10}\)) * [LN] \(\to \mathbf{C}\) (\(12_{10}\)) * [yˣ] \(\to \mathbf{D}\) (\(13_{10}\)) * [1/x] \(\to \mathbf{E}\) (\(14_{10}\)) * [Σ+] \(\to \mathbf{F}\) (\(15_{10}\))

To type 0xDEADBEEF: Key [yˣ] [1/x] [√x] [yˣ] [eˣ] [1/x] [1/x] [Σ+]!

Rapid Calculation & Equation Entry: Rapid Radix Conversion Without Stack Interruption

In high-speed computer science sprints and collegiate numerical exams, base conversion problems (such as evaluating $3\text{A}7_{16} + 452_8$ in decimal) can consume precious minutes if converted on scratch paper.

On the SC-32, the entire 4-register operational stack preserves all values when cycling base modes. You can convert radices mid-expression without losing running operands:

  1. Switch to Hex: [BASE] [HEX] → Key 3 [√x] 7 [ENTER] ($3\text{A}7_{16} = 935_{10}$).
  2. Switch to Octal: [BASE] [OCT] → Key 452 [+]. Register $X$ instantly sums them in octal: $2261_8$.
  3. Switch to Decimal: [BASE] [DEC] → Register $X$ immediately reads $1,201_{10}$ with zero intermediate scratchpad steps!

Because stack lift and numeric precision are invariant across base toggles, you never have to re-enter running totals or exit the calculation chain.

docs.title: 10.4.1 Why [↱] [÷R] Is a Bit-Field Superpower
docs.text: When you divide a binary word \(Y\) by a power of two \(M = 2^k\) using [↱] [÷R], the SC-32 splits the binary word right at bit boundary \(k\) in a single keystroke: * Register X (Quotient \(\lfloor Y / 2^k \rfloor\)): Holds the upper bits shifted right by \(k\) positions (\(Y \gg k\)). * Register Y (Remainder \(Y \bmod 2^k\)): Holds the lower \(k\) bits masked off (\(Y \ \& \ (2^k - 1)\)).

docs.title: 10.5 Engineering Design Briefing: Bare-Metal Embedded Firmware & High-Performance Network Switching (Problems 10.1 through 10.40)
docs.text:
Inside-Out Stack Architecture: Algebraic Trap vs. RPN Shortcut — 36-Bit Integer Registers & Subnet Boundary Partitioning via [↱] [÷R]

The Algebraic Parenthesis Trap: In network engineering and embedded firmware development, calculating IPv4 CIDR subnet IDs or decomposing packed hardware telemetry words on standard scientific calculators is fraught with difficulty. Algebraic scientific calculators lack native quotient-remainder separation, forcing developers to alternate between floating-point division, manual integer truncation, and re-multiplication to isolate remainder bits *([Shannon, 1938](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-shannon1938))*.

The RPN Stack Shortcut: The SC-32 provides native 36-bit two's complement integer architecture with instantaneous base conversions ([HEX], [DEC], [OCT], [BIN]) across all four stack registers *([IEEE, 2019](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-ieee754_2019))*. Dividing a binary word by a power of two ($2^k$) using simultaneous division with remainder ([↱] [÷R]) automatically isolates the upper network prefix bits in Register $X$ while depositing the lower host field remainder directly into Register $Y$ in a single instruction cycle, completely eliminating manual bitmask scratchwork.

The following 40 reference problems provide complete, publication-grade coverage across network engineering, microcontroller firmware, computer graphics, cryptography, and discrete mathematics.

docs.text:
Calculate LRC across message bytes 0x02, 0x41, 0x42: 2 [ENTER] 41 [+] 42 [+] \(\rightarrow\) 85h.

Step-by-Step RPN Reasoning & Stack Logic: 1. 2 [ENTER] — Deposit the initial message byte (0x02) onto the stack. 2. 41 [+] — Key the second message byte (0x41) and accumulate; the partial sum (0x43) appears on the display. 3. 42 [+] — Key the third message byte (0x42) and accumulate; total unmasked message sum (0x85) occupies Register \(X\). 4. 256 [↱] [÷R] — Execute modulo 256 division; the single-byte remainder (0x85) resides in Register \(Y\). 5. 256 [x⇄y] [-] — Compute the two's complement additive checksum (0x7B) in place.

docs.title: 10.5.26 Problem 10.26: UART Fractional Baud Rate Divisor at 150 MHz
docs.text:
A high-performance dual-core microcontroller runs its peripheral system clock at \(f_{\text{clk}} = 150.0\text{ MHz}\) (\(150,000,000\text{ Hz}\)). The hardware UART baud rate generator features an integer baud rate register (IBRD, 16-bit) and a fractional baud rate register (FBRD, 6-bit with divisor \(64\)) over an \(8\times\) oversampling receiver clock. Determine IBRD and FBRD to configure a target baud rate of \(115,200\text{ baud}\), and calculate the resulting baud rate error percentage.

\[\text{Baud Divider} = \frac{f_{\text{clk}}}{8 \times \text{Baud}} = \frac{150,000,000}{8 \times 115,200} = \frac{150,000,000}{921,600} \approx 162.760416667\]

docs.title: Keystrokes in [ALL] Mode:
docs.text:
1. 150000000 [ENTER] 8 [÷] 115200 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 162.760416667
  2. Integer divider IBRD: [ENTER] [↱] [PARTS] [IP] \(\rightarrow\) 162 (0xA2)
  3. Fractional divider FBRD: [x⇄y] [↱] [PARTS] [FP] 64 [×] [↱] [PARTS] [IP] \(\rightarrow\) 48 (or rounded: 49 0x31)
  4. Actual baud rate: \(150,000,000 / (8 \times (162 + 49/64)) = 150,000,000 / 1302.125 = \mathbf{115,196.3\text{ baud}}\)
  5. Baud Error: \((115196.3 - 115200) / 115200 \times 100\% = \mathbf{-0.0032\%}\) (Near zero error!).

docs.title: 10.5.27 Problem 10.27: SPI Clock Prescaler Selection
docs.text: A SPI peripheral runs from a \(75.0\text{ MHz}\) bus clock. The connected flash memory specifies a maximum operating frequency of \(10.0\text{ MHz}\). The SPI prescaler offers powers of two: \(2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128\). Determine the optimal prescaler divider and actual SPI operating frequency.

docs.text:
75 [ENTER] 10 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) \(7.5\).

Step-by-Step RPN Reasoning & Stack Logic: 1. 75.0 [ENTER] — Arm Register \(Y\) with the master SPI peripheral clock frequency (\(75.0\text{ MHz}\)). 2. 10.0 [÷] — Enter maximum peripheral flash frequency (\(10.0\text{ MHz}\)) and divide; minimum required divider ratio (\(7.50\)) condenses in \(X\). 3. 8 [ENTER] — Select the lowest power-of-two prescaler divider exceeding \(7.5\) (\(P = 8\)). 4. 75.0 [x⇄y] [÷] — Divide master clock by prescaler divider; the actual operational SPI bus clock frequency (\(f_{\text{SPI}} = 9.375\text{ MHz}\)) is verified.

Since the divider must be a power of two \(\ge 7.5\), select 8 (2³). Actual SPI frequency: 75 [ENTER] 8 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 9.375 (\(9,375,000\text{ Hz}\)).

docs.title: 10.5.28 Problem 10.28: I2C Fast-Mode Plus SCL Timing Register Calculations
docs.text: Target I2C clock frequency \(f_{\text{SCL}} = 1.0\text{ MHz}\) (\(1000\text{ ns}\) cycle time) derived from a \(150.0\text{ MHz}\) core clock period (\(T_{\text{clk}} = \frac{1}{150\times 10^6} \approx 6.6667\text{ ns}\)). Total clocks per SCL period: \(150\text{ cycles}\). In Fast-Mode Plus, asymmetric duty cycle allocates \(t_{\text{LOW}} \ge 500\text{ ns}\) and \(t_{\text{HIGH}} \ge 260\text{ ns}\). Allocating \(\frac{1}{3}\) high and \(\frac{2}{3}\) low: * \(t_{\text{HIGH}} = 50\text{ cycles} \times 6.6667\text{ ns} = \mathbf{333.3\text{ ns}}\) (\(> 260\text{ ns}\)) * \(t_{\text{LOW}} = 100\text{ cycles} \times 6.6667\text{ ns} = \mathbf{666.7\text{ ns}}\) (\(> 500\text{ ns}\)).

  2. High phase clocks: 3 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) \(50\) cycles

docs.title: 10.6.1 Two's Complement Foundations & Modulo Odometer Intuition
docs.text: Two's complement is often perceived as an arbitrary binary convention, but it is fundamentally the radix complement of base 2, mathematically isomorphic to ten's complement in decimal arithmetic. In a four-digit decimal register (\(0000 \dots 9999\)), subtracting \(1\) from \(0000\) rolls backward to \(9999\), which represents \(-1\). In a 36-bit binary word, subtracting \(1\) from \(0\) rolls over to all ones (0xFFFFFFFFF), which evaluates mathematically to \(-1\). In RPN computer science pedagogy, students inspect bitfield transformations sequentially: partitioning nibbles via simultaneous quotient and remainder with [↱] [÷R], executing bit shifts via power-of-two multiplication and division, and verifying register alignment without hidden precedence rules.

docs.title: 10.6.2 Bitfield Manipulation via Positional Weights
docs.text: Binary flags and bitmasks represent weighted combinations of powers of two (\(1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 \dots\)). Setting or clearing individual bits corresponds directly to adding or subtracting powers of two: 1. Setting Bit \(k\): Adding \(2^k\) sets bit \(k\) without altering adjacent fields. Switching to [BIN] confirms that bit \(k\) flips from 0 to 1. 2. Clearing Bit \(k\): Subtracting \(2^k\) clears bit \(k\) back to 0 while preserving surrounding state. 3. Partitioning Bitfields: Dividing by \(2^k\) via [↱] [÷R] separates the word: the upper bits shifted right reside in Register \(X\), while the lower \(k\) bits remain in Register \(Y\). This confirms that digital systems manipulate composite state registers through the positional mathematics of powers of two rather than isolated logic switches.

docs.title: 10.6.3 36-Bit Architecture & IPv4 Headroom
docs.text: The SC-32 advances classic base-conversion instruments (such as the HP-32SII) by employing a 36-bit two's complement integer word. On standard 32-bit signed architectures, the IPv4 broadcast address 0xFFFFFFFF (\(4,294,967,295\)) cannot be represented as a positive integer; its leading bit forces an overflow into \(-1\). On the SC-32, Bit 35 serves as the sign bit, providing 4 full bits of positive headroom above the standard 32-bit boundary. Furthermore, switching dynamically between [HEX], [DEC], [OCT], and [BIN] preserves all four operational stack levels (\(X, Y, Z, T\)) with zero truncation or register loss.

docs.title: 10.8 Summary & Looking Ahead
docs.text:
Chapter 10 demystified the low-level binary foundation of digital computation. Operating across an authentic 36-bit two's complement integer architecture, you navigated Hexadecimal, Decimal, Octal, and Binary modes while preserving multi-level stack register values intact. Without dedicated Boolean keys, you harnessed modular integer division via [↱] [÷R]—returning quotient in \(Y\) and remainder in \(X\)—alongside word length clipping, modular reduction, and powers-of-two arithmetic to configure microcontroller registers, construct IPv4 CIDR subnet masks, pack and extract RGB color channels, and analyze telemetry bit disparities. Finally, you unified discrete combinatorics (\(nPr\), \(nCr\), \(n!\)) and pseudorandom seeding into an essential mathematical toolkit for systems programming and digital electronics.

From discrete bits and memory registers, the principles of accumulation and mathematical modeling extend directly into financial decision-making and quantitative economics. In Chapter 11: Financial Mathematics & Time Value of Money (TVM), you will master the SC-32's dedicated five-variable compound interest solver (\(N, I\%YR, PV, PMT, FV\)). You will calculate mortgage amortization schedules, evaluate net present value (NPV) and internal rate of return (IRR), and apply actuarial sign discipline to model complex real-world capital flows.

docs.title: 11.1 The Application: The Time Value of Human Labor & William Kahan's Financial Invariant
docs.text:
Money is not merely abstract numbers printed on green paper or glowing as digits in a bank ledger. In the physical universe, money represents stored human time and labor.

When an engineer signs an employment contract, an entrepreneur secures an equipment lease, or a family signs a 30-year home mortgage, the mathematics of compound interest dictates whether that labor compounds into generational freedom or evaporates into perpetual interest debt.

docs.title: 11.1.1 William Kahan's Crusade: The War on Destructive Percentage Keys
docs.text:
In the late 1970s, UC Berkeley Professor and future Turing Award laureate William M. Kahan inspected the commercial handheld calculators sold to consumers and business executives. What he discovered appalled him.

On almost every algebraic calculator of the era, the percentage key was destructive. Suppose you were billing a corporate client for \(\$150.00\) of engineering consulting, plus an \(8.25\%\) state sales tax:

\[\text{Algebraic keystrokes: } 150 \ [\times] \ 8.25 \ [\%] \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \text{Displays } 12.38\]

The moment you pressed [↱] [%], the calculator obliterated your \(\$150.00\) base amount! To find the invoice total (\(\$162.38\)), you had to either manually re-enter \(\$150.00\), write it down on scratch paper, or rely on a clunky memory key ([M+]). If the client asked to test an alternative \(9.5\%\) tax rate, you had to start completely over from scratch.

Kahan declared war on this numerical incompetence. In 1979, writing in the Hewlett-Packard Journal (Kahan, 1979), he formulated what is now celebrated in numerical computing as the Kahan Percentage Invariant:

The Kahan Percentage Invariant

A percentage operator must be non-destructive and dyadic:

$$X \longleftarrow \frac{Y \times X}{100}, \qquad Y \longleftarrow Y \quad (\text{Preserved frozen on the stack!})$$

On the StackCalc SC-32, your base amount never disappears:

  1. Key in: 150 [ENTER] 8.25 [↱] [%] → Register $X$ displays 12.38 (the tax amount). → Register $Y$ silently holds 150.00 (the base invoice).
  2. Total Invoice? Just tap [+] → $162.38!
  3. Discount Subtracted? Just tap [-] → $137.62!
  4. Alternative Rate? Tap [↰] [LASTX] [x⇄y] or test alternate taxes directly without re-entry!

Figure 11.1: The SC-32 transflective display executing multi-variable financial calculations with continuous stack preservation.

Figure 11.2: The SC-32 precision aluminum chassis and tactile key switches, engineered for fatigue-free boardroom and field accounting.

Beyond simple percentages, all commercial banking, corporate bonds, and mortgages rest on the 5-variable Time Value of Money (TVM) equation:

\[PV + PMT \left[ \frac{1 - (1 + i)^{-N}}{i} \right] + FV (1 + i)^{-N} = 0\]

The SC-32's dedicated TVM register suite frees you from the tyranny of opaque amortization software. You control the five dials of capital. )

Inside-Out Stack Architecture: Algebraic Trap vs. RPN Shortcut — Compound TVM & Amortization Formulas

The Algebraic Parenthesis Trap: Consider evaluating the compound interest factor or monthly mortgage annuity payment manually from the fundamental closed-form equation:

$$PMT = PV \cdot \frac{i(1 + i)^N}{(1 + i)^N - 1}$$

On an algebraic textbook calculator, this formula is a minefield of nested parentheses, cognitive buffering, and operator precedence traps *([Sweller, 1988](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-sweller1988); [Dijkstra, 1961](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-dijkstra1961))*. An analyst must key:

PV * ( ( I / 1200 ) * ( 1 + I / 1200 ) ^ N ) / ( ( 1 + I / 1200 ) ^ N - 1 )

Notice the fatal vulnerabilities: ( I / 1200 ) must be recomputed or stored in scratch memory three separate times; five levels of open parentheses must remain balanced in working memory; and a single missing closing parenthesis triggers a syntax error or a silent erroneous amortization table *([Parker, 2019](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-parker2019); [Ellenberg, 2014](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-ellenberg2014))*.

The RPN Stack Shortcut: On the StackCalc SC-32, the computation proceeds from the inside out using The Inside-Out Growth Factor and The LASTX Dual-Branch Trick *([HP, 1982](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-hp15c1982); [HP, 1991](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-hp32sii1991))*. The periodic interest rate $i = I/1200$ is computed once. Adding 1 yields the base $(1 + i)$. Raising to the $N$-th power yields $G = (1 + i)^N$. Tap [ENTER] to duplicate $G$, subtract 1 to form the denominator $(G - 1)$ in Register $X$, and tap [÷] against the numerator branch or use The x⇄y Denominator Flip. Every intermediate subtotal is physically visible on the transflective dot-matrix LCD, requiring zero parentheses, zero scratchpad re-entry, and zero cognitive load *([Miller, 1956](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-miller1956))*.

CHAPTER BASELINE MODE: [FIX 2] (Fixed 2-decimal currency display; Standard Base-10 Arithmetic; Degrees angular mode default). TVM variables and four operational stack registers ($X, Y, Z, T$) are maintained continuously in non-volatile hardware memory.

docs.title: 11.2 The Executive's Guide to RPN: Speed, Flow & Cognitive Friction
docs.text:
In high-stakes corporate boardrooms, private equity deal evaluations, commercial contract negotiations, and dynamic field estimation, computational latency imposes immediate cognitive friction.

When an executive using an algebraic calculator (such as a smartphone app, spreadsheet formula line, or standard office desktop unit) attempts to evaluate compound financial relationships, they are forced to mentally manage parenthesis depth, worry about operator precedence, and frequently store intermediate results into disjointed memory keys (M+, MR, STO 1).

Reverse Polish Notation completely removes this cognitive overhead. The four-level operational stack acts as a visual, transparent ledger where operands are staged, intermediate results are automatically preserved, and dyadic operations consume inputs with zero syntax errors.

docs.title: 11.2.1 The Concrete-Representational-Abstract (CRA) Financial Continuum
docs.text: Financial comprehension on the SC-32 bridges three distinct pedagogical levels: 1. Concrete (The Cash Ledger): Physical dollar bills exchanged across a commercial transaction table or loan amortization ledger. Every outflow leaves the wallet (represented by negative sign [+/-]), and every inflow enters the wallet (positive sign). 2. Representational (The Operational 4-Stack): The vertical registers (\(X, Y, Z, T\)) represent distinct balance accounts. Register \(X\) represents active liquid cash in hand; Register \(Y\) preserves the pre-tax invoice baseline; Register \(Z\) holds cumulative tax reserves; Register \(T\) retains repeating scaling multipliers. 3. Abstract (The Actuarial Equations): Compound interest, annuity discount factors, and exponential discounting formulas operate behind simple single-key triggers ([↱] [%], [↱] [%CHG], [↰] [TVM], [PMT]).

docs.title: 11.3 The Base-Preserving Percentage Invariant ([↱] [%])
docs.text:
On standard commercial calculators, pressing the percentage key is fraught with peril: some models divide the entry by 100, others multiply the previous operand, and nearly all destroy the base operand, preventing subsequent addition or subtraction without re-typing.

On the StackCalc SC-32, the Percentage Function ([↱] [%]) is an invariant dyadic operator adhering strictly to William Kahan's non-destructive specification:

\[\text{Calculation: } \quad X \leftarrow \frac{Y \times X}{100}, \quad Y \leftarrow Y \text{ (Preserved!)}, \quad \text{Lift} \leftarrow \text{TRUE}\] Register State After Keying [Base] [ENTER] [Rate] [%] Executive Function Register \(Y\) Base Amount (Preserved frozen in \(Y\)) Base remains intact for subsequent total, discount, or alternative trial Register \(X\) Computed Percentage Amount: \((Y \times X) / 100\) Tax, tip, commission, or margin dollar value

Immediate Next Keystrokes: * Press [+]: Instantly yields Base + Amount (Total with Tax, Markup, Tip). * Press [-]: Instantly yields Base - Amount (Discounted Price, Net Proceeds). * Press [x⇄y]: Restores base to \(X\) for alternative tax rate trials.

docs.title: 11.3.1 Architectural Contrast with Infix Calculators
docs.text: In an algebraic calculator: * To compute tax on \(\$150.00\) at \(8.25\%\), the user types 150 × 0.0825 = to get \(\$12.38\). * To get the total, they must now type + 150 = \(\to \$162.38\). * If they also needed to see what the net total would be with a \(10\%\) discount instead, they must start completely over and re-enter 150. In RPN: * 150 [ENTER] 8.25 [↱] [%] puts \(\$12.38\) in \(X\) and preserves \(\$150.00\) in \(Y\). * Pressing [+] yields \(\$162.38\) in one stroke. * Pressing [↰] [LASTX] recovers \(\$12.38\), or rolling the stack allows immediate further analysis.

docs.title: 11.4 Period-over-Period & Year-over-Year Performance ([↱] [%CHG])
docs.text:
Evaluating corporate revenue growth, cost expansion, and quarterly margin velocity requires calculating the relative percentage change:

\[\%CHG = \frac{\text{New Value} - \text{Old Value}}{\text{Old Value}} \times 100\]

On the SC-32, the Percent Change Function ([↱] [%CHG]) is executed via Right Shift [↱] followed by [↱] [%CHG]:

\[\text{Protocol: } \quad \text{Old\_Value [ENTER] New\_Value [↱] [%CHG]}\] Register State Before [%CHG] State After [%CHG] Executive Role Register \(Y\) Old Value (Baseline) Old Value (Preserved in \(Y\)!) Allows instant variance check: [x⇄y] [LASTX] [-] Register \(X\) New Value (Current) \(\frac{\text{New} - \text{Old}}{\text{Old}} \times 100\) Relative rate of expansion/contraction (%) LASTX Previous operand New Value Retained for delta calculations

Because the Old Value is preserved in Register \(Y\) and the New Value is saved in LASTX, the executive can immediately compute the absolute dollar variance by pressing [x⇄y] [↰] [LASTX] [-].

docs.title: 11.5 Cross-Metric Elasticity & Spread: The Multi-Metric Stack Advantage
docs.text:
The true computational superiority of the RPN operational stack emerges during comparative multi-metric corporate analytics.

Consider an executive evaluating a software portfolio company: * Metric A (Annual Recurring Revenue - ARR): Grew from \(\$12.0\text{M}\) to \(\$15.6\text{M}\). * Metric B (Customer Acquisition Cost - CAC): Expanded from \(\$2.4\text{M}\) to \(\$2.88\text{M}\).

The executive must determine: 1. The ARR vs. CAC Growth Spread: The percentage point difference in expansion rates (\(\Delta \text{ARR}\% - \Delta \text{CAC}\%\)). 2. The Growth Elasticity Ratio: The sensitivity of revenue growth relative to acquisition spending (\(\Delta \text{ARR}\% \div \Delta \text{CAC}\%\)).

Stack Register Value Staged Financial Meaning Immediate Dyadic Operation Register \(T\) \(0.00\) Top of stack — Register \(Z\) \(0.00\) Holding register — Register \(Y\) \(+30.00\%\) Metric A YoY Growth (\(\Delta\text{ARR}\%\)) Base comparator Register \(X\) \(+20.00\%\) Metric B YoY Growth (\(\Delta\text{CAC}\%\)) Active metric
  • Press [-]: \(30.00 - 20.00 = \mathbf{+10.00\%}\) Growth Spread (ARR outgrew CAC by 10 percentage points!).
  • Press [÷]: \(30.00 \div 20.00 = \mathbf{1.50\times}\) Growth Elasticity Ratio (1.5x revenue leverage per CAC dollar!).

In an algebraic calculator, performing this analysis requires scribbling intermediate percentages on paper or entering a 30-character formula with nested parentheses: $\((((15.6 - 12.0) \div 12.0) \times 100) - (((2.88 - 2.40) \div 2.40) \times 100)\)$ On the SC-32, the stack natively holds both metrics side-by-side, allowing instant dyadic inspection.

docs.title: 11.6 The 5-Variable Time Value of Money (TVM) Architecture
docs.text:
The SC-32 features an onboard Five-Variable Time Value of Money (TVM) Engine accessed via Left Shift [↰] followed by [↰] [TVM] on the multi-action [x∥y] key (Row 7, Column 3), as specified in the HP32SII Deviation Rubric.

TVM Variable LFU Softkey Actuarial Description Computational Units \(N\) [N] Total number of compounding periods Integer or fractional periods \(I\%YR\) [I%YR] Annual nominal interest rate Percent per year (e.g. 6.5 for 6.5%) \(PV\) [PV] Present value (initial loan principal or investment) Currency ($) \(PMT\) [PMT] Periodic annuity payment amount Currency ($ per period) \(FV\) [FV] Future value (final balloon balance or accumulated savings) Currency ($)

docs.title: 11.6.1 The Master Actuarial TVM Equation
docs.text:
The five financial variables are bound by the universal compound interest annuity formula:

\[PV + PMT \left[ \frac{1 - (1 + i)^{-N}}{i} \right] (1 + i \cdot S) + FV (1 + i)^{-N} = 0\]

where: * \(i = \frac{I\%YR}{100 \times P/\text{YR}}\) is the periodic interest rate per compounding period. * \(N\) is the total integer count of compounding periods. * \(S = 0\) for End-of-Period payments (Ordinary Annuity, default). * \(S = 1\) for Beginning-of-Period payments (Annuity Due, flagged by the BEGIN annunciator).

docs.title: 11.6.2 Strict Cash Flow Sign Conventions
docs.text:
• Cash Inflow (\(+\)): Money received into your hands/account (e.g., bank loans, proceeds, receipts).
  • Cash Outflow (\(-\), [+/-]): Money paid out from your pocket (e.g., initial investment deposits, mortgage payments, maintenance costs).

docs.title: 11.7.37 Problem 11.37: Internal Rate of Return (IRR) on Uneven Cash Flows
docs.text:
An infrastructure venture requires an upfront outlay of \(C_0 = -\$100,000.00\). It generates subsequent year-end inflows: \(C_1 = \$30,000.00, C_2 = \$40,000.00, C_3 = \$50,000.00\). Determine the project's Internal Rate of Return (\(IRR\)) where \(NPV = 0\):

\[NPV(r) = -100000 + \frac{30000}{1+r} + \frac{40000}{(1+r)^2} + \frac{50000}{(1+r)^3} = 0\]

docs.title: 11.7.38 Problem 11.38: Net Present Value (NPV) Comparison of Capital Projects
docs.text:
A company evaluates two mutually exclusive industrial automation projects with a \(12.0\%\) hurdle rate: * Project Alpha: Initial Cost \(\$80,000.00\); Inflows: \(\$35,000/\text{yr}\) for 3 years. * Project Beta: Initial Cost \(\$120,000.00\); Inflows: \(\$52,000/\text{yr}\) for 3 years.

$\(\text{PV Annuity Factor} = \frac{1 - (1.12)^{-3}}{0.12} = \frac{1 - 0.71178}{0.12} \approx 2.40183\)$ * Project Alpha: \(35,000 \times 2.40183 - 80,000 = \$84,064.10 - \$80,000 = \mathbf{+\$4,064.10}\). * Project Beta: \(52,000 \times 2.40183 - 120,000 = \$124,895.22 - \$120,000 = \mathbf{+\$4,895.22}\). Project Beta delivers \(\$831.12\) more net present value to shareholders.

docs.title: 11.7.40 Problem 11.40: Macaulay and Modified Duration of an Investment-Grade Bond
docs.text: Calculate the interest rate sensitivity (Modified Duration) of a 3-year \(8.0\%\) annual coupon bond trading at par (\(\$1,000.00\)) with yield \(y = 8.0\%\): $\(\text{Macaulay Duration } D = \frac{1 \times 80/1.08 + 2 \times 80/1.08^2 + 3 \times 1080/1.08^3}{1000} = \mathbf{2.783\text{ years}}\)$ $\(\text{Modified Duration } D^* = \frac{D}{1 + y} = \frac{2.783}{1.08} = \mathbf{2.577\text{ years}}\)$ A \(100\text{ bps}\) (\(1.0\%\)) rise in market interest rates causes approximately a \(2.58\%\) decline in bond price.

docs.title: 11.8.1 Problem 11.43: The CEO's Gross Margin vs. Markup Trap
docs.text:
A hardware product has a landed bill-of-materials cost of \(C = \$60.00\). The board mandates a \(40.0\%\) Gross Margin on retail sales. * The Amateur Markup Trap: Adding \(40\%\) on top of \(\$60.00\) (60 [ENTER] 40 [↱] [%] [+] \(\rightarrow\) $84.00) yields only \(\$24.00 / \$84.00 = 28.57\%\) gross margin—destroying profitability!

Named RPN Stack Idiom: The Executive Margin vs. Markup Invariant — Contrast naive markup addition against genuine gross margin pricing using non-destructive stack registers (Parker, 2019; Ellenberg, 2014).

Step-by-Step RPN Reasoning & Stack Logic: 1. 60 [ENTER] — Enter unit manufacturing bill-of-materials cost (\(\$60.00\)) into Register \(Y\). 2. 40 [↱] [%] — Compute \(40\%\) markup (\(\$24.00\)) in Register \(X\), preserving \(\$60.00\) base in \(Y\). 3. [+] — Add markup to cost; displays the flawed markup price \(\mathbf{\$84.00}\) (which delivers only \(28.57\%\) margin).

  • True Gross Margin Pricing: Selling price must satisfy \(\text{Price} = \frac{\text{Cost}}{1 - \text{Margin}}\): 60 [ENTER] 1 [ENTER] 0.40 [-] [÷] \(\rightarrow\) $100.00.

A manufacturing line carries annual fixed overhead of \(F = \$420,000.00\). Each unit sells for \(P = \$85.00\) with variable unit cost \(V = \$35.00\) (contribution margin \(\$50.00/\text{unit}\)): $\(Q_{\text{BE}} = \frac{F}{P - V} = \frac{420,000}{85 - 35}\)$ * Keystrokes: 420000 [ENTER] 85 [ENTER] 35 [-] [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 8,400 units.

[÷] — Divide fixed overhead (\(Z\)) by unit contribution margin (\(X\)); breakeven volume resolves to \(\mathbf{8,400\text{ units}}\).
