docs.title: A.4 The Formal Register Delta Algebra
docs.text: To verify calculation pipelines with mathematical certainty, the effect of any operator \(\Omega\) on the four-register stack \(\mathbf{S} = [X, Y, Z, T]^T\) is expressed as a matrix or functional transformation \(\mathbf{S}' = \mathbf{f}_\Omega(\mathbf{S})\).

docs.title: A.4.1 Unary Operators (\(f(X)\))
docs.text: Unary functions include [√x], [1/x], [eˣ], [LN], [SIN], [COS], [TAN], [x²], [10ˣ], [LOG], [x!], and [|x|]: $\(\begin{bmatrix} X' \\ Y' \\ Z' \\ T' \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} f(X) \\ Y \\ Z \\ T \end{bmatrix}, \quad \text{LASTX}' = X, \quad \text{Lift}' = \text{TRUE}\)$

docs.title: A.4.2 Dyadic Operators (\(f(Y, X)\))
docs.text:
Standard binary operators include [+], [-], [×], [÷], [yˣ], [ˣ√y], and [x∥y]: $\(\begin{bmatrix} X' \\ Y' \\ Z' \\ T' \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} f(Y, X) \\ Z \\ T \\ T \end{bmatrix}, \quad \text{LASTX}' = X, \quad \text{Lift}' = \text{TRUE}\)$

[!IMPORTANT] The Top-Register Constant Replication Invariant: Observe that during any dyadic operation, Register \(T\) drops into \(Z\), while \(T\) retains its original value (\(T' \leftarrow T\)). This structural invariant allows a constant stored in \(T\) to be reused indefinitely across an unbounded series of operations without re-entry!

docs.title: A.4.3 Circular Stack Rotations
docs.text: Rotations rearrange registers without altering numerical values or updating LASTX: * Roll Down ([R↓]): $\(\begin{bmatrix} X' \\ Y' \\ Z' \\ T' \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} Y \\ Z \\ T \\ X \end{bmatrix}, \quad \text{LASTX}' = \text{LASTX}, \quad \text{Lift}' = \text{TRUE}\)$ * Roll Up ([↱] [R↑]): $\(\begin{bmatrix} X' \\ Y' \\ Z' \\ T' \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} T \\ X \\ Y \\ Z \end{bmatrix}, \quad \text{LASTX}' = \text{LASTX}, \quad \text{Lift}' = \text{TRUE}\)$ * Exchange \(X\) and \(Y\) ([x⇄y]): $\(\begin{bmatrix} X' \\ Y' \\ Z' \\ T' \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} Y \\ X \\ Z \\ T \end{bmatrix}, \quad \text{LASTX}' = \text{LASTX}, \quad \text{Lift}' = \text{TRUE}\)$

docs.title: A.4.4 Stack Elevator ([ENTER])
docs.text: The [ENTER] operation pushes the stack while replicating \(X\) into \(Y\): $\(\begin{bmatrix} X' \\ Y' \\ Z' \\ T' \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} X \\ X \\ Y \\ Z \end{bmatrix}, \quad \text{LASTX}' = \text{LASTX}, \quad \text{Lift}' = \text{FALSE}\)$

Under extended system flags ([↱] [FLAGS]), the user can expand the stack beyond 4 levels: * 4-LVL (Classic HP): 4 registers (\(X, Y, Z, T\)). \(T\) replicated on drop; values pushed off \(T\) are discarded. * 8-LVL (Extended STEM): 8 registers (\(X, Y, Z, T, A, B, C, D\)). Deeper parenthetical evaluations can occur without variable storage. \(D\) replicated on drop. * INF (Infinite Dynamic): Dynamic heap allocation. Stack grows unboundedly until system memory limit. docs.title: B.1 The Non-Destructive Error Recovery Principle
docs.text:
On vintage or poorly engineered consumer calculators, encountering an arithmetic singularity (such as division by zero or a domain overflow) triggers a catastrophic reset: the operational display flashes an error code, intermediate calculations are wiped, and the user is forced to re-key multi-step expressions from the beginning.

The StackCalc SC-32 enforces an absolute architectural invariant: The Non-Destructive Error Recovery Principle.

The Non-Destructive Error Recovery Guarantee

When any of the 12 hardware error conditions occurs:

  1. The error message is posted to the status line of the transflective LCD.
  2. The operation causing the error is halted before mutating operational memory.
  3. All four operational stack registers ($X, Y, Z, T$) are frozen intact.
  4. Pressing [C] or [<-] dismisses the error and restores your exact prior stack.

You can immediately inspect operands, swap values via [x⇄y], or re-key the correct operator without losing a single intermediate calculation!

Homeschooler & Student Verification:

If you accidentally divide by zero, do **not panic**! Do not turn off the calculator. Simply press `[C]`. Your numerator is still resting safely in Register $Y$, and the zero is in Register $X$. You can change the zero or swap registers immediately!

docs.title: B.2 Comprehensive Catalog of All 12 Hardware Errors
docs.text:
Every hardware error code on the SC-32 corresponds to a deterministic mathematical domain singularity or hardware constraint boundary.

Error Code Designation Error Code Designation Error Code Designation Code 01 DIVIDE BY 0 Code 05 STAT ERROR Code 09 MEMORY FULL Code 02 INVALID DATA Code 06 NO ROOT FOUND Code 10 TIMEOUT Code 03 OVERFLOW Code 07 A ≠ 0 Code 11 INTERRUPTED Code 04 TOO BIG Code 08 ERROR 5 Code 12 CANNOT BE < 0

docs.title: B.2.1 Code 01: DIVIDE BY 0
docs.text:
• Mathematical Classification: Essential singularity, pole of order 1, or undefined limit.
  • Triggering Conditions:
  • Direct division: \(y \div 0\)
  • Multiplicative reciprocal: \(1/0\)
  • Logarithmic singularity: \(\ln(0)\) or \(\log_{10}(0)\) (\(\lim_{x \to 0^+} \ln x = -\infty\))
  • Zero base with non-positive exponent: \(0^y\) where \(y \le 0\)
  • Trigonometric poles: \(\tan(90^\circ)\), \(\tan(270^\circ)\), \(\cot(0^\circ)\), \(\sec(90^\circ)\), \(\csc(0^\circ)\)
  • IEEE-754 Representation: Hardware trap prevents creation of unsigned or signed IEEE-754 \(\pm\infty\) or NaN in user registers.
  • Stack State upon Error:
  • Register \(X\): 0.0000 (the invalid divisor or argument)
  • Register \(Y\): Original numerator (e.g., \(145.80\))
  • Registers \(Z, T\): Undisturbed
  • LASTX: Unaltered (preserves the \(X\) value from the prior successful calculation)
  • Keystroke Recovery Procedure:
  • Press [C] to dismiss the DIVIDE BY 0 banner.
  • The display reveals 0.0000 in \(X\) and your numerator in \(Y\).
  • Key the intended non-zero divisor (e.g., [1] [2]).
  • Press [÷]. The calculation completes normally.

docs.title: B.2.2 Code 02: INVALID DATA
docs.text:
• Mathematical Classification: Function domain violation in the real field \(\mathbb{R}\).
  • Triggering Conditions:
  • Square root of negative number in real mode: \(\sqrt{-x}\) where \(x < 0\)
  • Logarithm of negative number: \(\ln(-x)\) or \(\log_{10}(-x)\)
  • Inverse trigonometric domain limits: \(\arcsin(x)\) or \(\arccos(x)\) where \(|x| > 1.0\)
  • Factorial of non-integer or negative integer: \((-n)!\) or non-positive integer gamma poles
  • Combinatorics boundaries: \(nCr\) or \(nPr\) where \(r > n\), \(n < 0\), or \(r < 0\)
  • Negative base with non-integer exponent: \((-2)^{0.5}\)
  • Stack State upon Error: All registers frozen. Offending argument rests in \(X\).
  • Keystroke Recovery Procedure:
  • Press [C] to clear the message.
  • If a complex result was desired, arm the complex prefix: press [↰] [CMPLX], then re-execute the function. For example, [↰] [CMPLX] [√x] converts \(\sqrt{-16}\) into \(0 + 4i\).
  • If the input was erroneous, press [+/-] to invert the sign or re-key the argument.

docs.title: B.2.3 Code 03: OVERFLOW
docs.text:
• Mathematical Classification: Magnitude exceeds IEEE-754 double-precision representation limits.
  • Triggering Conditions:
  • Absolute value \(|x| > 1.7976931348623157 \times 10^{308}\)
  • Factorial \(n!\) for \(n > 170\)
  • Exponential \(e^x\) for \(x > 709.782712893384\)
  • Power \(10^x\) for \(x > 308.2547155599167\)
  • Stack State upon Error: All registers frozen. Operands preserved prior to exponential scaling.
  • Keystroke Recovery Procedure:
  • Press [C] to dismiss.
  • Scale the calculation by factoring out exponential powers (e.g., convert units from meters to kilometers, or compute logarithms first: \(\ln(a \times b) = \ln a + \ln b\)).

docs.title: B.2.4 Code 04: TOO BIG
docs.text:
• Mathematical Classification: Integer boundary overflow in the 36-bit two's complement integer architecture.
  • Triggering Conditions:
  • Entering or computing an integer value outside the range \([-2^{35}, 2^{35}-1]\): $\(\text{Lower Limit: } -34,359,738,368 \quad (0\text{x}800000000)\)$ $\(\text{Upper Limit: } +34,359,738,367 \quad (0\text{x}7FFFFFFFF)\)$
  • Integer multiplications or power-of-two scaling that push values beyond the signed 36-bit range.
  • Attempting to switch base (HEX, OCT, BIN) with a floating-point number whose integer magnitude exceeds 36 bits.
  • Stack State upon Error: Operands preserved in full floating-point representation.
  • Keystroke Recovery Procedure:
  • Press [C] to dismiss.
  • Switch to standard decimal floating-point mode via [↰] [BASE] [DEC].
  • Apply modulo \(2^{36}\) or scale values appropriately.

docs.title: B.2.5 Code 05: STAT ERROR
docs.text:
• Mathematical Classification: Statistical degrees-of-freedom singularity or vertical geometric degeneracy.
  • Triggering Conditions:
  • Requesting sample means ([↱] [x̄,ȳ] [x̄]) when sample count \(n = 0\).
  • Requesting sample standard deviations (\(s_x, s_y\)) or linear regression ([↱] [L.R.]) when \(n < 2\) (degrees of freedom \(\nu = n - 1 \le 0\)).
  • Linear regression with zero variance in \(x\) (\(\sum x^2 - \frac{(\sum x)^2}{n} = 0\)), corresponding to a perfectly vertical line where slope \(m = \infty\).
  • Correlation coefficient \(r\) with zero variance in \(y\) or \(x\).
  • Stack State upon Error: Statistical accumulators intact. Stack preserved.
  • Keystroke Recovery Procedure:
  • Press [C] to dismiss.
  • Accumulate additional distinct data points using [Σ+].
  • Inspect accumulators via [↱] [SUMS] to verify data entry integrity.

docs.title: B.2.6 Code 06: NO ROOT FOUND
docs.text:
• Mathematical Classification: Root-finder iteration exhaustion or failure to bracket zero-crossing.
  • Triggering Conditions:
  • Richard Brent's hybrid root solver ([↱] [SOLVE]) executes 100 iterations without bracketing a sign change or satisfying convergence tolerance (\(\epsilon = 10^{-12}\)).
  • The target equation has no real roots (e.g., \(x^2 + 4 = 0\) in real domain).
  • The initial guesses in \(X\) and \(Y\) bracket a local minimum above the \(x\)-axis or a local maximum below the \(x\)-axis without crossing zero.
  • Stack State upon Error: Best candidate approximation returned in Register \(X\). Stack preserved.
  • Keystroke Recovery Procedure:
  • Press [C] to clear.
  • Press [x∥y] (PLOT) to visually graph the function on the LCD and inspect its zero-crossings.
  • Supply two new initial guesses that clearly straddle opposite sides of the root (\(f(a) \cdot f(b) < 0\)).
  • Press [↱] [SOLVE] again.

docs.title: B.2.7 Code 07: A ≠ 0
docs.text:
• Mathematical Classification: Cubic polynomial degeneracy.
  • Triggering Conditions:
  • Characteristic cubic polynomial solver ([XEQ] -> POLY) is executed (EXEC) with leading coefficient \(A = 0\) (\(0x^3 + Bx^2 + Cx + D = 0\)).
  • Stack State upon Error: Stored coefficients in registers \(A, B, C, D\) remain intact.
  • Keystroke Recovery Procedure:
  • Press [C] to dismiss.
  • If solving a true cubic, press A, enter the non-zero leading coefficient, and press EXEC.
  • If solving a quadratic equation \(Bx^2 + Cx + D = 0\), solve using Brent's root solver ([↱] [SOLVE]) or the standard quadratic formula.

docs.title: B.2.8 Code 08: ERROR 5
docs.text:
• Mathematical Classification: Non-convergent cash flow in Time Value of Money (TVM) compound interest iteration.
  • Triggering Conditions:
  • Unsolvable TVM financial configuration where cash flows cannot be balanced by any real interest rate \(I\% \ge -100\%\).
  • All cash flow variables (\(PV, PMT, FV\)) entered with the identical mathematical sign (e.g., all positive), violating the fundamental cash flow sign convention that inflows must balance outflows.
  • Stack State upon Error: Financial registers \(N, I\%YR, PV, PMT, FV\) remain frozen.
  • Keystroke Recovery Procedure:
  • Press [C] to dismiss.
  • Verify the cash flow signs: money leaving your hands (investments, loan payments) must be keyed negative ([+/-]), while money received (loan proceeds, withdrawals) must be positive.
  • Clear financial memory if starting a fresh problem via [↰] [CLEAR] [CLALL].

docs.title: B.2.9 Code 09: MEMORY FULL
docs.text:
• Mathematical Classification: Hardware non-volatile memory or equation bank exhaustion.
  • Triggering Conditions:
  • Attempting to store a 25th equation when the hardware limit of 24 equations is reached.
  • Equation step allocation exceeds available flash sector storage.
  • Stack State upon Error: Existing equations and stack remain 100% intact.
  • Keystroke Recovery Procedure:
  • Press [C] to dismiss.
  • Enter equation catalog, select obsolete or temporary equations, and delete them using [↰] [CLEAR] [CLEQN].

docs.title: B.2.10 Code 10: TIMEOUT
docs.text:
• Mathematical Classification: Numerical algorithm cycle exhaustion.
  • Triggering Conditions:
  • Romberg numerical quadrature ([XEQ] -> [↱] [∫]) exceeds 100,000 sub-interval function evaluations without reaching Richardson extrapolation tolerance.
  • Occurs with functions possessing infinite derivatives, sharp step discontinuities, or high-frequency oscillations (e.g., \(\sin(1/x)\) near \(x = 0\)).
  • Stack State upon Error: Current best numerical approximation preserved in \(X\).
  • Keystroke Recovery Procedure:
  • Press [C] to dismiss.
  • Narrow the integration interval \([a, b]\) to isolate smooth regions, or decompose the integral into piecewise segments around the singularity.

docs.title: B.2.11 Code 11: INTERRUPTED
docs.text:
• Mathematical Classification: Asynchronous user abort.
  • Triggering Conditions:
  • The user presses [C] during a running Romberg integration, Brent's root search, cubic solve, or graphic plot render.
  • Stack State upon Error: Completely clean operational state. Intermediate solver values cleared; user registers frozen at pre-execution state.
  • Keystroke Recovery Procedure:
  • Press [C] to return directly to interactive RPN calculation.

docs.title: B.2.12 Code 12: CANNOT BE < 0
docs.text:
• Mathematical Classification: Unsigned integer underflow in educational / elementary mode.
  • Triggering Conditions:
  • Subtracting a larger unsigned whole number from a smaller unsigned whole number (\(Y < X\) on [-]) while operating in constrained elementary educational profile.
  • Stack State upon Error: Operands \(X\) and \(Y\) preserved.
  • Keystroke Recovery Procedure:
  • Press [C] to dismiss.
  • Press [x⇄y] to exchange operands, or switch to standard signed scientific mode.

docs.title: B.3 Hardware Reset, Diagnostics & Recovery Protocols
docs.text:
For standardized collegiate exams (such as AP, SAT, or FE exams), laboratory baseline resets, or severe power anomalies, the SC-32 provides hardware-level diagnostic and memory wipe sequences:

SC-32 Hardware Recovery Protocols

  1. Soft Reset (Status Clear): Press [C] twice. Cancels active prompts, dismisses error banners, and clears pending shift flags without erasing variables or the stack.
  2. Memory Initialization (Factory Baseline Reset): Hold [C] while powering on, or press [↰] [CLEAR] [CLALL]. Erases all variables A-Z, statistical accumulators, TVM registers, and stack. Resets angular mode to DEGREES, display format to ALL.
  3. Dual-Slot NVM Ping-Pong Recovery: On boot, the microcontroller validates both non-volatile memory slots via 32-bit FNV-1a checksums. If the active slot fails due to battery removal during a write cycle, the firmware automatically rolls back to the standby slot, preventing data corruption.

docs.title: B.4 Verification & Implementation Parity
docs.text: The 12 hardware error codes and non-destructive recovery mechanisms are verified in the engine unit tests: * The Calculator Engine Error Handling Test Suite (CalculatorEngineTests_Errors)

docs.title: C.1.1 Tactile Snap-Dome Mechanics & Debouncing Algorithm
docs.text:
• Actuation Force: \(400\,\text{g}\) tactile stainless steel snap domes providing an unambiguous mechanical snap threshold.
  • Key Travel: \(0.35\,\text{mm}\) short-stroke actuation ensuring zero lost motion.
  • Firmware Debounce Architecture: Eager actuation on leading falling edge (\(0\,\text{ms}\) latency) followed by a \(20\,\text{ms}\) lockout window. This eliminates double-strike bounce artifacts even under aggressive 50-problem contest bursts.

docs.title: C.2 Electrical Matrix & Keypad Scanning Bus
docs.text:
The switch matrix is wired as an \(8 \times 6\) crossbar scanned by the dual-core 32-bit microcontroller:

  • Row Lines (Strobed Outputs): GPIO pins [6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 14, 18, 19]. Strobed low sequentially in round-robin sequence at \(1\,\text{kHz}\) scanning frequency.
  • Column Lines (Sensed Inputs): GPIO pins [11, 12, 13, 15, 16, 17]. Pulled high internally by \(50\,\text{k}\Omega\) resistors; active-low detection.
  • Hardware Sleep Wake Interrupt: Row 7, Column 0 ([C]/ON switch) is routed to an asynchronous edge-triggered interrupt. When the calculator is in deep \(11.8\,\mu\text{A}\) sleep, depressing this key immediately wakes the system clock within \(5\,\text{ms}\).

docs.title: C.4 Authoritative HP32SII Deviations Master Index
docs.text:
The SC-32 intentionally deviates from the 1988 vintage HP-32SII in exact alignment with the project button rubric:

  1. [↱] + +/- = |x| (Absolute Value):
  2. HP32SII Original: ( (open parenthesis for algebraic equation editor).
  3. SC-32 Rationale: Parentheses are redundant in direct RPN mode; direct absolute value is far more useful in applied engineering.
  4. [↱] + E = ÷R (Integer Division & Remainder):
  5. HP32SII Original: ) (close parenthesis for algebraic equation editor).
  6. SC-32 Rationale: Returns integer quotient in \(Y\) and remainder in \(X\) in a single keystroke.
  7. [↱] + <- = Unassigned:
  8. HP32SII Original: = (equals for algebraic equation editor).
  9. SC-32 Rationale: Equality comparison belongs in the x?y and x?0 menus; left unassigned.
  10. [↰] + 0 = REGS (Register Viewer):
  11. HP32SII Original: INPUT (program input prompt).
  12. SC-32 Rationale: Programming prompts are replaced by dynamic equation parameters; REGS allows instant inspection of all variables.
  13. Key Row 7, Col 3 (Multi-Action Key):
  14. HP32SII Original: R/S (Run/Stop program execution).
  15. SC-32 Assignment: Primary: x∥y, Left Shift [↰]: TVM, Right Shift [↱]: PLOT, Alpha: (i).
  16. SC-32 Rationale: Traditional line programming is replaced by RPN step equations, numerical quadrature, root finding, and financial solvers.
  17. [↰] + + = LBL:
  18. Restored equation safety key ensuring equations retain explicit labels.
  19. [↱] + XEQ = POLY:
  20. Cubic polynomial solver workspace (A B C D EXEC CLR on LFU softkeys).
  21. Top 6 LFU Dynamic Softkeys:
  22. Context-aware softkey strip permanently positioned above the primary math rows.

SC-32 APPENDIX D // MATHEMATICAL CONSTANTS, SI UNITS & MASTER STEM EQUATION DIRECTORY ● IMMUTABLE MATHEMATICAL CONSTANTS • 58 STEM EQUATIONS • PARENTHESIS-FREE RPN SEQUENCING

Figure D.1: The StackCalc SC-32 technical reference bench instrument: rapid parenthesis-free evaluation of fundamental engineering and mathematical equations.

DIRECTORY BASELINE: Immutable mathematical constants; Complete BIPM SI prefixes (10³⁰ to 10⁻³⁰); Exact international unit conversions; Scientific notation entry syntax via [E]; Full 12-digit mantissa stack precision.

docs.title: D.1 The Architecture of Precision: Constants and Equations in RPN
docs.text:
A scientific calculator is not merely a tool for performing isolated arithmetic operations; it is a computational laboratory for modeling the physical universe. On the StackCalc SC-32, the synergy of Reverse Polish Notation (RPN), continuous four-register stack visibility (\(X, Y, Z, T\)), and dedicated scientific functions provides an unparalleled environment for STEM calculations.

SC-32 Scientific Register Hierarchy & Data Flow

> [ REGISTER T ] Top / Constant Buffer <-- Retains constant factor during drop > │ > [ REGISTER Z ] Third Stack Level <-- Holds intermediate vector/matrix term > │ > [ REGISTER Y ] Second Stack Level <-- Stores dyadic base, dividend, angle > │ > [ REGISTER X ] Active / Display <-- Direct keyboard entry & live readout > > [ LASTX REG ] Recovery Buffer <-- Automatically captures previous X > [ STATS BANK ] 6 Accumulators <-- Σx, Σy, Σx², Σy², Σxy, n > [ MEMORY A-Z ] 26 Global Registers <-- Persistent storage via [STO] / [RCL]

docs.title: D.1.1 The Concrete-Representational-Abstract (CRA) Framework
docs.text:
1. Concrete (Key Entry & Hardware Tactility): Scientific magnitudes are keyed using the tactile 400g snap-dome keys. Entering a power-of-ten scale factor such as \(6.62607015 \times 10^{-34}\) is accomplished cleanly via 6.62607015 [E] 34 [+/-].
  2. Representational (Four-Register Visual Feedback): As operations execute, intermediate physical quantities (such as angular frequency \(\omega\) in \(Y\) and capacitance \(C\) in \(X\)) remain continuously visible on the transflective \(132 \times 65\) LCD, eliminating memory ambiguity.
  3. Abstract (Parenthesis-Free Formula Decomposition): Equations with complex nesting (such as blackbody radiation laws or relativistic Lorentz transformations) are evaluated inside-out or bottom-up, completely avoiding algebraic parentheses.

docs.title: D.2 Fundamental Mathematical Constants
docs.text:
Unlike empirical physical measurements (such as the Newtonian gravitational constant \(G\), the fine-structure constant \(\alpha\), or subatomic particle masses, which are periodically revised by international CODATA adjustments and are therefore stated explicitly within individual problem benchmarks in Section D.4), pure mathematical constants are timeless invariants. The table below lists the fundamental mathematical constants and their exact SC-32 RPN generation sequences.

docs.title: D.3 International Standard Unit Conversions & BIPM SI Prefixes

docs.title: D.5 Specialized RPN Idioms & Stack Optimization Patterns
docs.text: Mastery of the SC-32 involves recognizing recurring computational structures and leveraging dedicated hardware keys to minimize button presses and eliminate redundant variable stores.

docs.title: D.5.1 The Harmonic Mean Idiom ([x∥y])
docs.text: The SC-32 provides a dedicated primary key [x∥y] which calculates: $\(X = \frac{X \cdot Y}{X + Y} = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{X} + \frac{1}{Y}}\)$ In algebraic calculators, entering a reciprocal sum requires 12 to 16 keystrokes with fractions and parentheses. On the SC-32, it takes exactly one keystroke: * Parallel Resistors: \(R_{\text{eq}} = R_1 \parallel R_2 \parallel R_3\) \(\rightarrow\) R1 [ENTER] R2 [x∥y] R3 [x∥y]. * Series Capacitors: \(C_{\text{eq}} = C_1 \parallel C_2\) \(\rightarrow\) C1 [ENTER] C2 [x∥y]. * Thin Lens Optics: Focal length \(f = d_o \parallel d_i\) \(\rightarrow\) do [ENTER] di [x∥y]. * Spring Series Compliance: \(k_{\text{eq}} = k_1 \parallel k_2\) \(\rightarrow\) k1 [ENTER] k2 [x∥y]. * Reduced Mass in Two-Body Problem: \(\mu = m_1 \parallel m_2\) \(\rightarrow\) m1 [ENTER] m2 [x∥y].

docs.title: D.5.2 The Difference-of-Squares Idiom
docs.text: When evaluating expressions of the form \(a^2 - b^2\) (such as Pythagorean legs \(b = \sqrt{c^2 - a^2}\) or numerical aperture \(NA = \sqrt{n_1^2 - n_2^2}\)): * Traditional RPN: c [↰] [x²] a [↰] [x²] [-] [√x] (6 keystrokes). * Stack Factoring Alternative: c [ENTER] a [ENTER] [+] [↰] [LASTX] c [x⇄y] [-] [×] [√x]. When numbers are large multi-digit values, entering them once and using [x⇄y] and [↰] [LASTX] avoids re-typing.

docs.title: D.5.3 Constant Factor Replication in Register T
docs.text: When evaluating a formula with a repeated scalar factor \(K\) across multiple variables (e.g. converting several values from feet to meters using \(0.3048\), or multiplying items by sales tax \(1.0825\)): 1. Load the constant into the stack: 1.0825 [ENTER] [ENTER] [ENTER] (fills \(X, Y, Z, T\)). 2. Enter Price 1: 10 [×] \(\rightarrow\) Displays result \(10.825\). Register \(T\) drops to \(Z\) and replicates \(1.0825\) in \(T\)! 3. Enter Price 2: [CLx] 25 [×] \(\rightarrow\) Displays \(27.0625\). Register \(T\) continues to supply \(1.0825\) indefinitely without ever touching memory registers!

docs.title: D.6 Equation Bank Programming & Automatic Variable Prompting
docs.text:
The StackCalc SC-32 provides a non-volatile Equation Bank accessed via [↱] [EQN]. Any standard formula can be stored as a symbolic expression and evaluated repeatedly, solved numerically via Brent's root finder, or integrated via Romberg quadrature.

Equation Bank Workflow: Entry, Solving & Integration

  1. Create Equation: [↱] [EQN] → Type formula using named variables $A$–$Z$. Example: Y = A × X² + B × X + C
  2. Evaluate (Prompt): [XEQ] → SC-32 sequentially prompts: A? → enter value → [R/S], X? → enter value → [R/S], B? → enter value → [R/S], C? → enter value → [R/S]. Result displays in Register $X$.
  3. Numerical Root: [↱] [SOLVE] X → Solves for $X$ when $Y = 0$ using Richard Brent's hybrid algorithm.
  4. Numerical Integral: [↱] [∫] → Prompts for variable, lower, upper. Evaluates Romberg adaptive quadrature.

docs.title: D.6.1 Benchmark Example: Parabolic Motion Integration
docs.text: Evaluate \(\int_0^4 3 X^2 \, dX = [X^3]_0^4 = 64.0\): 1. Enter Equation mode: [↱] [EQN] 2. Enter keystrokes: 3 [ENTER] X [↰] [x²] [×] 3. Assign label: PARABOLA 4. Set integration bounds: Lower bound \(0.0\), Upper bound \(4.0\). 5. Press [↱] [∫] X 6. The transflective screen indicates active Romberg convergence steps and halts with 64.0000 in Register \(X\).

docs.title: D.7.1 Dimensional Dependency Tracking & Conceptual Grounding
docs.text: In collegiate engineering and physics education, learners often struggle with algebraic syntax friction, losing sight of physical scaling relationships while navigating nested parentheses. Formulating standard reference equations—from relativistic dynamics to thermodynamic cycles—into step-by-step RPN pipelines reveals physical dimensional dependencies directly. Intermediate operands in Registers \(Y\) and \(Z\) anchor dimensional analysis, allowing students to inspect intermediate physical products (such as momentum, kinetic energy, or pressure heads) before collapsing terms into final units.

docs.title: D.7.2 2022 CODATA Physical Constants & Verification Precision
docs.text: The SC-32 hardcodes fundamental physical constants according to the latest 2022 CODATA recommendations (including the Planck constant \(h\), speed of light \(c\), elementary charge \(e\), and Avogadro constant \(N_A\)). Because these values are defined with exact SI definitions or high-precision mantissas, computing physical benchmarks with 4-level stack traces ensures that experimental calculations and textbook derivations match standard reference tables to full floating-point precision without compounding rounding errors.

docs.title: D.7.3 Hardware Stack Persistence & Register Flow Control
docs.text: Translating multidisciplinary equations into pure postfix execution highlights the architectural efficiency of the 4-register operational stack (\(X, Y, Z, T\)). In operations requiring constant reuse, filling Register \(T\) provides perpetual constant replication, while the single-cycle parallel harmonic key ([x∥y]) and one-touch recovery via [↰] [LASTX] eliminate scratchpad register allocation. The deterministic behavior of the stack ensures rapid, error-free execution across all 58 core scientific formulas.

docs.title: D.8 Diagnostic Checkpoints & Singularity Handling
docs.text:
Diagnostic Checkpoint D.1: Scientific Exponent Entry Syntax

Never press `[×] 10 [yˣ]` to enter scientific notation! Doing so pushes an extra operator onto the stack, consuming two stack levels.

Always use the dedicated [E] (Exponent) key: * Correct: 1.602176634 [E] 19 [+/-] (Single atomic number entered into Register \(X\)). * Incorrect: 1.602176634 [ENTER] 10 [ENTER] 19 [+/-] [yˣ] [×] (Consumes 4 stack registers and risks stack overflow).

Diagnostic Checkpoint D.2: Trigonometric Angular Modes in Physical Laws

Physical formulas involving wave motion, optics, and projectile trajectories demand careful attention to the active angular mode:

  • Geometric & Surveying Formulas (Snell's Law, Law of Cosines, Great Circle): Require Degrees mode ([↰] [MODES] [DEG]).
  • Analytical Calculus & Fourier Syntheses (Pendulum period, Harmonic oscillations): Require Radians mode ([↰] [MODES] [RAD]). Verify the LCD annunciator at the top of the display before running chained trigonometric sequences.

Diagnostic Checkpoint D.3: Mathematical Singularity and Boundary Handling

* **Division by Zero ($x / 0$):** The SC-32 halts chained execution and displays `DIV BY ZERO`. Press `[<-]` to recover prior stack state.

  • Square Root of Negative Real (\(\sqrt{-x}\)): In Real mode, displays INVALID ARG. In Complex mode ([↰] [CMPLX]), returns pure imaginary result \(i\sqrt{x}\) into \((x, y)\) coordinate representation.
  • Logarithm of Non-Positive Real (\(\ln(0)\) or \(\ln(-x)\)): Displays DOMAIN ERROR.

docs.title: Appendix E: Primary Sources & Annotated Further Reading Guide
docs.text:
SC-32 SCHOLARSHIP // ANNOTATED FURTHER READING & PRIMARY SOURCES ● 1914–2026 CHRONOLOGY • THEMATIC PATHWAYS • BIBTEX CATALOG

The architecture of the StackCalc SC-32 does not exist in isolation. It represents the conscious convergence of more than a century of research across mathematical logic, stack-oriented computer organization, numerical error analysis, cognitive science, and scientific instrument craftsmanship.

While the detailed historical narratives of William Hewlett's 1972 Corvallis genesis, John Napier's 1614 logarithms, Cody & Waite's range reduction, Eratosthenes' geodesy, Carl Friedrich Gauss's 1801 orbital recovery of Ceres, and Claude Shannon's 1937 boolean algebra have been woven directly into the opening chapters of this manual, this appendix provides an authoritative, automatically indexed guide to the primary literature, complete with chapter cross-references and verified BibTeX citations.

Annotation: Introduces parenthesis-free prefix and postfix notation, demonstrating that operator position alone uniquely determines evaluation order without grouping symbols. Cited in Chapters: Ch 02, Foreword

docs.title: 1. Welcome, Explorer! (Wait—Did Your Parents Buy You This Book?)
docs.text:
If an adult handed you this book and said, "Here, read this math manual," you probably wanted to groan and hide it under your bed. We get it! Most school math books are torture: pages of boring drills, confusing rules like "borrow from the neighbor," and giant tangles of parentheses ( ( 15 - 3 ) × ( 4 + 2 ) ) ÷ 6 = ? where one tiny mistake ruins your whole page.

Here is the secret: this is not a normal school math book, and the calculator in your hands is not a normal calculator.

Look closely at the bottom-right corner of the StackCalc SC-6. Notice anything missing? There is no equals (=) button.

Why? Because on a normal calculator, the = button is a trap. You type a long chain of numbers and parentheses, cross your fingers, hit =, and hope it doesn't flash SYNTAX ERROR. On the SC-6, you use Reverse Polish Notation (RPN)—the exact same "inside-out" secret code used by rocket engineers, tournament math champions, and computer scientists.

Want to beat every grown-up in your house at a 5th-grade math challenge right now? Hand a parent their phone calculator, pick up your SC-6, and race them on: $\((15 - 3) \times (4 + 2) \div 6\)$

While they are still hunting for the ( and ) brackets on their glass screen, you tap: 15 [ENTER] 3 [-] 4 [ENTER] 2 [+] [×] 6 [÷] \(\longrightarrow\) 12!

Zero parentheses. Zero scrap paper. Done in five seconds flat. Flip to Chapter 2 to see how Stack Math and your 4-level number stack work, or jump straight to Chapter 8 to test your reflexes against the built-in Arithmetic Sprint Game ([f] [?])!

Unlocked Keycaps Ribbon — Master Grade Progression

You don't need to learn all 43 keys at once! As you level up from Kindergarten to Grade 6, you unlock new superpowers on your keypad: • Grades K–1: [▦] Ten-Frame, [g] [COUNT] Step Counter / Rack, [f] [LINE] Number Line, [+], [-], [ENTER], [C], [<-], Digits [0]–[9]. • Grade 2: [PV] Place Value Mode, Doubles (N [ENTER] [+]), [g] [REP] Skip-Counting. • Grade 3: [×], [÷], [f] [RECT] Rectangle Area, [🕒] Planetary Clock, Unit Fractions ([.] n [.] d). • Grade 4: [g] [÷R] Quotient & Remainder, [g] [SIMP] Factor Reduction, Mixed Numbers [a ᵇ/c], Improper Fractions [f] [d/c], Decimals. • Grade 5: Unlike Fractions, [f] [LCM] Least Common Denominator, [f] [PRISM] Volume, [Σ+] Surface Area Accumulation, Unit Conversions. • Grade 6 (Pre-Algebra & Rapid Math Sprint): [+/-] Signed Numbers, [g] [|x|] Absolute Value, [g] [FACT] Prime Decomposition, [GCF], [f] [LCM], Ratios ([g] [a:b]), Geometric [x²] and [f] [√x] Inverses, Descriptive Statistics ([g] [x̄], [f] [MED], [g] [MODE], [IQR], [g] [MAD]). Strict Gatekeeping Directive: 5th graders and younger NEVER see logarithms (LOG, LN) or abstract powers (yˣ). Advanced functions are segregated exclusively into secondary advanced math extensions.

docs.title: 2. Foreword: The Renaissance of Tactile Mathematics
docs.text:
For Parents & Teachers: The Crisis of Frictionless Computation & The RPN Solution

In an era dominated by glowing glass tablets, cloud-connected mobile applications, and opaque computer algebra engines, children frequently encounter school mathematics as an arbitrary ritual of keystrokes followed by an equal sign (=). A student types 7 + 5 = on a touchscreen; the digits vanish instantly, replaced by 12. What happened between the input and the output? In the traditional algebraic calculator paradigm, the mathematical transformation is completely hidden from view. The physical regrouping of five loose counters with seven counters to form a complete ten and two units never occurs in the child's mind. The intermediate subtotal is swallowed by internal hardware buffers. If the child makes a mistake, the screen flashes SYNTAX ERROR, providing zero spatial evidence of where the reasoning derailed. The StackCalc SC-6 Elementary Calculator & Classroom Companion was engineered to end this era of black-box computation. Drawing inspiration from the mechanical clarity celebrated by David Macaulay *([Macaulay, 2016](sc6/appendix-c-formulas-and-conversions.md#cite-macaulay2016))* and the intuitive wonder of mathematics championed by Steven Strogatz *([Strogatz, 2012](sc6/appendix-c-formulas-and-conversions.md#cite-strogatz2012))*, it restores physical intuition, spatial clarity, and tactile joy to mathematics from Kindergarten through Grade 6. Designed around a crisp $400\text{g}$ tactile stainless-steel snap-dome matrix, an ambient-light transflective dot-matrix LCD, and dark impact-resistant technical thermoplastics, the SC-6 is not a disposable toy or a passive consumer tablet. It is an authentic, durable scientific instrument built for young hands and curious minds.

| Paradigm | Keystroke Sequence | Cognitive & Pedagogical Reality | |---|---|---| | **Traditional Algebraic (Infix)** | `7` `+` `5` `=` $\longrightarrow 12$ | The `+` key hides `7` in invisible memory while waiting for `5`. The `=` key destroys the problem structure. The learner never sees where intermediate numbers live. | | **Reverse Polish Notation (RPN)** | `7` `[ENTER]` `5` `[+]` $\longrightarrow 12$ | `7` rises visibly to Register $Y$; `5` enters Register $X$; `[+]` fuses them visibly into `12`. Every number is a visible object; zero hidden buffers; zero syntax errors. |

docs.title: 2.1 For the Skeptical Parent: Why Not Just Use a $10 Calculator or Tablet App?
docs.text:
If you are a parent looking at the StackCalc SC-6 and its companion 3D-printed block kits, you should ask a blunt question: "Why shouldn't my child just use a $10 four-function calculator or a free iPad math game?"

Here is the honest answer: 1. Tablet apps hijack attention; tactile instruments build focus. Even the best-intentioned tablet app lives one swipe away from video feeds, pop-up badges, and slot-machine sound effects. The SC-6 has zero Wi-Fi, zero notifications, and zero ads. When your child sits at the kitchen table with physical blocks and the SC-6, their entire attention is on the math in their hands. 2. A $10 calculator hides the work; the 4-level stack shows every step. On a drugstore calculator, typing 7 + 5 = makes the 7 and 5 vanish into 12. When a child makes a mistake on a multi-step word problem, they have no idea what went wrong and have to start over from scratch. On the SC-6, four levels of numbers (\(T, Z, Y, X\)) stay visible on the screen at once, and [f] [LASTX] lets them undo or check their last step immediately. 3. Three 5-Minute Kitchen-Table Lightbulb Moments You Will See in Week One: - The "Make-a-Ten" Snap (Grades K–2): Your child places 8 red counters and 2 gold counters into the physical Ten-Frame tray (10), leaves 3 gold counters beside it (13), and sees the exact same tray light up on the SC-6 screen via [▦]. Finger-counting disappears because they can see \(8 + 5\) as \(10 + 3\). - The Bus Remainder Aha! (Grades 3–4): Instead of getting lost in 3.2222222 when dividing 145 campers into 45-seat buses, your child taps 145 [ENTER] 45 [g] [÷R] and sees 3 full buses on line \(X\) and 10 campers left over on line \(Y\)—matching what happens in real life. - The Fraction Tower Match (Grades 3–6): Before touching a common-denominator rule, your child drops a \(\frac{1}{2}\) block and a \(\frac{1}{3}\) block into the Fraction Studio comparator well, slides five \(\frac{1}{6}\) blocks beside them until the tops are flush, and then verifies \(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3} = \frac{5}{6}\) right on the SC-6.

docs.title: 2.2 The Equals-Sign Trap vs. The Stack Ladder
docs.text:
Decades of educational research in early mathematics education (Jerome Bruner (Bruner, 1966), Zoltan Dienes (Dienes, 1960), and Liping Ma (Ma, 1999)) identify the "equals-sign trap" as the single greatest cognitive stumbling block transitioning from elementary arithmetic to pre-algebra. In typical elementary classrooms, students see = at the end of every line on a worksheet. Consequently, children come to view the equals sign not as a relational statement of balance, but as an urgent command meaning "produce the answer right now!"

When these students later encounter algebraic expressions such as: $\(8 + 4 = \Box + 5\)$ an alarming majority of students write \(12\) in the box (or \(17\)), because their eyes lock onto \(8 + 4\) and treat the equals sign as an immediate trigger to compute (Strogatz, 2012).

The StackCalc SC-6 dismantles this trap by replacing the equals sign with the Stack Ladder. There is no [=] button on the faceplate. Instead, mathematical quantities sit as physical objects on visible shelves: 1. Quantity First: You pick up an object or measure a quantity onto the active shelf (\(X\)). 2. The Elevator Lift: Tapping [ENTER] lifts that object smoothly onto the upper mezzanine shelf (\(Y\)). 3. Second Quantity: You bring another quantity into contact on the ground shelf (\(X\)). 4. Operational Action: Tapping an operator ([+], [-], [×], [÷]) causes the upper shelf to drop down, fusing the objects into a new composite quantity immediately.

On the Stack Ladder, computation is never an opaque command—it is a tangible running balance of physical objects that can be grouped, scaled, and inspected at will.

docs.title: 2.3 Five Stack Math Super-Moves
docs.text:
Throughout this textbook and classroom companion, students and mentors master five foundational Stack Math Super-Moves that bond physical manipulatives to the RPN stack: 1. The Make-a-Ten Snap: Using 3D-printed Ten-Frames ([▦]) to bridge to 10 before chaining addition, turning mental carrying into an intuitive tactile click (Singapore MOE, 2014). 2. The Elevator Stack Drop: Watching intermediate numbers drop floor-by-floor down the 4-register stack (\(T \to Z \to Y \to X\)) as operations execute, eliminating parenthetical clutter entirely (Macaulay, 2016). 3. The Remainder-You-Can-Hold: Using integer division [g] [÷R] to place the whole quotient in \(X\) and the physical leftover remainder in \(Y\) simultaneously—preserving the discrete reality of egg crates, bus seats, and bakery trays (Ma, 1999). 4. The Equal-Fraction Tower Alignment: Testing equivalence and simplifying fractions directly in the 84 mm Fraction Studio comparator well ([g] [SIMP]), where equal fractions physically match in height (Strogatz, 2012). 5. The Skip-Counting Ladder: Locking a constant step increment across registers via [g] [REP] so repeated taps of [+] scale rhythmic times-table ladders without re-entering numbers (Gauss, 1809).

For Parents & Teachers: The Concrete-Representational-Abstract (CRA) Framework

Jerome Bruner's foundational cognitive research established that deep mathematical fluency develops through a three-stage cognitive progression: Concrete → Representational → Abstract (CRA) *([Bruner, 1966](sc6/appendix-c-formulas-and-conversions.md#cite-bruner1966))*. The StackCalc SC-6 is the first physical calculating instrument designed specifically to embody and accelerate the CRA sequence within every mathematical domain.

| CRA Stage | Physical / Digital Medium | Classroom & Studio Examples | |---|---|---| | **Stage 1: Concrete (Hands-On Manipulatives)** | 3D-Printed Gridfinity Studio Kits | Ten-Frame Trays, $84\text{ mm}$ Fraction Towers & Comparator Well, 144 Four-Color Counting Tiles, Prime Factor Studio, Planetary Geared Clock. | | **Stage 2: Representational (LCD Sandboxes)** | Transflective Dot-Matrix Visual Modes | Ten-Frame Studio `[▦]`, Step Counter & Bead Rack `[g] [COUNT]`, Number Line Jump Arcs `[LINE]`, Place Value `[PV]`, Geared Clock Dial `[🕒]`. | | **Stage 3: Abstract (RPN Stack Dynamics)** | Multi-Register Stack-Order (RPN) Stack ($X, Y, Z, T$) | Two-Number stack drop, $T$-register constant replication, parenthesis-free order of operations `(15-3)×(4+2)÷6`, multi-face surface area accumulation via `[Σ+]`. |

Stage 1: Concrete (Physical Manipulative Kits): Before you ever press a key on the SC-6, mathematical quantities exist in three dimensions. In Kindergarten and Grade 1, you place solid counters into tactile Ten-Frame trays. In Grade 2 and Grade 3, you dock and stack $19\text{ mm}$ four-color Gridfinity counting tiles to construct physical rectangular arrays for multiplication ($4 \times 6$) and explore planar region coloring without fragile friction snaps. In Grade 4 and Grade 5, you align $84\text{ mm}$ Fraction Towers, physically feeling that two $1/4$ blocks have the exact same height as one $1/2$ block. In Grade 6, you place proportional prime factor blocks into the Prime Factor Studio logarithmic comparator box, physically experiencing Napierian logarithmic addition where stacking a [2] and a [3] block lands exactly on the "6" tick mark of the back-wall slide rule comparator ($h(2) + h(3) = 12.64\text{ mm} + 20.04\text{ mm} = 32.68\text{ mm} = h(6)$). The physical manipulatives share identical geometric dimensions and naming conventions with the SC-6 hardware interface, anchoring subsequent symbolic reasoning. Stage 2: Representational (Visual LCD Sandboxes): The SC-6 graphic LCD features a high-contrast $132 \times 65$ dot-matrix transflective panel. When you enter a visual tool mode, the screen shifts seamlessly from raw numerals into high-resolution vector diagrams that mirror your physical manipulatives (Ten-Frames via [▦], dynamic jumping number line via [f] [LINE], bead rack via [g] [COUNT], and dual geared analog clocks via [🕒]). In this representational stage, numbers are visible, countable objects living directly within the dual-stack columns of the calculator. Stage 3: Abstract (RPN Operational Stack Dynamics): Once you understand the underlying physical and visual behavior, you transition effortlessly to the abstract stage. The visual frames give way to standard numerical registers ($T, Z, Y, X$). Now you harness the true power of Reverse Polish Notation: chaining multi-step problems without intermediate scratch paper, utilizing two-number stack drops to carry intermediate answers automatically into the next operation, replicating constants through the top register ($T$) for rhythmic skip-counting ladders, and accumulating multi-face geometric surface areas directly into hardware statistical memory ([Σ+]).

docs.title: 4. Three Foundational RPN Breakthroughs for Your Math Journey
docs.text:
Three core operational capabilities illustrate why a dedicated tactile RPN instrument and physical manipulative studio transform elementary mathematics:

  1. Parenthesis-Free Multi-Step Evaluation: In standard curriculum problems such as \(((18 + 6) \times (15 - 7)) \div 8\), algebraic calculators require balancing nested parentheses, where a single missing bracket produces a syntax error. On the SC-6, you evaluate the expression from the inside out: 18 [ENTER] 6 [+] 15 [ENTER] 7 [-] [×] 8 [÷] \(\longrightarrow\) 24! The first sub-expression \((18 + 6 = 24)\) lifts cleanly into Register \(Y\); the second sub-expression \((15 - 7 = 8)\) forms in Register \(X\). Tapping [×] multiplies them into \(192\), and tapping 8 followed by [÷] produces \(24\). The calculation requires zero parentheses, zero scratch paper, and zero memory register overhead.

  2. Visible Unreduced Fractions and Deliberate Simplification ([g] [SIMP]): When exploring fraction equivalence, you place a \(1/2\) block (\(42.0\text{ mm}\)) beside three \(1/6\) blocks (\(3 \times 14.0\text{ mm} = 42.0\text{ mm}\)) in the Fraction Studio comparator well. On traditional calculators, typing 3/6 immediately forces an automatic reduction to 0.5 or 1/2, erasing the unreduced state. The SC-6 preserves the unreduced fraction on screen when entering . 3 . 6 [ENTER]. You deliberately press [g] [SIMP] to divide out common factors step-by-step, observing how both numerator and denominator scale down until the annunciator confirms LOWEST TERMS.

  3. Discrete Integer Division with Remainders ([g] [÷R]): In real-world sharing—such as distributing 17 counting tiles equally among 5 friends—a decimal quotient (\(3.4\)) obscures the concrete outcome. Tapping 17 [ENTER] 5 [g] [÷R] displays the whole quotient 3 in Register \(X\) and the exact remainder 2 in Register \(Y\) simultaneously. Pressing [x⇄y] swaps the two values on the screen, allowing you to verify both the grouped units and the leftover items in a single keystroke.

docs.title: 5. The Four SC-6 RPN Superpowers
docs.text:
The StackCalc SC-6 equips you with four unique operational tools—referred to throughout this manual as the Four RPN Superpowers. These capabilities are completely absent from traditional consumer calculators, transforming difficult elementary math concepts into effortless, rhythmic operations.

THE FOUR SC-6 RPN SUPERPOWERS

SUPERPOWER 1: [g] [REP] / [REP] Rhythmic Skip-Counting & Times Tables Replicates X into all registers; rhythmic [+] builds times tables (7, 14, 21, 28...). SUPERPOWER 2: [g] [÷R] / [÷R] Simultaneous Whole Quotient & Remainder Divides in 1 stroke: Quotient in X, Remainder in Y. [x⇄y] swaps to inspect. SUPERPOWER 3: [SIMP] Step-by-Step Fraction Factor Reduction Divides out prime factors one at a time; announces "LOWEST TERMS" when irreducible. SUPERPOWER 4: [f] [LASTX] Self-Checking Inverse Arithmetic Recalls the prior number into X to verify operations via inverse math (add -> sub).

docs.title: 5.1 Superpower 1: Rhythmic Skip-Counting Ladders ([g] [REP])
docs.text:
• Keycap: Row 3, Col 5 ([g] [REP], mapped to executeRep())
  • The Challenge in Early Math: Memorizing multiplication tables through rote chanting often fails because you do not experience the steady, rhythmic accumulation of equal groups.
  • The RPN Solution: When you enter a number (e.g. 7) and press [g] [REP], the value 7 is instantly replicated across all four stack registers: $\(X = 7, \quad Y = 7, \quad Z = 7, \quad T = 7\)$
  • Now, every tap of the [+] key adds another group of 7. As you tap [+] rhythmically, the screen climbs: $\(7 \xrightarrow{[+]} 14 \xrightarrow{[+]} 21 \xrightarrow{[+]} 28 \xrightarrow{[+]} 35 \xrightarrow{[+]} 42 \xrightarrow{[+]} 49 \xrightarrow{[+]} 56 \dots\)$
  • Because the top register (\(T\)) automatically duplicates upon every two-number drop, you can skip-count indefinitely! Multiplication is no longer an abstract flashcard; it is an active, rhythmic ladder.

docs.title: 5.2 Superpower 2: Simultaneous Whole Quotient and Remainder ([g] [÷R])
docs.text:
• Keycap: Row 4, Col 6 ([g] [÷R], mapped to intDiv)
  • The Challenge in Early Math: When you learn division, standard calculators produce confusing decimals. Dividing \(17 \div 5\) produces 3.4. But what does 0.4 mean when you are packing 17 eggs into 5-egg cartons, or sharing 17 cookies among 5 friends? It means 3 cookies each and 2 cookies left over! Decimal calculators force you to perform messy scratch-paper long division just to find the remainder.
  • The RPN Solution: Entering 17 [ENTER] 5 [g] [÷R] executes integer division in a single stroke:
  • Register \(X\): Displays the whole quotient \(Q = 3\) (each friend gets 3 cookies).
  • Register \(Y\): Holds the exact remainder \(R = 2\) (2 cookies left over in the jar).
  • Tapping [x⇄y] (Row 3, Col 3) instantly swaps registers, allowing you to inspect the remainder and swap back. Sharing and packaging problems are solved in seconds with absolute conceptual clarity.

docs.title: 5.3 Superpower 3: Step-by-Step Fraction Factor Reduction ([g] [SIMP])
docs.text:
• Keycap: Row 1, Col 2 ([g] [SIMP])
  • The Challenge in Early Math: Traditional fraction calculators automatically reduce every fraction to lowest terms immediately upon entry. If you key \(4/8\), the calculator instantly displays \(1/2\). While convenient for an engineer, you never see that \(4/8\) has a common factor of 2 or 4, missing the entire conceptual bridge of equivalent fractions.
  • The RPN Solution: StackCalc SC-6 enforces unreduced fraction arithmetic by default. When you key . 12 . 18 [ENTER], the screen displays 12/18. The fraction remains unreduced through additions and multiplications until you deliberately press [g] [SIMP]:
  • First press of [g] [SIMP]: Divides numerator and denominator by their greatest common factor, displaying 2/3.
  • Second press of [g] [SIMP]: Detects that \(\gcd(2, 3) = 1\), leaves 2/3 intact, and momentarily flashes LOWEST TERMS across the screen.
  • You retain complete ownership over the simplification process.

docs.title: 5.4 Superpower 4: Self-Checking Inverse Arithmetic ([f] [LASTX])
docs.text:
• Keycap: Row 3, Col 1 ([f] [LASTX])
  • The Challenge in Early Math: Teachers constantly urge students to "check your work." But checking addition via subtraction or checking multiplication via division requires re-typing numbers, creating new opportunities for typing errors and cognitive fatigue.
  • The RPN Solution: The SC-6 hardware automatically preserves the value that was in Register \(X\) immediately prior to any arithmetic operation inside a dedicated hardware register called LAST x.
  • Suppose you calculate \(47 + 36 = 83\): 47 [ENTER] 36 [+] \(\implies \mathbf{83}\)
  • To verify the calculation, you simply press [f] [LASTX]:
  • The previous number (\(36\)) is recalled into Register \(X\), automatically pushing the result (\(83\)) into Register \(Y\).
  • You press [-]: $\(83 - 36 = 47\)$
  • The original starting number (\(47\)) reappears! You have independently verified your work in two keystrokes without writing down a single intermediate digit.

docs.text:

docs.title: 6.2 Three Foolproof Ways to Return to Regular Number Mode
docs.text:
Students and teachers never get "trapped" inside a visual mode. The SC-6 provides three foolproof, frictionless pathways to return immediately to standard numbers: 1. Universal [C] (Clear / Cancel) Key: Pressing [C] (Row 7, Col 1) when no digits are actively being typed instantly dismisses any active visual mode and restores Regular Number Mode ([NUM]). 2. Mode Key Toggle: Tapping the active mode key a second time acts as an immediate toggle back to Regular Number Mode (e.g. in [▦], pressing [▦] returns to numbers). 3. Number Display Keys ([g] [FIX], [f] [ALL], [FDISP]): Pressing any standard numerical formatting key immediately exits visual graphics and renders the active stack in that numerical format.

Strict Data Preservation Guarantee: Switching between visual modes and number mode is 100% non-destructive. The stack registers (\(X, Y, Z, T\)), LAST x, and continuous memory are never altered. Visual modes are simply alternative optical lenses for viewing the exact same underlying RPN stack values.

docs.title: 8. Quick-Start Adventure Showcase: 30 Things You Will Master Across K–6
docs.text:
To show you the fun, speed, and superpower clarity of Stack Math across your entire elementary math journey, here are 30 exciting hands-on adventures! Each adventure features an authentic mission, step-by-step keystrokes, a full 4-register stack trace table (\(T, Z, Y, X\)), and a pointer to the chapter where you can explore the topic in depth.

QUICK-START ADVENTURE SHOWCASE DIRECTORY

Adventures 01–05 : Grades K–1 Counting, Number Bonds & Single-Digit Addition (Explore in Chapter 03) Adventures 06–10 : Grade 2 Place Value Bundling, Doubling & Subtraction (Explore in Chapters 03 & 04) Adventures 11–15 : Grade 3 Array Multiplication & Rhythmic Skip-Counting (Explore in Chapter 04) Adventures 16–20 : Grade 4 Division with Remainder & Sharing Scenarios (Explore in Chapters 04 & 05) Adventures 21–25 : Grade 5 Fraction Arithmetic, Towers & Reduction (Explore in Chapters 05 & 06) Adventures 26–30 : Grade 6 Mixed Operations, Time & Surface Area Memory (Explore in Chapters 06, 07 & 09)

docs.title: 8.1 Adventure 01: The Ten-Frame Number Bond (Making 10)
docs.text:
• Grade Band: Kindergarten – Grade 1
  • Chapter Pointer: Chapter 03: Counting, Number Lines & Place Value Studio
  • Problem Statement: Maya has 7 red counters in her ten-frame tray. How many more blue counters does she need to fill the frame of 10?
  • Hands-On Manipulative: Place 7 red counters into the physical wooden Ten-Frame tray (fill top row of 5, then 2 in bottom row). Notice 3 empty cells.
  • Visual Sandbox Keystrokes: Press [▦], then enter 7.
  • Abstract RPN Keystrokes: 10 [ENTER] 7 [-] \(\implies \mathbf{3}\)
  • 4-Register Stack Trace Table:
Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X Operational Commentary [C] 0 0 0 0 Clean baseline stack in [NUM] mode. 10 0 0 0 10 Key target capacity (\(10\)) into Ground Floor \(X\). [ENTER] 0 0 10 10 Target capacity lifts smoothly into Mezzanine Floor \(Y\). 7 0 0 10 7 Enter red counters into Ground Floor \(X\). [-] 0 0 0 3 Subtraction combines \(Y - X = 3\). Result in \(X\)!
  • Diagnostic Checkpoint: Did you see \(Y = 10\) and \(X = 7\) before pressing [-]? If your display shows \(17\), you pressed [+] instead of [-]. Press [f] [LASTX] to recall \(7\), then press [-] twice!

docs.title: 8.2 Adventure 02: Number Line Addition (Hopping Forward)
docs.text:
• Grade Band: Grade 1
  • Chapter Pointer: Chapter 03: Counting, Number Lines & Place Value Studio
  • Problem Statement: A grasshopper sits on tick mark 6 of a number line. It makes a forward leap of 5 units. Where does it land?
  • Visual Sandbox Keystrokes: Press [f] [LINE], key 6 [ENTER] 5 [+].
  • Abstract RPN Keystrokes: 6 [ENTER] 5 [+] \(\implies \mathbf{11}\)
  • 4-Register Stack Trace Table:
Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X Operational Commentary 6 0 0 0 6 Starting coordinate entered into Ground Floor \(X\). [ENTER] 0 0 6 6 Coordinate 6 slides into Mezzanine Floor \(Y\) (start anchor). 5 0 0 6 5 Jump magnitude keyed into Ground Floor \(X\). [+] 0 0 0 11 Forward hop executes: \(6 + 5 = 11\). Stack drops cleanly.

docs.title: 8.3 Adventure 03: Seeing Groups at a Glance (5-Grouping on the Bead Rack)
docs.text:
• Grade Band: Kindergarten – Grade 1
  • Chapter Pointer: Chapter 03: Counting, Number Lines & Place Value Studio
  • Problem Statement: Show 8 beads on a Rekenrek rack. How many are dark and how many are light?
  • Visual Sandbox Keystrokes: Press [g] [COUNT], then press 8.
  • LCD Display Output: The left column shows 5 solid beads (●●●●●) and 3 light beads (○○○) slid across to the active left rail. The rest rail holds 2 light beads (○○).
  • Abstract RPN Check: Decompose 8 into \(5 + 3\): 8 [ENTER] 5 [-] \(\implies \mathbf{3}\)
  • 4-Register Stack Trace Table:
Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X Operational Commentary 8 0 0 0 8 Total beads entered into Ground Floor \(X\). [ENTER] 0 0 8 8 Total bead count lifts to Mezzanine Floor \(Y\). 5 0 0 8 5 First group of 5 dark beads keyed into \(X\). [-] 0 0 0 3 \(8 - 5 = 3\) light beads left over on the rail!

docs.title: 8.4 Adventure 04: Self-Checking Inverse Addition ([f] [LASTX])
docs.text:
• Grade Band: Grade 1 – Grade 2
  • Chapter Pointer: Chapter 02: RPN for Young Learners & Chapter 04: Whole Number Operations
  • Problem Statement: Solve \(24 + 15 = 39\). Immediately verify your result using Superpower 4 without re-entering any numbers.
  • Abstract RPN Keystrokes: 24 [ENTER] 15 [+] \(\to\) [f] [LASTX] [-]
  • 4-Register Stack Trace Table:
Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X Operational Commentary 24 [ENTER] 0 0 24 24 First number committed to Mezzanine Floor \(Y\). 15 [+] 0 0 0 39 Addition completed; LAST x preserves \(15\) in hardware. [f] [LASTX] 0 0 39 15 Prior number (\(15\)) recalled into \(X\); sum lifts to \(Y\)! [-] 0 0 0 24 Inverse check: \(39 - 15 = 24\). Starting number verified!

docs.title: 8.5 Adventure 05: Comparing Two Sets ([≠])
docs.text:
• Grade Band: Kindergarten – Grade 1
  • Chapter Pointer: Chapter 03: Counting, Number Lines & Place Value Studio
  • Problem Statement: Box A has 9 apples. Box B has 12 apples. Test whether the two boxes have the same number of apples.
  • Abstract RPN Keystrokes: 9 [ENTER] 12 [≠]
  • LCD Display Output: Screen displays NO (9 ≠ 12). Register \(X\) retains \(12\); Register \(Y\) retains \(9\).
  • Follow-Up Difference: Press [-] immediately to find the difference: $\(12 - 9 = 3 \text{ apples more in Box B!}\)$
  • 4-Register Stack Trace Table:
Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X Operational Commentary 9 0 0 0 9 Box A quantity entered into Ground Floor \(X\). [ENTER] 0 0 9 9 Box A lifts to Mezzanine Floor \(Y\). 12 0 0 9 12 Box B quantity entered into Ground Floor \(X\). [≠] 0 0 9 12 Test displays NO (9 ≠ 12); values preserved on stack. [-] 0 0 0 -3 \(12 - 9 = 3\) apples difference. Stack drops cleanly.

docs.title: 8.6 Adventure 06: Place Value Digit Extraction ([PV])
docs.text:
• Grade Band: Grade 2
  • Chapter Pointer: Chapter 03: Counting, Number Lines & Place Value Studio
  • Problem Statement: In the number \(4,520\), identify the digit occupying the hundreds place and the tens place using the hardware [PV] key.
  • Hardware Formula: \(\lfloor (|Y| \bmod (10 \times X)) / X \rfloor\)
  • Abstract RPN Keystrokes:
  • 4520 [ENTER] 100 [PV] \(\implies \mathbf{5}\) (hundreds digit)
  • 4520 [ENTER] 10 [PV] \(\implies \mathbf{2}\) (tens digit)
  • 4-Register Stack Trace Table (Hundreds Place):
Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X Operational Commentary 4520 0 0 0 4520 Full number entered into Ground Floor \(X\). [ENTER] 0 0 4520 4520 Full number lifts to Mezzanine Floor \(Y\). 10 0 0 4520 10 0 Place value target (\(100\)) entered into Ground Floor \(X\). [PV] 0 4520 10 0 Hardware extracts hundreds digit: 5 hundreds!

docs.title: 8.7 Adventure 07: Bundling Tens into Hundreds (Regrouping)
docs.text:
• Grade Band: Grade 2
  • Chapter Pointer: Chapter 03: Counting, Number Lines & Place Value Studio
  • Problem Statement: A school supply closet has 8 boxes of 10 pencils, and an educator brings in 4 more boxes of 10 pencils. How many total pencils are there?
  • RPN Keystrokes: 8 [ENTER] 4 [+] 10 [×] \(\implies \mathbf{120}\)
  • 4-Register Stack Trace Table:
Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X Operational Commentary 8 0 0 0 8 Initial 8 boxes entered into Ground Floor \(X\). [ENTER] 0 0 8 8 Box count lifts to Mezzanine Floor \(Y\). 4 0 0 8 4 Additional 4 boxes entered into Ground Floor \(X\). [+] 0 0 0 12 Total boxes calculated: \(12\) tens. 10 0 0 12 10 Pencils per box (\(10\)) entered into \(X\). [×] 0 0 0 120 \(12 \times 10 = 120\) total pencils!

docs.title: 8.8 Adventure 08: Doubling Ladders via [ENTER] [+]
docs.text:
• Grade Band: Grade 2
  • Chapter Pointer: Chapter 04: Whole Number Operations & Skip-Counting
  • Problem Statement: Generate the sequence of geometric powers of 2 starting from 1: \(1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64\).
  • RPN Keystrokes: 1 [ENTER] [+] [ENTER] [+] [ENTER] [+]
  • Mechanics: Pressing [ENTER] duplicates Register \(X\) into Register \(Y\). Pressing [+] immediately doubles the value!
  • 4-Register Stack Trace Table:
Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X Operational Commentary 1 0 0 0 1 Seed starting value \(1\) into Ground Floor \(X\). [ENTER] 0 0 1 1 Duplicate \(1\) into Mezzanine Floor \(Y\). [+] 0 0 0 2 \(1 + 1 = 2\). First doubling complete! [ENTER] 0 0 2 2 Duplicate \(2\) into Mezzanine Floor \(Y\). [+] 0 0 0 4 \(2 + 2 = 4\). Second doubling complete! [ENTER] 0 0 4 4 Duplicate \(4\) into Mezzanine Floor \(Y\). [+] 0 0 0 8 \(4 + 4 = 8\). Third doubling complete!

docs.title: 8.9 Adventure 09: Three-Digit Subtraction with Regrouping Check
docs.text:
• Grade Band: Grade 2
  • Chapter Pointer: Chapter 04: Whole Number Operations & Skip-Counting
  • Problem Statement: Calculate \(523 - 287 = 236\). Verify via [f] [LASTX] [+].
  • RPN Keystrokes:
  • 523 [ENTER] 287 [-] \(\implies \mathbf{236}\)
  • [f] [LASTX] [+] \(\implies \mathbf{523}\)
  • Verification: Adding the second number back to the difference restores the starting number (\(523\)) with zero re-typing.
  • 4-Register Stack Trace Table:
Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X Operational Commentary 523 0 0 0 523 Starting number entered into Ground Floor \(X\). [ENTER] 0 0 523 523 Starting number lifts to Mezzanine Floor \(Y\). 287 0 0 523 287 Second number entered into Ground Floor \(X\). [-] 0 0 0 236 Subtraction evaluates: \(523 - 287 = 236\). [f] [LASTX] 0 0 236 287 Superpower 4 recalls prior number (\(287\)) into \(X\)! [+] 0 0 0 523 Inverse check: \(236 + 287 = 523\) verified!

docs.title: 8.10 Adventure 10: Step-Counting by Fives (2-LV Stack Mode)
docs.text:
• Grade Band: Grade 2
  • Chapter Pointer: Chapter 02: RPN for Young Learners & Chapter 04: Whole Number Operations
  • Problem Statement: In 2-Stack mode (2-LV), configure a constant step counter of 5 starting from 0.
  • RPN Keystrokes:
  • 5 [ENTER] 0 [+] \(\implies \mathbf{5}\)
  • [+] \(\implies \mathbf{10}\), [+] \(\implies \mathbf{15}\), [+] \(\implies \mathbf{20}\), [+] \(\implies \mathbf{25}\)
  • Mechanics: In 2-stack mode, Register \(Y\) preserves the top constant (\(5\)) upon every two-number drop, creating an automatic step counter.
  • 4-Register Stack Trace Table (2-LV Mode):
Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X Operational Commentary 5 0 0 0 5 Step constant (\(5\)) entered into Ground Floor \(X\). [ENTER] 0 0 5 5 Constant lifts to Register \(Y\). 0 0 0 5 0 Starting origin (\(0\)) entered into Register \(X\). [+] 0 0 0 5 \(5 + 0 = 5\); Register \(Y\) preserves constant \(5\)! [+] 0 0 0 5 Next tap of + adds constant: \(5 + 5 = 10\). [+] 0 0 0 5 Next tap of + adds constant: \(10 + 5 = 15\). [+] 0 0 0 5 Next tap of + adds constant: \(15 + 5 = 20\).

docs.title: 8.11 Adventure 11: Array Multiplication (Rectangular Garden)
docs.text:
• Grade Band: Grade 3
  • Chapter Pointer: Chapter 04: Whole Number Operations & Skip-Counting
  • Problem Statement: A community garden has 6 rows of tomato plants with 8 plants in each row. How many total plants are in the garden?
  • Hands-On Manipulative: Build a \(6 \times 8\) grid using \(20\text{ mm}\) interlocking cubes.
  • RPN Keystrokes: 6 [ENTER] 8 [×] \(\implies \mathbf{48}\)
  • 4-Register Stack Trace Table:
Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X Operational Commentary 6 0 0 0 6 Row count entered into Ground Floor \(X\). [ENTER] 0 0 6 6 Row count lifts to Mezzanine Floor \(Y\). 8 0 0 6 8 Column count entered into Ground Floor \(X\). [×] 0 0 0 48 Array area calculates: \(6 \times 8 = 48\) total plants!

docs.title: 8.12 Adventure 12: Superpower 1 — Skip-Counting Times Tables ([g] [REP])
docs.text:
• Grade Band: Grade 3
  • Chapter Pointer: Chapter 04: Whole Number Operations & Skip-Counting
  • Problem Statement: Practice the 7-times table up to \(7 \times 10 = 70\) using Superpower 1.
  • RPN Keystrokes:
  • 7 [g] [REP]
  • Rhythmic Taps: [+] \(\to 14\), [+] \(\to 21\), [+] \(\to 28\), [+] \(\to 35\), [+] \(\to 42\), [+] \(\to 49\), [+] \(\to 56\), [+] \(\to 63\), [+] \(\to 70\)
  • 4-Register Stack Trace Table:
Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X Operational Commentary 7 0 0 0 7 Step size entered into Ground Floor \(X\). [g] [REP] 7 7 7 7 Superpower 1 replicates \(7\) across all 4 floors! [+] 7 7 7 14 \(7 + 7 = 14\) (\(2 \times 7\)); \(T\) replicates constant \(7\)! [+] 7 7 7 21 \(14 + 7 = 21\) (\(3 \times 7\)). [+] 7 7 7 28 \(21 + 7 = 28\) (\(4 \times 7\)). Rhythmic ladder climbs!

docs.title: 8.13 Adventure 13: Area of a Rectangle ([f] [RECT])
docs.text:
• Grade Band: Grade 3
  • Chapter Pointer: Chapter 06: Geometry, Surface Area & Planetary Time
  • Problem Statement: Find the area of a classroom rug measuring \(9\text{ ft}\) long by \(7\text{ ft}\) wide.
  • RPN Keystrokes: 9 [ENTER] 7 [f] [RECT]
  • Display Output: Displays AREA: 63 SQ FT. Register \(X\) holds \(63.0\).
  • 4-Register Stack Trace Table:
Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X Operational Commentary 9 0 0 0 9 Length (\(9\text{ ft}\)) entered into Ground Floor \(X\). [ENTER] 0 0 9 9 Length lifts to Mezzanine Floor \(Y\). 7 0 0 9 7 Width (\(7\text{ ft}\)) entered into Ground Floor \(X\). [f] [RECT] 0 0 0 63 Area computes: \(9 \times 7 = 63\text{ sq ft}\).

docs.title: 8.14 Adventure 14: Planetary Clock Continuous Hands ([🕒])
docs.text:
• Grade Band: Grade 3
  • Chapter Pointer: Chapter 06: Geometry, Surface Area & Planetary Time
  • Problem Statement: Display 3:30 on the analog clock face. Confirm the continuous hour hand angle.
  • RPN Keystrokes: 3.30 [🕒]
  • LCD Verification: The analog clock dial renders the minute hand pointing directly at 6 (\(180^\circ\)). The hour hand points halfway between 3 and 4 (\(105^\circ\), or \(1.8326\text{ rad}\)), confirming that the hour hand moves continuously between numbers rather than staying frozen at 3:00.
  • 4-Register Stack Trace Table:
Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X Operational Commentary 3.30 0 0 0 \(3.30\) Time string 3.30 entered into Ground Floor \(X\). [🕒] 0 0 0 \(3.3000\) Clock sandbox launches: continuous hands display!

docs.title: 8.15 Adventure 15: Unit Fraction Entry (. n . d)
docs.text:
• Grade Band: Grade 3
  • Chapter Pointer: Chapter 05: Fractions, Decimals & Proportional Towers
  • Problem Statement: Enter the unit fraction \(1/4\) into Register \(X\) and convert it to decimal format.
  • RPN Keystrokes:
  • . 1 . 4 [ENTER] \(\implies \mathbf{1/4}\)
  • [FDISP] \(\implies \mathbf{0.25}\)
  • [FDISP] \(\implies \mathbf{1/4}\)
  • 4-Register Stack Trace Table:
Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X Operational Commentary . 1 . 4 0 0 0 \(0.2500\) Two-dot notation builds fraction \(1/4\) in \(X\). [ENTER] 0 0 \(0.2500\) \(0.2500\) Fraction committed and lifts to Mezzanine Floor \(Y\). [FDISP] 0 0 \(0.2500\) \(0.25\) Instant decimal conversion: \(1/4 = 0.25\)! [FDISP] 0 0 \(0.2500\) \(0.2500\) Instant toggle back to fraction representation!

docs.title: 8.16 Adventure 16: Superpower 2 — Field Trip Bus Division ([g] [÷R])
docs.text:
• Grade Band: Grade 4
  • Chapter Pointer: Chapter 04: Operations, Skip-Counting & Number Sense
  • Problem Statement: 125 students and chaperones are going on a science museum field trip. Each school van holds 8 passengers. How many vans will be completely filled, and how many passengers will be in the final partial van?
  • RPN Keystrokes: 125 [ENTER] 8 [g] [÷R]
  • Dual-Stack Output:
  • Register \(X\): \(15\) (Quotient: 15 full vans).
  • Register \(Y\): \(5\) (Remainder: 5 passengers in the remaining van).
  • Total vans needed: \(15 + 1 = 16\text{ vans}\).
  • 4-Register Stack Trace Table:
Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X Operational Commentary 12 5 0 0 12 5 Total passengers entered into Ground Floor \(X\). [ENTER] 0 12 5 5 125 committed and copied to Mezzanine Floor \(Y\). 8 0 12 5 8 Capacity per van keyed into \(X\). [g] [÷R] 0 12 5 0 Integer division with remainder: \(X = 15\) full vans, \(Y = 5\) leftover passengers!

docs.title: 8.17 Adventure 17: Superpower 3 — Step-by-Step Fraction Simplification ([g] [SIMP])
docs.text:
• Grade Band: Grade 4
  • Chapter Pointer: Chapter 05: Fractions, Decimals & Proportional Towers
  • Problem Statement: Simplify the unreduced fraction \(12/18\) step-by-step.
  • RPN Keystrokes:
  • . 12 . 18 [ENTER] \(\implies \mathbf{12/18}\)
  • [g] [SIMP] \(\implies \mathbf{2/3}\)
  • [g] [SIMP] \(\implies\) Flashes "LOWEST TERMS", display remains \(\mathbf{2/3}\)
  • 4-Register Stack Trace Table:
Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X Operational Commentary . 12 . 1 8 0 0 12 \(8.0000\) Enter fraction \(12/18\) into Ground Floor \(X\). [ENTER] 0 12 \(8.0000\) \(8.0000\) Fraction committed to stack. [g] [SIMP] 0 12 \(8.0000\) \(8.0000\) Reduced by common factor: \(12/18\) simplifies to \(2/3\)! [g] [SIMP] 0 12 \(8.0000\) \(8.0000\) Flashes "LOWEST TERMS"; fraction is already irreducible!

docs.title: 8.18 Adventure 18: Mixed Number to Improper Fraction Conversion ([f] [d/c] / [a ᵇ/c])
docs.text:
• Grade Band: Grade 4
  • Chapter Pointer: Chapter 05: Fractions, Decimals & Proportional Towers
  • Problem Statement: A recipe calls for \(2\ 3/4\) cups of flour. Convert this quantity to an improper fraction for bulk measuring, then restore mixed notation.
  • RPN Keystrokes:
  • 2 . 3 . 4 [ENTER] \(\implies \mathbf{2\ 3/4}\)
  • [f] [d/c] \(\implies \mathbf{11/4}\)
  • [a ᵇ/c] \(\implies \mathbf{2\ 3/4}\)
  • 4-Register Stack Trace Table:
Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X Operational Commentary 2 . 3 . 4 0 0 2 \(0.7500\) Mixed number \(2\ 3/4\) keyed into Ground Floor \(X\). [ENTER] 0 2 \(0.7500\) \(0.7500\) Mixed number committed to stack. [f] [d/c] 0 2 \(0.7500\) \(0.7500\) Converted to improper fraction: \(11/4\). [a ᵇ/c] 0 2 \(0.7500\) \(0.7500\) Converted back to mixed fraction: \(2\ 3/4\).

docs.title: 8.19 Adventure 19: Currency Division with Remaining Cents
docs.text:
• Grade Band: Grade 4
  • Chapter Pointer: Chapter 04: Operations, Skip-Counting & Number Sense
  • Problem Statement: Four children earn \(\$17.50\) washing cars together. How much whole money does each child receive, and what is the remaining loose change?
  • RPN Keystrokes: 17.50 [ENTER] 4 [g] [÷R]
  • Result:
  • Register \(X\): \(\$4.00\) each.
  • Register \(Y\): \(\$1.50\) remaining change (\(37.5\text{¢}\) each when divided further).
  • 4-Register Stack Trace Table:
Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X Operational Commentary 17.50 0 0 0 \(17.50\) Total car wash earnings \(\$17.50\) entered into \(X\). [ENTER] 0 0 \(17.50\) \(17.50\) Committed and lifted to Mezzanine Floor \(Y\). 4 0 0 \(17.50\) 4 Number of children keyed into \(X\). [g] [÷R] 0 0 \(1.50\) \(4.00\) \(X = \$4.00\) whole dollars each, \(Y = \$1.50\) remaining change!

docs.title: 8.20 Adventure 20: Adding Like Denominators (Unreduced Invariant)
docs.text:
• Grade Band: Grade 4
  • Chapter Pointer: Chapter 05: Fractions, Decimals & Proportional Towers
  • Problem Statement: Calculate \(2/4 + 2/4\). Verify that the SC-6 preserves the unreduced sum of \(4/4\) before manual reduction.
  • RPN Keystrokes: . 2 . 4 [ENTER] . 2 . 4 [+]
  • Display Output: Displays 4/4 (does not auto-reduce to 1).
  • Simplification: Press [g] [SIMP] \(\implies \mathbf{1}\).
  • 4-Register Stack Trace Table:
Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X Operational Commentary . 2 . 4 0 0 0 \(0.5000\) First fraction \(2/4\) keyed into Ground Floor \(X\). [ENTER] 0 0 \(0.5000\) \(0.5000\) First fraction committed to Floor \(Y\). . 2 . 4 0 0 \(0.5000\) \(0.5000\) Second fraction \(2/4\) keyed into Ground Floor \(X\). [+] 0 0 0 \(1.0000\) Unreduced invariant preserved: displays \(4/4\)! [g] [SIMP] 0 0 0 1 Manual simplification reduces \(4/4\) to whole number \(1\)!

docs.title: 8.21 Adventure 21: Unlike Fraction Addition via LCD ([f] [LCM])
docs.text:
• Grade Band: Grade 5
  • Chapter Pointer: Chapter 05: Fractions, Decimals & Proportional Towers
  • Problem Statement: Add \(3/8 + 5/12\). Find the least common denominator using the hardware [f] [LCM] key before evaluating.
  • RPN Keystrokes (Finding LCD): 8 [ENTER] 12 [f] [LCM] \(\implies \mathbf{24}\)
  • RPN Keystrokes (Direct Sum): . 3 . 8 [ENTER] . 5 . 12 [+] \(\implies \mathbf{19/24}\)
  • 4-Register Stack Trace Table:
Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X Operational Commentary 8 [ENTER] 12 0 0 8 12 Denominators 8 and 12 loaded into stack. [f] [LCM] 0 0 0 24 Least common denominator found: \(\text{LCM}(8, 12) = 24\). . 3 . 8 0 0 24 \(0.3750\) First fraction \(3/8\) entered into \(X\). [ENTER] 0 24 \(0.3750\) \(0.3750\) Pushed to Mezzanine Floor \(Y\). . 5 . 12 0 24 \(0.3750\) \(0.4167\) Second fraction \(5/12\) entered into \(X\). [+] 0 0 24 \(0.7917\) Added with common denominator: \(3/8 + 5/12 = 19/24\)!

docs.title: 8.22 Adventure 22: Parenthesis-Free Order of Operations
docs.text:
• Grade Band: Grade 5
  • Chapter Pointer: Chapter 02: RPN for Young Learners: The Tower Elevator
  • Problem Statement: Evaluate the multi-step expression \((15 - 3) \times (4 + 2) \div 6 = 12\) without parentheses.
  • RPN Keystrokes:
  • 15 [ENTER] 3 [-] \(\implies \mathbf{12.0}\) (subtotal 1)
  • 4 [ENTER] 2 [+] \(\implies \mathbf{6.0}\) (subtotal 2)
  • [×] \(\implies \mathbf{72.0}\) (\(12 \times 6\))
  • 6 [÷] \(\implies \mathbf{12.0}\)
  • 4-Register Stack Trace Table:
Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X Operational Commentary 15 [ENTER] 3 [-] 0 0 0 12 First group evaluated: \(15 - 3 = 12\). 4 [ENTER] 2 [+] 0 0 12 6 Second group evaluated: \(4 + 2 = 6\), subtotal 1 rests safely on \(Y\)! [×] 0 0 0 72 Multiplied together: \(12 \times 6 = 72\). 6 [÷] 0 0 0 12 Divided by 6: \(72 \div 6 = 12\), zero parenthesis keys required!

docs.title: 8.23 Adventure 23: Master Surface Area via Stats Mode ([Σ+])
docs.text:
• Grade Band: Grade 5
  • Chapter Pointer: Chapter 06: Geometry, Surface Area & Planetary Time
  • Problem Statement: Find the total surface area of a rectangular wooden jewelry box measuring \(5\text{ cm}\) long, \(4\text{ cm}\) wide, and \(3\text{ cm}\) high without scratch paper.
  • Mathematical Decomposition: $\(\text{Face Pair 1 (Top/Bottom): } 2 \times (5 \times 4) = 40\text{ cm}^2\)$ $\(\text{Face Pair 2 (Front/Back): } 2 \times (5 \times 3) = 30\text{ cm}^2\)$ $\(\text{Face Pair 3 (Left/Right): } 2 \times (4 \times 3) = 24\text{ cm}^2\)$ $\(\text{Total Surface Area: } 40 + 30 + 24 = 94\text{ cm}^2\)$
  • RPN Keystrokes:
  • [g] [CLΣ]
  • 5 [ENTER] 4 [×] 2 [×] [Σ+] (\(N=1\), subtotal \(40\))
  • 5 [ENTER] 3 [×] 2 [×] [Σ+] (\(N=2\), subtotal \(30\))
  • 4 [ENTER] 3 [×] 2 [×] [Σ+] (\(N=3\), subtotal \(24\))
  • [f] [Σx] \(\implies \mathbf{94.0\text{ cm}^2}\)
  • 4-Register Stack Trace Table:
Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X Operational Commentary [g] [CLΣ] 0 0 0 0 Clear statistical registers before accumulation. 5 [ENTER] 4 [×] 2 [×] [Σ+] 0 0 0 1 Face Pair 1 (\(40\)) accumulated into \(\Sigma\). Register \(X\) shows sample count \(N=1\). 5 [ENTER] 3 [×] 2 [×] [Σ+] 0 0 0 2 Face Pair 2 (\(30\)) accumulated into \(\Sigma\). Register \(X\) shows \(N=2\). 4 [ENTER] 3 [×] 2 [×] [Σ+] 0 0 0 3 Face Pair 3 (\(24\)) accumulated into \(\Sigma\). Register \(X\) shows \(N=3\). [f] [Σx] 0 0 0 \(94.0\) Recall sum \(\Sigma x\): total surface area \(94\text{ cm}^2\) without scratch paper!

docs.title: 8.24 Adventure 24: Modulo-60 Flight Elapsed Time Arithmetic
docs.text:
• Grade Band: Grade 5
  • Chapter Pointer: Chapter 06: Geometry, Surface Area & Planetary Time
  • Problem Statement: A flight departs at 9:45 AM and has a flight duration of 2 hours and 35 minutes. Calculate the arrival time.
  • RPN Keystrokes:
  • 9.45 [f] [▸HR] \(\implies \mathbf{9.75\text{ hr}}\)
  • [ENTER]
  • 2.35 [f] [▸HR] \(\implies \mathbf{2.5833\text{ hr}}\)
  • [+] \(\implies \mathbf{12.3333\text{ hr}}\)
  • [g] [▸HMS] \(\implies \mathbf{12.20}\) (\(12:20\text{ PM}\))
  • 4-Register Stack Trace Table:
