docs.title: 1.2 Anatomy of the Instrument: Screen, Stack & Shift Keys
docs.text: Before exploring the silicon and material engineering beneath the surface, it is essential to understand the operational anatomy of the StackCalc SC-32 as a tactile calculating instrument. Unlike algebraic calculators that obscure calculations behind scrolling textual formula lines, parentheses, and hidden operator precedence hierarchies, the SC-32 provides continuous, physical visibility into every intermediate value through its four-register operational stack and tri-state key matrix.

docs.title: 1.2.1 The Transflective Graphic Display & The 4 Operational Registers (\(T, Z, Y, X\))
docs.text:
The transflective graphic liquid-crystal display is optically bonded beneath non-glare mineral glass, rendering four dedicated numerical shelves that correspond 1-to-1 with the four operational registers of the RPN engine (Cochran, 1972; HP, 1982):

Stack Register Display Shelf Readout Operational Architecture & Role \(T\) 0.000000000000 Top of stack; replicates downward on dyadic drop for constant calculations \(Z\) 0.000000000000 Intermediate storage shelf; holds nested sub-totals without memory registers \(Y\) 0.000000000000 Staged operand register; paired with \(X\) during two-variable operations (\(Y - X, Y \div X\)) \(X\) 0.000000000000 Primary working register; displays keyed digits and immediate function results
  • Register \(X\) (Primary Working Register & Active Display): The ground floor of the stack. When you type numerical digits, they accumulate directly in Register \(X\). Every single-variable (monadic) function (such as [SIN], [LN], [√x], or [1/x]) executes immediately in place upon the value in Register \(X\), preserving the higher registers unchanged.
  • Register \(Y\) (Staged Operand Register): The second level of the stack. Register \(Y\) holds the prior operand, ready to be paired with Register \(X\) when a two-variable (dyadic) operator ([+], [-], [×], [÷], [yˣ]) is pressed. In non-commutative operations, the operand in Register \(Y\) is the dividend or minuend (\(Y - X\) or \(Y \div X\)).
  • Register \(Z\) (Intermediate Storage Register): The third level of the stack. During chained, nested expressions, Register \(Z\) holds intermediate sub-totals without requiring memory register assignment (STO / RCL) or scratch paper.
  • Register \(T\) (Top of Stack & Constant Factor Pipeline): The uppermost operational shelf. When a dyadic operation combines Registers \(Y\) and \(X\), the stack drops: Register \(Z\) drops to \(Y\), and Register \(T\) drops to \(Z\). Crucially, Register \(T\) preserves its contents and replicates downward. This classic architectural feature allows an engineer to load a conversion factor or physical constant into \(T\) and apply it repeatedly across successive data points without re-entering the number.

docs.title: 1.2.2 The ENTER Key: Stack Lift Automaton
docs.text:
The large central [ENTER] key is the heartbeat of RPN calculation. It performs three synchronized actions in a single machine cycle (HP, 1991): 1. Terminates Number Entry: It signals to the input parser that the current number in Register \(X\) is complete. 2. Executes Stack Lift: It copies the contents of Register \(X\) into Register \(Y\), while simultaneously lifting the previous contents of Register \(Y\) into \(Z\), and Register \(Z\) into \(T\) (the previous contents of Register \(T\) are overwritten). 3. Disables Stack Lift on Next Digit: It arms an internal state machine flag so that the very next digit keyed by the user immediately overwrites Register \(X\) rather than lifting the stack again.

Because dyadic operators (+, -, ×, ÷) evaluate immediately on the contents of \(Y\) and \(X\) and replace \(X\) with the result, there is no = key on the SC-32. Combining numbers is the answer.

docs.title: 1.2.3 The 43-Key Tri-State Topology: Direct, Left Shift [↰], and Right Shift [↱]
docs.text:
The physical keyboard consists of 43 laser micro-foamed snap-dome keys organized into an ergonomic 6-row by 7-column matrix (plus a wide [ENTER] bar). Rather than forcing users to navigate nested LCD menus during time-critical calculations, the SC-32 maps 129 direct scientific and engineering primitives across three primary operational planes:

  • Primary Key Face (Direct Keypress): Printed in high-contrast white on the keycap face. Provides instant, single-stroke access to digits 0–9, fundamental arithmetic operators ([+], [-], [×], [÷]), [ENTER], backspace [<-], clear [C], and primary scientific primitives ([SIN], [COS], [TAN], [LN], [eˣ], [√x], [1/x], [yˣ]).
  • Left Shift [↰] (Row 5, Col 0): Activates inverse trigonometric functions (ASIN, ACOS, ATAN), exponential complements (10ˣ, LOG), powers and roots (x², ˣ√y), factorial (x!), complex evaluation (CMPLX), display modes (FIX, SCI, ENG, ALL), and mantissa inspection (SHOW).
  • Right Shift [↱] (Row 6, Col 0): Activates advanced numerical solvers and hardware modes: Richard Brent's root finder (SOLVE), Romberg numerical quadrature (∫), the polynomial root extractor (POLY), function curve tracing (PLOT), polar/rectangular vector conversions (→POL, →REC), stack roll manipulation (x⇄y, R↓, R↑), prior-argument recovery (LASTX), and power-off (OFF).

docs.title: 1.3 Dual-Core Silicon Architecture & Cold-Boot Dynamics
docs.text:
The computational engine of the StackCalc SC-32 is built upon a dedicated dual-core embedded 32-bit microcontroller, a high-performance, low-power processing architecture featuring twin ARM Cortex-M33 cores clocked symmetrically at 150 MHz.

Unlike consumer graphing calculators that rely on general-purpose microprocessors burdened by Linux operating systems, complex virtual memory managers, and non-deterministic background daemons, the SC-32 operates as a bare-metal, deterministic scientific instrument.

Subsystem Component Hardware Allocation Clock / Bus Rate Primary Functional Responsibilities Core 0: Computation Engine ARM Cortex-M33 (32-bit RISC) 150 MHz Embedded Swift RPN kernel, Brent's root finder, Romberg quadrature, IEEE-754 transcendentals Core 1: Real-Time I/O ARM Cortex-M33 (32-bit RISC) 150 MHz 200 Hz eager matrix key scanner, debounce automaton, 8.0 MHz SPI display bus driver, power monitor On-Chip SRAM 520 KiB Multi-Bank RAM System Bus 64 KiB tightly coupled data RAM, 350 KiB heap (stack & history), 106 KiB dual-core shared buffers Non-Volatile QSPI Flash 4 MiB High-Speed Flash 66 MHz QSPI 3.936 MiB firmware & vector font bitmaps, 64 KiB continuous ping-pong state slots

docs.title: 1.3.1 Symmetric Task Partitioning
docs.text: The twin processing cores divide system responsibilities with zero thread contention: * Core 0 (Computational Engine): Dedicated strictly to mathematical evaluation, RPN stack mechanics, arbitrary precision floating-point algorithms, polynomial root extraction, numerical quadrature, and bivariate regression. Core 0 executes the deterministic Embedded Swift runtime (RPNCore), where arithmetic operations are compiled into direct machine code with soft-float whole-module optimization. * Core 1 (Real-Time I/O Subsystem): Operates as an independent peripheral controller. It continuously scans the 43-key matrix at a 200 Hz frame rate, manages the eager debounce state machine, and drives the high-speed 8.0 MHz SPI display bus to refresh the transflective LCD. Because Core 1 handles display rendering and keyboard polling asynchronously, long-running numerical operations on Core 0 (such as a 64-step Romberg integral) never cause keystroke drops or stuttering display updates.

docs.title: 1.3.2 Sub-5-Millisecond Cold Boot
docs.text:
Traditional graphing calculators require between 5 and 15 seconds to boot a bulky software stack. In contrast, the SC-32 achieves an instantaneous sub-5-millisecond cold boot:

  1. \(T + 0.00\text{ ms}\) (Power-On Reset): POR triggers on keypress; internal 3.3V low-dropout regulator rail stabilizes.
  2. \(T + 0.45\text{ ms}\) (Clock Synchronization): Main crystal oscillator locks; system Phase-Locked Loop (PLL) accelerates to 150 MHz.
  3. \(T + 1.20\text{ ms}\) (Core 0 Initialization): Core 0 initializes the vector table, configures memory protection, and maps the 520 KiB SRAM array.
  4. \(T + 2.10\text{ ms}\) (Display Subsystem Release): Core 1 initializes the 8.0 MHz SPI bus master and deasserts the transflective LCD hardware reset line.
  5. \(T + 3.40\text{ ms}\) (Continuous Memory Verification): The non-volatile storage engine computes and verifies the 32-bit FNV-1a checksum of the active flash ping-pong slot (Slot A or Slot B).
  6. \(T + 4.10\text{ ms}\) (Stack & Register Restoration): All four operational stack registers (\(X, Y, Z, T\)), LASTX, user registers \(A\dots Z\), statistical accumulators, and equation buffers are restored into SRAM.
  7. \(T + 4.85\text{ ms}\) (Frame Refresh & Keypad Arming): The LCD frame buffer is refreshed with the restored stack image, and the 200 Hz eager key matrix scanner is armed. Total elapsed cold boot: \(4.85\text{ ms}\).

Pressing [C] from power-off instantly awakens the calculator. The display illuminates with your exact prior stack, variables, and mode settings, ready for high-speed calculation without delay.

docs.title: 1.3.3 Power Management & Battery Budget
docs.text:
The SC-32 is engineered for extreme power efficiency, operating for 6 to 12 months on a single standard CR2032 3V lithium coin cell (\(3.0\text{ V}\), \(225\text{ mAh}\) nominal). In compliance with postal hazardous materials and consumer safety regulations (Reese's Law), units ship with the coin cell omitted; standard CR2032 cells are readily available locally.

Operating Mode Active Subsystems System Clock Current Draw Typical Endurance Active Calculation Dual Cores running, math solvers active 150 MHz \(18.2\text{ mA}\) 25 hours continuous heavy computation Idle Typing Display active, keyboard polling at 200 Hz 48 MHz \(4.8\text{ mA}\) 95 hours active classroom use Standby Pause Screen static, keyboard interrupt armed 12 MHz \(850\,\mu\text{A}\) 530 hours standby Deep Sleep (Off) Transflective LCD static, low-power oscillator 32.768 kHz \(11.8\,\mu\text{A}\) 18+ months shelf life

The battery discharge curve remains exceptionally flat throughout 90% of the coin cell's life, transitioning from \(3.0\text{ V}\) down to \(2.2\text{ V}\). An internal analog-to-digital converter (ADC) samples the power rail through a precision voltage divider every 60 seconds. When battery voltage reaches \(2.15\text{ V}\), a low-battery annunciator ([BAT]) illuminates on the top status line, providing approximately 10 hours of advance warning before the brownout protection circuit safely commits all state to non-volatile flash memory and suspends execution.

[!WARNING] COIN CELL BATTERY INGESTION HAZARD (REESE'S LAW / 16 CFR PART 1263): This instrument uses a CR2032 \(3.0\,\text{V}\) lithium coin cell battery. DEATH or serious injury can occur if ingested. A swallowed button or coin cell battery can cause Internal Chemical Burns in as little as 2 hours. KEEP new and used batteries OUT OF REACH of children. Always secure the dovetail service cover and M2 retention screws before use. Seek immediate medical attention if a battery is suspected to be swallowed or inserted inside any part of the body (U.S. National Battery Ingestion Hotline: 1-800-498-8666).

docs.title: 1.4.1 The Strict "Zero White Enclosures" Rule
docs.text: In adherence to professional laboratory and flight deck standards, the SC-32 strictly prohibits white exterior enclosures: 1. Chemical Resistance: White thermoplastics are rapidly degraded, yellowed, and stained by skin oils, isopropyl alcohol, flux removers, and common bench chemicals. 2. Optical Glare: Under harsh overhead laboratory fluorescent lights or direct outdoor sunlight, white bezels generate high-angle specular glare that impairs visual focus on the display. 3. Contrast Optimization: A dark chassis provides an immediate, high-contrast visual frame that accentuates the light transflective LCD screen and the stark-white laser-foamed keycap legends. 4. Classroom Segregation: White polymers (such as archival white PLA and PETG) are strictly quarantined to classroom STEM manipulatives (such as Fraction Towers and Ten-Frame trays); all handheld calculator bodies are constructed from dark technical polymers.

docs.title: 1.4.2 Physical Geometry & Mechanical CAD
docs.text:
The physical dimensions of the SC-32 have been precision-engineered for balanced single-handed palm retention and absolute benchtop stability:

  • Printed Circuit Board (PCB): \(72.0\text{ mm}\) width \(\times 142.4\text{ mm}\) length \(\times 1.6\text{ mm}\) thickness. 4-layer FR4 construction with a matte black solder mask and Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold (ENIG) surface finish for corrosion-proof contact pads.
  • Chassis Outer Footprint: \(80.0\text{ mm}\) width \(\times 148.0\text{ mm}\) length.
  • Ergonomic Planar Incline: The chassis profile measures \(16.0\text{ mm}\) in thickness at the upper display envelope and tapers down to \(11.9\text{ mm}\) at the lower keypad base. This produces a built-in \(1.60857^\circ\) planar tilt angle, aligning the LCD screen perpendicular to the user's line of sight when resting flat upon a work table.
  • Fastener Torque Specifications: The faceplate and lower tub are assembled using six M2.5 \(\times 8\text{ mm}\) black-oxide socket head cap screws driven into ultrasonic heat-set brass threaded inserts at a calibrated tightening torque of \(0.28\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}\).
  • Drop Durability: The combination of internal perimeter gussets (\(2.4\text{ mm}\) wall thickness) and an elastomeric TPU 95A perimeter bumper ensures structural integrity through repeated \(1.2\text{-meter}\) drops onto reinforced industrial concrete.

docs.title: 1.6 1064nm Infrared Fiber Laser Micro-Foaming Physics & Photothermal Kinetics
docs.text:
All physical legends on the SC-32 keycaps, bezel borders, and faceplate annunciators are permanently marked using a pulsed 1064nm near-infrared fiber laser.

Physics of 1064nm Infrared Laser Micro-Foaming

Optical Energy Delivery: A pulsed 1064nm Nd:YVO4/fiber laser delivers 1.2W peak power focused down to a 35 μm spot. Subsurface Gas Nucleation: Near-IR photons penetrate the outer smooth technical polymer (surface roughness $R_a < 0.4\,\mu\text{m}$) and are absorbed at a depth of $50\text{--}100\,\mu\text{m}$. Rapid photothermal heating vaporizes trace foaming agents into $10\text{--}20\,\mu\text{m}$ spherical micro-cavities. Omnidirectional Mie Scattering: When ambient photons strike these microscopic subsurface gaseous voids, refractive index contrast ($n=1.54$ polymer vs. $n=1.00$ gas) triggers complete Mie scattering, creating an indelible chalk-white legend with zero surface ablation.

docs.title: 1.6.1 The Subsurface Foaming Mechanism
docs.text:
Traditional pad printing, silk screening, and UV-curable inkjet printing deposit a thin film of ink on top of the plastic. Within months of heavy typing, finger oils and friction wear the ink away.

The SC-32 employs an advanced photothermal process known as subsurface laser micro-foaming: 1. Near-IR Absorption: The laser produces short pulses (pulse width \(\tau = 100\text{ ns}\)) at a pulse repetition frequency between \(20\text{ kHz}\) and \(80\text{ kHz}\) at a wavelength of \(\lambda = 1064\text{ nm}\). The beam focuses to a precision spot diameter of \(35\,\mu\text{m}\). 2. Localized Subsurface Heating: The near-IR photons pass through the outermost polymer layer and are absorbed by carbon black pigments approximately \(50\text{--}100\,\mu\text{m}\) below the surface. 3. Controlled Gas Evolution: Rapid thermal excitation briefly melts a micro-volume of polymer, vaporizing trace foaming additives to create spherical micro-cavities (\(10\text{--}20\,\mu\text{m}\) diameter) without puncturing or ablating the smooth outer surface. 4. Mie Optical Scattering: When ambient light enters these trapped gaseous micro-voids, the sharp refractive index boundary between the polymer matrix (\(n \approx 1.54\)) and the gas inside the cavity (\(n \approx 1.00\)) causes omnidirectional Mie scattering. The scattered light reflects all visible wavelengths equally, generating an indelible, brilliant chalk-white legend.

docs.title: 1.6.2 Photothermal Kinetics & Optimal Fluence Regimes
docs.text:
The high-contrast legends of the SC-32 keycaps rely on exact photothermal control during laser processing:

Fluence Regime Radiant Energy Range Polymer Reaction Visual & Mechanical Result Thermal Ablation \(> 4.5\text{ J/cm}^2\) Surface vaporization & carbon charring Rough surface, scorched gray/black mark; unserviceable Optimal Micro-Foaming \(2.5\text{--}4.5\text{ J/cm}^2\) Subsurface gaseous void nucleation Pure chalk-white 15.2:1 AAA mark; smooth \(R_a < 0.4\,\mu\text{m}\) Sub-Threshold Regime \(< 2.5\text{ J/cm}^2\) Insufficient photothermal rise No gas evolution; plastic remains unmarked dark substrate

The radiant energy delivered per unit area is defined as fluence \(F\): $\(F = \frac{E_{\text{pulse}}}{\pi w_0^2} = \frac{P_{\text{avg}}}{f_{\text{rep}} \cdot \pi w_0^2} \quad \left[\frac{\text{J}}{\text{cm}^2}\right]\)$ where: * \(P_{\text{avg}} = 1.20\text{ W}\): Average laser output power. * \(f_{\text{rep}} = 35,000\text{ Hz}\) (\(35\text{ kHz}\)): Pulse repetition rate. * \(w_0 = 17.5\,\mu\text{m} = 1.75 \times 10^{-3}\text{ cm}\): Gaussian beam focal spot radius.

Evaluating on the SC-32 stack yields: $\(E_{\text{pulse}} = \frac{1.20}{35000} \approx 3.4286 \times 10^{-5}\text{ J} = 34.29\,\mu\text{J}\)$ $\(\text{Area} = \pi (1.75 \times 10^{-3})^2 \approx 9.6211 \times 10^{-6}\text{ cm}^2\)$ $\(F = \frac{3.4286 \times 10^{-5}}{9.6211 \times 10^{-6}} \approx 3.5636\text{ J/cm}^2\)$ This places the operational point squarely within the optimal micro-foaming window (\(2.5\text{--}4.5\text{ J/cm}^2\)), guaranteeing pure chalk-white legends with zero surface ablation.

docs.title: 1.6.3 Optical & Mechanical Testing
docs.text:
• Contrast Ratio: Measured via a spectrophotometer at a 15.2:1 AAA Champion contrast ratio against Midnight Navy and Space Gray backgrounds, comfortably exceeding ISO 9241-303 ergonomic legibility requirements.
  • CIE Color Coordinates: The foamed legend achieves a lightness rating of \(L^* \ge 88.0\), \(a^* = -0.4\), \(b^* = 1.2\), providing pure white visibility under both yellow incandescent light and harsh blue daylight.

docs.title: 1.7.1 Snap-Dome Mechanics
docs.text: Beneath each keycap sits a custom four-legged stainless-steel snap-dome: * Actuation Force: Calibrated to \(3.92\text{ N}\) (\(400\text{ grams}\)). This substantial actuation threshold prevents accidental keypresses when resting fingers across the keypad. * Actuation Travel: \(0.80\text{ mm}\) downward travel before bottoming out. * Snap Ratio: \(62\%\) snap ratio (\(\frac{F_{\text{peak}} - F_{\text{contact}}}{F_{\text{peak}}}\)), providing an unambiguous mechanical and acoustic click that confirms entry long before visual feedback registers. * Schottky Diode Isolation: Every switch is isolated by a dedicated 1N4148 or BAT54 Schottky diode, preventing electrical "ghosting" or phantom keystrokes when multiple keys are held simultaneously during high-speed contest entry.

docs.title: 1.7.2 The Eager Debounce Engine
docs.text:
Conventional debounce firmware waits 20 to 50 milliseconds after an electrical contact closure before validating the keystroke, adding frustrating input latency.

The SC-32 implements an Eager Debounce Engine running on Core 1: 1. 0 ms Actuation Latency: On the initial rising edge transition of any matrix cross-point (\(0 \to 1\)), the key event is dispatched immediately to Core 0's RPN execution queue. 2. 20 ms Lockout Window: Following immediate dispatch, Core 1 ignores all subsequent contact chatter and rebound oscillations on that switch coordinate for a continuous 20 ms window. 3. Release Confirmation: The key is marked as released only after the matrix line indicates an open circuit across two consecutive 5 ms scan frames after the lockout window expires.

This architecture enables championship competitors to burst-type at speeds exceeding 15 keystrokes per second without dropped inputs or double-digit bounces.

docs.title: 1.8 High-Contrast Transflective Graphic LCD Architecture & Optical Physics
docs.text:
The SC-32 visual subsystem features a high-density \(132 \times 65\) pixel monochrome dot-matrix liquid crystal display module in an ERC12864-1 envelope:

docs.title: 1.8.2 Transflective Ambient-Light Performance & Luminance Physics
docs.text:
The display incorporates film-compensated Super Twisted Nematic (FSTN) liquid crystals providing sharp, high-contrast black pixels with wide viewing angles (\(+60^\circ / -60^\circ\) horizontal, \(+40^\circ / -50^\circ\) vertical). In direct sunlight or under bright desk lamps, incoming photons traverse the liquid crystal cells, reflect off the rear transflector, and pass back through to the eye. Consequently, the brighter the ambient light, the crisper and more legible the display appears. There is zero washed-out screen glare, zero high-drain LED backlight power consumption during daytime operation, and zero eye fatigue.

The total perceived luminance \(L_{\text{total}}\) of the display is governed by the superposition of reflected ambient illumination and transmitted backlight luminance: $\(L_{\text{total}} = R \cdot E_{\text{ambient}} + T \cdot L_{\text{backlight}}\)$ where: * \(R = 0.55\): Reflectance coefficient of the rear transflective polymer matrix. * \(E_{\text{ambient}}\): Ambient illuminance in lux (\(\text{lm/m}^2\)). * \(T = 0.45\): Transmittance coefficient for rear-illuminated photons. * \(L_{\text{backlight}}\): Active backlight luminance (typically \(0\text{ cd/m}^2\) during daytime to preserve battery power).

Under direct outdoor sunlight (\(E_{\text{ambient}} \approx 80,000\text{ lux}\)), the reflected luminance reaches: $\(L_{\text{total}} = 0.55 \times \frac{80,000}{\pi} \approx 14,000\text{ cd/m}^2\)$ This provides stark, paper-like legibility without consuming a single microwatt of active backlighting power!

docs.title: 1.9 Dual-Slot Ping-Pong Continuous Flash Memory (NVM)
docs.text:
The SC-32 provides true non-volatile Continuous Memory. When the calculator turns off, enters deep sleep, or has its batteries removed during replacement, your entire calculation state is preserved.

Figure 1.3: Tool-free sliding dovetail battery door providing instantaneous coin cell service while continuous memory preserves all stack registers. Flash Memory Parameter Allocation / Setting Operational Reliability Mechanism Base QSPI Address 0x3F0000 (Top 64 KiB of Flash) Dedicated wear-leveled sector region isolated from code Slot A Allocation Sectors 1008–1015 (32 KiB) Holds serialized state: Magic 0x5743324D, Seq Counter, CRC Slot B Allocation Sectors 1016–1023 (32 KiB) Mirrored ping-pong alternate; active slot has higher valid seq Integrity Algorithm 32-bit FNV-1a Hash Checksum Validated on every boot; invalid CRC forces automatic fallback Endurance Rating 200,000 ping-pong erase cycles Over 27 years of lifetime under 20 full power-downs daily

docs.title: 1.9.1 Ping-Pong Power-Loss Immunity
docs.text: To guarantee absolute protection against data corruption, the memory system utilizes a dual-slot ping-pong architecture across the upper 64 KiB of QSPI Flash: 1. Magic Header: Every state record begins with the 4-byte signature 0x5743324D ("WC2M"). 2. FNV-1a 32-Bit Hash Checksum: The entire serialized state payload is hashed using the Fowler-Noll-Vo 32-bit algorithm: $\(\text{hash} \leftarrow 2166136261\)$ $\(\text{For each byte } b: \quad \text{hash} \leftarrow (\text{hash} \oplus b) \times 16777619\)$ 3. Monotonic Sequence Increment: Each save increments a 32-bit sequence counter. On boot, the firmware inspects both Slot A and Slot B: * It calculates the FNV-1a checksum of each slot. * If both slots have valid magic headers and intact checksums, the slot with the higher sequence counter is loaded into SRAM. * If a sudden battery disconnection occurred mid-write, the interrupted slot's checksum fails, and the system automatically falls back to the previous intact slot with zero data corruption. 4. Flash Endurance & Longevity: The high-speed QSPI flash is rated for 100,000 erase/write cycles per sector. Because writes alternate between Slot A and Slot B, the system supports 200,000 full state saves. An engineer performing 20 manual power-downs every single day will operate the memory safely for over 27 years without sector wear-out.

docs.title: 1.10 Diagnostic Checkpoints & Self-Test Protocols
docs.text:
For classroom instructors, homeschoolers, and lab technicians, the SC-32 provides built-in hardware diagnostic routines:

Diagnostic Checkpoint 1.1: Power Rail & Battery Inspection To verify internal battery voltage: 1. Press [↰] followed by [↱] [FLAGS]. 2. Use the arrow keys [↓] to navigate to SYSTEM INFO. 3. Verify that VBAT displays between 2.70V and 3.05V (for fresh coin cells) or 3.60V to 4.20V (for LiPo). If VBAT reads below \(2.20\text{ V}\), install fresh CR2032 cells to avoid unexpected shutdowns.

Diagnostic Checkpoint 1.2: 43-Key Matrix Continuity Test To confirm that all snap-domes and Schottky diodes are functioning with zero electrical contact bounce: 1. Power off the calculator. 2. Press and hold [ENTER] and press [C]. 3. The display enters KEYPAD TEST mode, showing a graphic representation of the 8 × 6 matrix. 4. Press each key sequentially from top-left to bottom-right; each box will invert on the display with an audible click confirmation.

Diagnostic Checkpoint 1.3: Display Contrast Adjustment 1. Press [↰] followed by [CONTRAST]. 2. Press [+] to darken pixel contrast for bright outdoor environments, or [-] to lighten contrast for shaded indoor desks. The setting is automatically saved to non-volatile continuous memory.

docs.title: 1.11.1 CR2032 Internal Impedance & Peukert Derating
docs.text:
The nominal capacity of a CR2032 lithium-manganese dioxide (\(\text{Li/MnO}_2\)) coin cell is rated at \(225\text{ mAh}\) under a continuous light load (\(0.2\text{ mA}\)). When subjected to active calculation bursts (\(18.2\text{ mA}\) at \(150\text{ MHz}\)), the cell's internal impedance \(R_{\text{int}}\) increases non-linearly: $\(R_{\text{int}}(DOD) = R_0 + k \cdot \left(\frac{DOD}{1 - DOD}\right)\)$ where \(R_0 \approx 15\,\Omega\) for fresh cells and \(DOD\) is the depth of discharge (\(0.0 \le DOD < 1.0\)).

To prevent voltage sag below the \(2.10\text{ V}\) brownout threshold during high-speed Romberg integration bursts, the power rail incorporates an array of low-ESR ceramic decoupling capacitors (\(3 \times 22\,\mu\text{F}\) X7R) acting as an energy reservoir, supplying instantaneous pulse current without stressing the high-impedance lithium chemistry.

docs.title: 1.12 Engineering Design Briefing: The Semiconductor Cleanroom & Avionics Stress Chamber (Problems 1.1 through 1.25)
docs.text:
Mastery of scientific instrumentation requires understanding the physical principles of the hardware itself. In this engineering expedition, you step into the role of a hardware reliability engineer qualifying the SC-32 for extreme field service. From calculating coin cell longevity under mixed duty cycles to auditing optical reflectance in direct sunlight, every problem deconstructs the physical reality of the instrument in your hands.

Inside-Out Stack Architecture: Algebraic Trap vs. RPN Shortcut — Hardware Energy Budgets & Multi-Rail Power Envelopes

The Algebraic Parenthesis Trap: When qualifying an embedded instrument for field service, an avionics or reliability engineer must integrate multi-term power budgets across heterogeneous operating duty cycles *([Horowitz & Hill, 2015](appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-horowitz2015))*:

Q_daily = ( 18.2 * 0.5 ) + ( 4.8 * 1.5 ) + ( 0.85 * 2.0 ) + ( 0.0118 * 20.0 )

On an algebraic calculator, evaluating this sum forces the engineer to manage four separate sets of parenthesis pairs or continuously write down intermediate values onto scratch paper. If a field technician misses a single closing parenthesis or accidentally clears the display halfway through the four-term entry, the entire multi-rail integration must be restarted from the beginning, introducing transcription latency and operational error *([Miller, 1956](appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-miller1956); [Sweller, 1988](appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-sweller1988))*.

The RPN Stack Shortcut: On the StackCalc SC-32, hardware energy equations resolve from the inside out with zero parentheses and zero scratchpad memory *([HP, 1982](appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-hp15c1982); [HP, 1991](appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-hp32sii1991))*. The engineer keys current and duration for the first state, multiplies in place ($18.2 \times 0.5 = 9.10\text{ mAh}$), enters the second rail, multiplies, and taps [+]. The running total accumulates continuously in Register $X$. Intermediate sub-rail totals remain visible in Registers $Y, Z, T$, enabling instant verification of each subsystem's contribution before committing the final battery lifetime division.

If Core 1 scans the matrix at \(f_{\text{scan}} = 200\text{ Hz}\) (\(T_{\text{frame}} = 5.0\text{ ms}\)) with a \(20\text{ ms}\) lockout window, calculate the safety margin ratio: $\(M = \frac{T_{\text{lockout}}}{t_{\text{bounce}}}\)$

Step-by-Step RPN Reasoning & Stack Dynamics: 1. The stack drops, leaving safety margin \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{4.1667})\) in Register \(X\)—proving the switch settles four times faster than the lockout cutoff without requiring scratchpad storage.

docs.title: 1.12.4 Problem 1.4: 8.0 MHz SPI Display Bus Refresh Frame Latency
docs.text:
Computer Engineering Context: The \(132 \times 65\) dot-matrix LCD requires 9 command bytes and 1,056 display RAM data bytes (\(8 \text{ pages} \times 132 \text{ columns}\)). Calculate transmission time at \(f_{\text{SPI}} = 8.0\text{ MHz}\) (\(1\text{ bit} = 125\text{ ns}\)): $\(T_{\text{frame}} = \frac{(9 + 1056) \times 8\text{ bits}}{8.0 \times 10^6\text{ bits/s}}\)$

Keystrokes: 1065 [ENTER] 8 [×] 8 [E] 6 [÷] 1000 [×]\(\to \mathbf{1.065\text{ ms}}\).

Named RPN Stack Idiom: The x⇄y Denominator Flip & Bus Bandwidth Pipeline — Scale payload bit count directly in the stack, divide by transmission clock frequency, and convert to milliseconds with zero intermediate storage (Horowitz & Hill, 2015).

The stack drops, evaluating peak instantaneous spark current \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{5.3333}\text{ A})\) directly—explaining why dedicated TVS diodes guard all external I/O pins.

docs.title: 1.12.23 Problem 1.23: Keypad Matrix Phantom Key Sneak Current Analysis
docs.text:
Circuit Design Context: Three keys are pressed simultaneously forming three corners of a rectangle in a matrix without diodes. With row pull-up \(R_{\text{pu}} = 10\text{ k}\Omega\) to \(3.3\text{ V}\), trace the sneak path current that causes a false "ghost" key: $\(I_{\text{sneak}} = \frac{V_{\text{cc}}}{R_{\text{pu}} + 3 R_{\text{contact}}} \approx \frac{3.3}{10000} = 0.33\text{ mA}\)$ Because Schottky diodes are placed in series with every keycap in the SC-32, the reverse-biased diode blocks sneak current completely (\(I_{\text{leak}} < 0.1\,\mu\text{A}\)), providing 100% anti-ghosting rollover.

Step-by-Step RPN Reasoning & Stack Dynamics: 1. Keying 3.3 [ENTER] 10000 [÷] loads logic supply potential (\(3.3\text{ V}\)) into Register \(Y\) and divides by row pull-up resistance (\(10,000\,\Omega\)). The stack drops, resolving the unmitigated sneak current \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{3.3000 \times 10^{-4}}\text{ A} = 0.33\text{ mA})\) in Register \(X\).

docs.title: 1.12.24 Problem 1.24: Ambient Light Sensor ADC Resolution and Lux Mapping
docs.text:
Sensor Interface Context: An ambient light photodiode produces current \(I_{\text{photo}} = 0.25\,\mu\text{A} / 100\text{ lux}\) through transimpedance resistor \(R_f = 2.4\text{ M}\Omega\). The 12-bit ADC (\(4096\text{ counts}\)) measures against a \(3.30\text{ V}\) reference. Calculate lux per ADC count: $\(V_{\text{out}} = I_{\text{photo}} \cdot R_f = \left(\frac{0.25 \times 10^{-6}\text{ A}}{100\text{ lux}}\right) \times 2.4 \times 10^6\,\Omega = 0.0060\text{ V/lux} = 6.0\text{ mV/lux}\)$ $\(V_{\text{LSB}} = \frac{3.30\text{ V}}{4096} \approx 0.80566\text{ mV}\)$ $\(\text{Resolution} = \frac{V_{\text{LSB}}}{0.0060\text{ V/lux}} = \frac{0.80566}{6.0} \approx \mathbf{0.1343\text{ lux/count}}.\)$

Step-by-Step RPN Reasoning & Stack Dynamics: 1. Keying 3.3 [ENTER] 4096 [÷] evaluates 12-bit ADC voltage step \(V_{\text{LSB}} = 8.0566 \times 10^{-4}\text{ V}\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: 8.0566 \times 10^{-4})\). 2. Striking 0.006 [÷] divides by the transimpedance transfer factor (\(6.0\text{ mV/lux}\)), resolving optical measurement resolution \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{0.1343}\text{ lux/count})\) directly.

docs.title: 1.12.25 Problem 1.25: Chassis Thermal Equilibrium Temperature Rise
docs.text:
Thermodynamics Context: At full continuous 150 MHz dual-core computation, the board dissipates \(P = 60.0\text{ mW} = 0.060\text{ W}\). The chassis has total heat radiating area \(A = 0.024\text{ m}^2\) with natural convection heat transfer coefficient \(h_c = 6.5\text{ W/m}^2\text{K}\): $\(\Delta T = \frac{P}{h_c \cdot A}\)$

Keystrokes: 0.060 [ENTER] 6.5 [ENTER] 0.024 [×] [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 0.3846\(\text{ K} \approx 0.38^\circ\text{C}\).

Step-by-Step RPN Reasoning & Stack Dynamics: 1. Keying 0.060 [ENTER] 6.5 [ENTER] 0.024 [×] loads continuous thermal dissipation (\(0.060\text{ W}\)) into \(Z\) and evaluates convection conductance \(h_c A = 0.1560\text{ W/K}\) in Register \(X\) \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0600, X: 0.1560)\). 2. Striking [÷] divides dissipation by conductance, determining steady-state equilibrium temperature rise \((T: 0.0000, Z: 0.0000, Y: 0.0000, X: \mathbf{0.3846}\text{ K} \approx 0.38^\circ\text{C})\)—proving the chassis remains cool to the touch with zero throttling.

docs.title: 1.13.1 Physical Hardware Determinism & Tactile Switch Dynamics
docs.text:
In laboratory metrology and precision engineering, calculating devices must behave with absolute physical determinism. Rather than mushy conductive-rubber membranes that produce variable contact resistance and bounce times exceeding \(15\text{ ms}\), the SC-32 employs 400-gram nickel-plated stainless-steel snap-domes seated over Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold (ENIG) contact pads. The force-displacement profile delivers a crisp, tactile snap that eliminates hesitation during high-speed numerical entry.

Key matrix scanning is completely decoupled from computation: Core 1 scans the 43-key matrix at 200 Hz with an eager debounce automaton, while Core 0 executes mathematical evaluations with soft-float whole-module optimization. This symmetric dual-core partitioning guarantees that keystrokes are never lost, even during long-running numerical quadrature or root-finding iterations.

docs.title: 1.13.2 Optical & Thermal Boundary Invariants
docs.text:
The physical instrument operates across demanding environmental conditions with zero thermal throttling. Under continuous 150 MHz dual-core processing, the board dissipates just \(60.0\text{ mW}\), yielding an equilibrium chassis temperature rise of less than \(0.4^\circ\text{C}\) above ambient in still air.

The transflective graphic liquid-crystal display relies on ambient light reflection rather than an emissive backlight, eliminating visual fatigue and delivering a photopic contrast ratio exceeding 15:1 in direct sunlight. Subsurface 1064nm laser micro-foamed key legends achieve permanent high-contrast markings that resist chemical degradation and mechanical wear across decades of field use.

docs.title: 1.13.3 Continuous Non-Volatile State Preservation
docs.text: An instrument must maintain readiness without state loss across battery replacement cycles. The SC-32 employs dual ping-pong flash sectors protected by 32-bit FNV-1a checksums. Upon cold boot, Core 0 verifies sector integrity and restores the four operational stack registers (\(X, Y, Z, T\)), LASTX, all 26 storage registers (\(A\dots Z\)), and statistical accumulators in under 5 milliseconds. If battery terminal voltage drops below \(2.15\text{ V}\), the brownout supervisor safely commits all active registers to non-volatile memory before suspending execution.

docs.title: 1.14 Summary & Looking Ahead
docs.text:
Chapter 1 established the physical foundation of the StackCalc SC-32: an instrument crafted from aerospace-grade technical polymers, actuated by 400-gram snap-domes with an eager debounce automaton, illuminated by high-contrast transflective liquid-crystal optics, and anchored by power-loss-immune continuous flash memory. Every mechanical dimension, optical coefficient, and thermal boundary condition was qualified through first-principles engineering calculations, demonstrating that physical reliability and tactile determinism are prerequisite to computational excellence.

With the physical instrument in your hands, the stage is set to master its computational engine. In Chapter 2: RPN Stack Dynamics & Operational Mechanics, you will leave algebraic parenthesis syntax behind to explore the four-level operational stack (\(X, Y, Z, T\)). You will discover how numbers lift, drop, roll, and replicate during postfix evaluation, transforming complex nested expressions into an intuitive, visual, and frictionless stream of tactile keystrokes.

docs.title: 2.1 Thinking in Stacks: How Engineers Deconstruct the Physical World
docs.text:
In an age dominated by large language models, ubiquitous smartphones, and instant chat interfaces, a fundamental question arises: Why do serious engineers, scientists, and contest mathematicians still reach for an RPN pocket calculator, and why do people still read books like this one?

The answer touches the very core of human cognition.

Asking a chatbot or a smartphone for an isolated number does not teach you how to think. An AI can output an answer, but it leaves you mathematically blind to the internal gears of the problem. When you stand before a real-world engineering challenge—an overheating motor on a factory floor, a fluctuating rocket combustion chamber, or an acoustic crossover distorting in an auditorium—reality never presents itself as a multiple-choice question.

Reality is a continuous, interconnected web of physical causality: - Electrical current generates resistive heat; - Heat elevates component temperature; - Temperature alters semiconductor resistance; - Resistance changes the operational bias point.

To solve real problems, you cannot be a passive spectator asking questions into a void. You must be able to deconstruct physical reality into a chronological sequence of irreducible, verifiable transformations.

docs.title: 2.1.1 The Cognitive Mismatch: Algebraic Precedence vs. Human Reasoning
docs.text:
Standard algebraic infix notation (\(A + B \times C\)) was invented in the 16th century for handwriting on static parchment, not for real-time human or electronic calculation.

Consider how you calculate a common electrical voltage divider: $\(V_{\text{out}} = V_{\text{in}} \times \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}\)$

In algebraic calculators, you write from left to right, but you are forced to evaluate from the inside out:

[ V_in ] [ * ] [ R2 ] [ / ] [ ( ] [ R1 ] [+] [ R2 ] [ ) ] [ = ]

Notice the cognitive trap inherent in infix machines: 1. The Execution Freeze: When you key [ / ] [ ( ], the calculator freezes. It cannot calculate because it has no idea what lies on the other side of the parenthesis. 2. Internal Buffering: It must store your numerator in an internal memory buffer. 3. Parenthesis Counting: You must mentally track open and closed parentheses: ( ... ). 4. Catastrophic Failure: If you miss a single closing parenthesis, the whole calculation either throws a syntax error or produces silent numerical garbage.

Educational psychologist John Sweller (1988) termed this extraneous cognitive load (Sweller, 1988). Your scarce human working memory—which George Miller (1956) proved is limited to only \(7 \pm 2\) chunks (Miller, 1956)—is wasted acting as a human syntax parser instead of focusing on the physical circuit!

The Algebraic Parenthesis Trap vs. The RPN Stack Shortcut: Anatomy of a Parenthesis-Free Mind

Why did William Hewlett and David Cochran choose a 4-level operational stack for the HP-35 in 1972 instead of standard algebraic infix notation *([Hewlett, 1972](appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-hewlett1972); [Cochran, 1972](appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-cochran1972))*? The Algebraic Parenthesis Trap: To evaluate an infix expression like $(A + B) / (C + D / (E - F))$, an algebraic calculator must implement Dijkstra's Shunting-Yard algorithm in silicon *([Dijkstra, 1961](appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-dijkstra1961))*. It allocates an internal operator stack and operand buffer. Until the final = keystroke is pressed, no intermediate values are verified. The user must hold 6 to 8 open parentheses in mind, acting as a human syntax validator. A missing bracket produces a syntax fault or uncatchable numerical error *([Parker, 2019](appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-parker2019))*. The RPN Stack Shortcut: By contrast, Reverse Polish Notation—grounded in Jan Łukasiewicz's parenthesis-free logic *([Łukasiewicz, 1924](appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-lukasiewicz1924))* and Charles Hamblin's addressless computer architecture *([Hamblin, 1957](appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-hamblin1957))*—operates chronologically. Operands arrive first; operators act immediately. Register $T$ replicates down, Register $X$ displays every intermediate subtotal in real time, and intermediate results are naturally positioned for subsequent operations with zero register allocation *([Knuth, 1997](appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-knuth1997); [HP, 1982](appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-hp15c1982))*.

docs.title: The RPN Revelation: Chronological Causality
docs.text:
In Reverse Polish Notation, there are zero parentheses and zero deferred equals: * R1 [ENTER] R2 [+] \(\to\) Total loop resistance is immediately visible on the LCD! * R2 [x⇄y] [÷] \(\to\) Exact voltage division ratio is instantly resolved! * V_in [×] \(\to\) Output voltage resolved!

Every single keystroke executes immediately. Cause precedes effect. The 4-level operational stack (\(X, Y, Z, T\)) acts as an externalized piece of your working memory. You do not remember numbers—the stack holds them. You are liberated to think.

Figure 2.1: Real-time 4-register operational stack ($T, Z, Y, X$) displaying intermediate calculation states with zero deferred parentheses. CHAPTER BASELINE MODE: [ALL] (Full 12-digit scientific mantissa; Standard Base-10 Arithmetic; Degrees angular mode default).

docs.title: 2.2 The Core Axiom: Operands Precede Operators
docs.text:
In traditional algebraic calculators, mathematical expressions are evaluated in infix notation: an operator is entered between its two operands, requiring the calculator to defer execution until closing parentheses or an equals sign (=) is pressed: $\((14 + 6) \times (9 - 4) = 100\)$

In Reverse Polish Notation (RPN), also known as postfix notation, operands are loaded into the operational registers first, followed immediately by the operator that acts upon them: $\(14 \quad \text{[ENTER]} \quad 6 \quad \text{[+]} \quad 9 \quad \text{[ENTER]} \quad 4 \quad \text{[-]} \quad \text{[×]}\)$

Calculation Paradigm Keystroke Sequence Keystrokes Syntactic Overhead Subtotal Visibility Algebraic (Infix) ( 1 4 + 6 ) * ( 9 - 4 ) = 13 4 parentheses, deferred evaluation Zero intermediate feedback Reverse Polish (RPN) 14 [ENTER] 6 [+] 9 [ENTER] 4 [-] [×] 9 Zero parentheses, direct execution 100% visible subtotals (\(20\), \(5\), \(100\))

docs.title: 2.2.1 The Three Axioms of Reverse Polish Notation
docs.text:
1. Zero Parentheses: Because operators act immediately on the numbers present in the operational registers, expressions are evaluated strictly from the inside out. Complex rational polynomials with multi-level nested brackets collapse without a single parenthesis.
  2. Intermediate States are Tangible: Every keystroke produces an immediate, verified subtotal on the liquid crystal display. You never wonder whether an operator was registered, and you can visually audit intermediate physics parameters at every step.
  3. The Operator is the Execution Command: There is no = key on the SC-32. Arithmetic operators (+, -, ×, ÷) combine numbers instantly upon actuation.

docs.title: 2.2.2 The Cult of RPN: The Hacker's Secret Weapon & The Astronaut's Choice
docs.text:
In 1924, Polish logician Jan Łukasiewicz (Łukasiewicz, 1924) invented prefix and postfix notation to solve a fundamental problem in mathematical philosophy: could formal symbolic logic be evaluated with total mathematical purity, entirely free of parentheses?

Between 1954 and 1957, Arthur Burks, Don Warren, and Jesse Wright (Burks et al., 1954) formalized postfix notation in computer science, and Australian philosopher Charles Leonard Hamblin (Hamblin, 1957) proposed the push-down store—the hardware operational stack. In 1961, Edsger Dijkstra (Dijkstra, 1961) showed in his famous Shunting-Yard paper that computers cannot evaluate infix notation directly; they must compile infix into postfix before execution.

Forty-eight years after Łukasiewicz, in 1972, Hewlett-Packard engineers Bill Hewlett and Tom Whitney faced a severe physical constraint: how to fit a complete scientific computer into a shirt pocket with only 256 words of ROM. Algebraic calculators required massive memory buffers just to parse operator precedence and store unclosed parentheses. RPN eliminated the parser entirely. Operands entered the hardware stack directly; binary operations executed on the silicon arithmetic-logic unit (ALU) in place.

When Apollo astronauts flew into orbit and later space shuttle pilots trained on emergency descent trajectories, their instrument of choice was an RPN machine: the HP-35, HP-41C, and HP-48. Why? In an emergency at Mach 25, you cannot afford to wonder if you closed three sets of parentheses or whether PEMDAS will interpret your fraction correctly. In RPN, what you see is what the machine has.

docs.title: The Bare-Metal Reality of Modern Computing
docs.text:
Today, every high-performance computing system secretly converts code into postfix stack operations: * The Java Virtual Machine (JVM): Executes postfix bytecode instructions (iload, iadd) on an abstract stack. * WebAssembly (Wasm): Powering high-speed browser graphics and game engines, Wasm is a pure postfix stack architecture. * Adobe PostScript: Renders every laser-printed page and PDF document via postfix stack commands. * The Forth Language: Powers deep-space planetary probes, bootloaders, and automotive engine control units.

When you calculate in RPN, you are not learning a quirky interface—you are thinking in the native language of computing machines.

The 30-Second Watercooler Challenge: The 4-Second Parallel Resistor

Pose this problem to any engineer or colleague using a smartphone calculator: "Three resistors are wired in parallel: 12 Ω, 20 Ω, and 30 Ω. What is $R_{\text{eq}}$?"

The Algebraic Nightmare (24 Keystrokes): ( 1 / ( 1 / 1 2 + 1 / 2 0 + 1 / 3 0 ) ) = They will miscount a bracket, lose their place on the glass screen, or spend 20 seconds squinting.

The StackCalc RPN Triumph (4 Seconds): Method A (Classical Reciprocal Stack): 12 [1/x] 20 [1/x] [+] 30 [1/x] [+] [1/x] → 6.0 Ω! Method B (Dedicated Hardware Parallel Key [x∥y]): 12 [ENTER] 20 [x∥y] 30 [x∥y] → 6.0 Ω!

Four seconds. Zero parentheses. The intermediate parallel equivalent of the first two resistors (7.5 Ω) is clearly visible on the LCD before the third is added!

docs.title: 2.3 The 4-Level Operational Stack (\(X, Y, Z, T\))
docs.text:
The default operating environment of the SC-32 provides four hardware operational registers displayed simultaneously on the high-contrast transflective dot-matrix screen:

Display Line Screen Output Operational Role Line T T: 12.0000000000_ Top of stack constant reservoir Line Z Z: 45.5000000000_ Deep subtotal and intermediate holding level Line Y Y: 8.0000000000_ Dyadic second operand (\(Y \text{ op } X\)) Line X X: 128.0000000000_ Primary accumulator, active input line, and displayed result Status [DEG] Annunciator line (active mode flags)

docs.title: 2.3.1 Functional Roles of the Operational Registers
docs.text:
• Register X (Bottom Display Line): The active input and primary working accumulator. When you enter numeric digits, they form directly within Register \(X\). Single-argument (monadic) functions (√x, 1/x, LN, eˣ, SIN, COS, ABS) act directly upon Register \(X\) in place, replacing its argument with the computed result without disturbing \(Y, Z,\) or \(T\).
  • Register Y (Second Display Line): The second operand for two-variable (dyadic) operations. When you press an arithmetic operator:
  • [+] evaluates \(Y + X\)
  • [-] evaluates \(Y - X\)
  • [×] evaluates \(Y \times X\)
  • [÷] evaluates \(Y \div X\)
  • [yˣ] evaluates \(Y^X\)
  • [↰] [ˣ√y] evaluates \(\sqrt[X]{Y}\)
  • [x∥y] evaluates \(\frac{X \times Y}{X + Y}\)
  • Register Z (Third Display Line): The intermediate holding register. When a dyadic operation drops the stack, the value in \(Z\) drops down to become the new \(Y\).
  • Register T (Top Display Line): The top of the operational stack and constant factor reservoir. During stack drops, Register \(T\) drops into \(Z\) while simultaneously copying its own value back into \(T\). This unique duplication property makes Register \(T\) the cornerstone of iterative engineering calculations.

docs.title: 2.4 Stack Lift Mechanics & The Elevator Metaphor
docs.text:
Understanding Stack Lift (stackLiftEnabled) is the key to effortless RPN proficiency.

Imagine the four registers as a vertical elevator shaft with four transparent floors (\(T\) on the 4th floor, \(Z\) on the 3rd, \(Y\) on the 2nd, and \(X\) on the ground floor).

Stack State Phase Stack Lift Flag Elevator Mechanism Keypress Consequence Post-Calculation / Function TRUE Elevator Primed: Typing any digit pushes all existing values upward \(T \leftarrow Z, Z \leftarrow Y, Y \leftarrow X, X \leftarrow \text{digit}\). Previous \(T\) discarded. Post-ENTER / Post-Clear FALSE Elevator Parked: Typing a digit directly overwrites Register \(X\) \(T \leftarrow T, Z \leftarrow Z, Y \leftarrow Y, X \leftarrow \text{digit}\). No stack movement.

docs.title: 2.4.1 Key Categories Governing Stack Lift
docs.text: Every physical key and function on the SC-32 falls into one of three distinct categories regarding stack lift:

docs.title: 1. Keys That Enable Stack Lift (stackLiftEnabled = true)
docs.text: All operations that produce a completed result arm the stack elevator. When you subsequently begin typing digits for the next number, the previous result is automatically preserved in Register \(Y\): * Arithmetic Operators: [+], [-], [×], [÷], [yˣ], [↰] [ˣ√y], [x∥y], [↱] [÷R]. * Monadic Functions: [√x], [↰] [x²], [1/x], [LN], [↰] [LOG], [eˣ], [↰] [10ˣ], [SIN], [COS], [TAN]. * Mathematical Constants: [↱] [π], [E]. * Memory Recalls: [RCL] A–Z, [↰] [LASTX]. * Summation Commands: [Σ+], [↰] [Σ-].

docs.title: 2. Keys That Disable Stack Lift (stackLiftEnabled = false)
docs.text: Keys that prepare Register \(X\) for fresh digit entry park the elevator, preventing premature stack movement: * The Stack Commit Key: [ENTER] copies \(X\) into \(Y\) (\(Y \leftarrow X\)) and immediately disables stack lift. When you type the next digit, it replaces \(X\) directly, leaving your copied value safely in \(Y\). * Clear X: [C] (when clearing an active entry line).

docs.title: 3. Keys That Preserve Stack Lift State
docs.text: Utility keys that inspect or rearrange registers without altering the computational phase preserve whatever stackLiftEnabled state was previously active: * Register Exchanges: [x⇄y]. * Stack Rotations: [R↓], [↱] [R↑]. * Full Precision Inspection: [↱] [SHOW]. * Sign Toggle: [+/-] (toggles mantissa or exponent sign without triggering lift).

docs.title: 2.5 Dyadic Stack Drop Mechanics
docs.text:
When any two-variable (dyadic) operator executes, two operands (\(Y\) and \(X\)) collapse into a single result in \(X\), and the upper registers drop downward:

\[\begin{aligned} X_{\text{new}} &\leftarrow Y_{\text{old}} \text{ [op] } X_{\text{old}} \\ Y_{\text{new}} &\leftarrow Z_{\text{old}} \\ Z_{\text{new}} &\leftarrow T_{\text{old}} \\ T_{\text{new}} &\leftarrow T_{\text{old}} \quad \text{(Duplicated)} \end{aligned}\] Register Level Value Before [+] Dyadic Operation Transition Value After [+] Status / Provenance Line T 10.000 Replicates downward while holding value 10.000 Replicated from previous \(T\) Line Z 25.000 Drops into Register \(Y\) 10.000 Dropped from previous \(T\) Line Y 7.000 Operates with \(X\): (\(7 + 3 = 10\)) 25.000 Dropped from previous \(Z\) Line X 3.000 Becomes primary accumulator 10.000 Evaluated sum (\(Y + X\))

Figure 2.2: The StackCalc SC-32 scientific instrument: tactile 400g snap-domes and transflective display optimized for rapid postfix execution.

docs.title: 2.5.1 Trace Example: Evaluating a Rational Expression
docs.text:
Evaluate the rational engineering fraction: $\(\text{Result} = \frac{(45 \times 3) + (18 \times 4)}{15 - 3} = \frac{135 + 72}{12} = \frac{207}{12} = 17.25\)$

Step Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X Notes & State Analysis 1 [4] [5] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(45.0000\) Enter numerator term 1 2 [ENTER] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(45.0000\) \(45.0000\) Stack lift disabled; \(X\) copied to \(Y\) 3 [3] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(45.0000\) \(3.0000\) Overwrites \(X\) directly 4 [×] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(135.0000\) \(45 \times 3 = 135\); Stack lift armed 5 [1] [8] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(135.0000\) \(18.0000\) Stack lifts! 135 preserved in \(Y\) 6 [ENTER] \(0.0000\) \(135.0000\) \(18.0000\) \(18.0000\) Stack lift disabled; 135 pushed to \(Z\) 7 [4] \(0.0000\) \(135.0000\) \(18.0000\) \(4.0000\) Overwrites \(X\) directly 8 [×] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(135.0000\) \(72.0000\) \(18 \times 4 = 72\); \(Z\) drops to \(Y\) 9 [+] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(207.0000\) \(135 + 72 = 207\) (Numerator complete) 10 [1] [5] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(207.0000\) \(15.0000\) Stack lifts! 207 preserved in \(Y\) 11 [ENTER] \(0.0000\) \(207.0000\) \(15.0000\) \(15.0000\) Stack lift disabled; 207 pushed to \(Z\) 12 [3] \(0.0000\) \(207.0000\) \(15.0000\) \(3.0000\) Overwrites \(X\) directly 13 [-] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(207.0000\) \(12.0000\) \(15 - 3 = 12\); \(Z\) drops to \(Y\) 14 [÷] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(17.2500\) \(207 \div 12 = 17.25\) (Final result)

Homeschooler Diagnostic Checkpoint 2.1: Notice how in Steps 5 and 10, typing a new number automatically pushed the intermediate subtotal into Register \(Y\) without pressing [ENTER]. If you accidentally pressed [ENTER] before typing 18 in Step 5, your stack will have an extra copy of 135. If this happens, press [R↓] to inspect the stack or press [C] to clear Register \(X\).

docs.title: 2.6 Constant Factor Arithmetic in Register T (\(T\)-Duplication)
docs.text:
One of the most powerful and revered features inherited from the Corvallis HP-32SII is \(T\)-Register Duplication.

When the stack drops during dyadic arithmetic, Register \(T\) drops into \(Z\) and simultaneously duplicates itself back into \(T\). The value in \(T\) is never lost during downward operations; it acts as an infinite constant reservoir.

docs.title: 2.6.1 Repeated Multiplication & Exponential Growth
docs.text:
Suppose you want to compute the growth of an investment over 4 consecutive periods at an annual compounding growth rate of \(5\%\) (\(1.05\) factor), starting with \(\$1,000.00\):

To prime Register \(T\) with the constant factor \(1.05\): Key: 1.05 [ENTER] [ENTER] [ENTER] 1000

Operational Register Register Value Operational Role in Repeated Multiplication Line T 1.0500000000 Replicating constant factor reservoir Line Z 1.0500000000 Intermediate constant layer Line Y 1.0500000000 Active multiplier for first dyadic operation Line X 1000.0000000000 Initial investment principal

Now, repeatedly press [×] to evaluate successive years: * Press [×] \(\rightarrow\) \(X = 1,050.0000\) (Year 1). \(T\) duplicates \(1.05\) into \(T\) and \(Z\). * Press [×] \(\rightarrow\) \(X = 1,102.5000\) (Year 2). \(T\) duplicates \(1.05\) into \(T\) and \(Z\). * Press [×] \(\rightarrow\) \(X = 1,157.6250\) (Year 3). \(T\) duplicates \(1.05\) into \(T\) and \(Z\). * Press [×] \(\rightarrow\) \(X = 1,215.5063\) (Year 4). \(T\) duplicates \(1.05\) into \(T\) and \(Z\).

\[\text{Principal} \times 1.05^4 = 1,215.50625\]

docs.title: 2.6.2 Streamlined Unit Conversion Pipeline
docs.text:
In engineering drafting, you frequently need to convert a series of dimensions from inches to millimeters (\(1\text{ in} = 25.4\text{ mm}\)).

Prime Register \(T\) with \(25.4\): 25.4 [ENTER] [ENTER] [ENTER]

Now convert successive dimensions by typing the measurement in inches and pressing [×]: * 0.75 [×] \(\rightarrow\) \(19.0500\text{ mm}\) * 1.25 [×] \(\rightarrow\) \(31.7500\text{ mm}\) * 2.50 [×] \(\rightarrow\) \(63.5000\text{ mm}\) * 4.125 [×] \(\rightarrow\) \(104.7750\text{ mm}\)

Because typing a new number automatically triggers stack lift, the new dimension lifts into \(X\), pushing the previous millimeter answer into \(Y\), and the next [×] pulls another \(25.4\) down from \(T\)! You can convert hundreds of blueprint dimensions without ever re-entering the factor or consuming a storage register.

docs.title: 2.7 Stack Manipulation Keys & Architectural Elegance
docs.text: The SC-32 provides dedicated hardware keys for rearranging register contents:

docs.title: 2.7.1 Register Exchange: [x⇄y]
docs.text:
Pressing [x⇄y] swaps the contents of Registers \(X\) and \(Y\) while leaving \(Z\) and \(T\) completely undisturbed:

\[\begin{aligned} X_{\text{new}} &\leftarrow Y_{\text{old}} \\ Y_{\text{new}} &\leftarrow X_{\text{old}} \\ Z_{\text{new}} &\leftarrow Z_{\text{old}} \\ T_{\text{new}} &\leftarrow T_{\text{old}} \end{aligned}\]

docs.title: Primary Use Cases:
docs.text:
• Order of Division/Subtraction Correction: If you entered operands in reverse order (e.g. you entered \(12\) and \(4\) and want \(4 \div 12\) instead of \(12 \div 4\)), pressing [x⇄y] swaps them before pressing [÷].
  • Polar/Rectangular Coordinate Inspection: In complex or vector mode, \(Y\) holds the imaginary/vertical coordinate (\(y\) or \(\theta\)) and \(X\) holds the real/horizontal coordinate (\(x\) or \(r\)). Pressing [x⇄y] alternates between them instantly.

docs.title: 2.7.2 Stack Roll Down: [R↓]
docs.text:
Pressing [R↓] cyclically rotates the contents of all four operational registers downward:

\[\begin{aligned} X_{\text{new}} &\leftarrow Y_{\text{old}} \\ Y_{\text{new}} &\leftarrow Z_{\text{old}} \\ Z_{\text{new}} &\leftarrow T_{\text{old}} \\ T_{\text{new}} &\leftarrow X_{\text{old}} \quad \text{(Bottom wraps to Top)} \end{aligned}\]

Pressing [R↓] four consecutive times restores the stack to its exact initial configuration. It allows you to inspect all four registers without altering any values.

docs.title: 2.7.3 Stack Roll Up: [↱] [R↑]
docs.text:
Pressing Right Shift [↱] followed by [↱] [R↑] (on the [R↓] keycap) rotates the stack in reverse:

\[\begin{aligned} X_{\text{new}} &\leftarrow T_{\text{old}} \quad \text{(Top wraps to Bottom)} \\ Y_{\text{new}} &\leftarrow X_{\text{old}} \\ Z_{\text{new}} &\leftarrow Y_{\text{old}} \\ T_{\text{new}} &\leftarrow Z_{\text{old}} \end{aligned}\]

docs.title: 2.8 The [↰] [LASTX] Register & Error Recovery Archetypes
docs.text:
Whenever any operation alters Register \(X\), the calculator automatically preserves the previous value of Register \(X\) in a dedicated hardware storage buffer called LASTX.

Pressing [↰] [LASTX] (Right Shift [↱] followed by [ENTER]) pushes the stack upward and places the preserved operand back into Register \(X\).

The Three Archetypes of [↰] [LASTX] Error Recovery

Archetype 1: Wrong Arithmetic Operator Recovery • Scenario: You meant to evaluate $500 - 35$, but mistakenly pressed [+]. • Stack currently displays: $X = 535.0000$. • Recovery Keystrokes: [↰] [LASTX] [-] [-] • Mechanism: [↰] [LASTX] recalls $35$ into $X$, while $Y$ holds $535$. First [-] evaluates $535 - 35 = 500$ (restoring your original base operand into $X$). Tapping [↰] [LASTX] [-] then computes $500 - 35 = 465.0000$ without re-entering numbers!

Archetype 2: Wrong Function Key Recovery • Scenario: You had $45.000$ in $X$ and accidentally pressed [LN] instead of [√x]. • Stack currently displays: $X = 3.806662$. • Recovery Keystrokes: [↰] [LASTX] [√x] • Mechanism: [↰] [LASTX] restores $45.0000$ into $X$, and [√x] immediately computes $\sqrt{45} = 6.708204$.

Archetype 3: Operand Reuse in Multi-Term Formulas • Scenario: Evaluate $f(x) = \frac{\sin x}{x}$ for $x = 0.42\text{ radians}$. • Keystrokes: 0.42 [SIN] [↰] [LASTX] [÷] • Mechanism: Step 1 calculates $\sin(0.42) = 0.407760$. Step 2 recalls $0.42$ back into $X$, automatically lifting $\sin(0.42)$ into $Y$. Step 3 divides them: $0.407760 \div 0.42 = 0.970857$. Zero variable storage required!

docs.title: 2.8.1 Stack Trace: Operand Reuse for Sinc Function \(\frac{\sin x}{x}\)
docs.text:
Step Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X LASTX Notes 1 [0] [.] [4] [2] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(0.420000\) \(0.0000\) Enter argument \(x\) 2 [SIN] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(0.407760\) \(0.420000\) \(\sin(0.42)\); \(0.42\) saved to LASTX 3 [LASTX] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(0.407760\) \(0.420000\) \(0.420000\) Stack lifts; \(x\) restored into \(X\) 4 [÷] \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(0.0000\) \(0.970857\) \(0.420000\) \(\frac{\sin(0.42)}{0.42} = 0.970857\)

Notice how [↰] [LASTX] eliminated the need to type 0.42 twice or store it in variable register A.

docs.title: 2.9 The [SHOW] Key: 15-Digit Precision & IEEE-754 vs. BCD Architecture
docs.text:
While the transflective LCD displays numbers rounded to 12 significant decimal digits in standard [ALL] mode, the SC-32 calculates internally using full 64-bit IEEE-754 double-precision (binary64) floating-point arithmetic (\(1\) sign bit, \(11\) exponent bits, and \(53\) explicit + implicit significand bits, delivering \(\log_{10}(2^{53}) \approx 15.955\) decimal digits of precision).

Pressing Right Shift [↱]followed by [SHOW] ([↱] [SHOW] on the [ENTER] key) temporarily overrides the active display format and renders the full 15-digit internal significand across two display lines:

Display Header Internal Mantissa Readout Status Instruction SHOW X: 3.141592653589793 E+00 Release key to resume normal display mode

[!NOTE] Architectural Note for HP Purists — IEEE-754 binary64 with Guard Rounding vs. Classic Saturn BCD: Vintage Corvallis calculators (such as the HP-32SII and HP-15C) used the custom 4-bit Saturn processor to execute Binary-Coded Decimal (BCD) arithmetic with a 12-digit decimal mantissa (and 15-digit internal scratchpad registers). While hardware BCD represents base-10 fractions such as \(0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3\) exactly in storage, it limits dynamic range and requires tens of thousands of clock cycles per transcendental evaluation. The StackCalc SC-32 executes native 64-bit IEEE-754 binary64 floating-point math (\(\approx 15.95\) decimal digits) coupled with a 12-digit decimal display guard-rounding layer. Because the last 3 to 4 binary-derived decimal digits act as hidden guard digits during standard 12-digit display formatting ([ALL], [FIX], [SCI], [ENG]), base-10 arithmetic such as 0.1 [ENTER] 0.2 [+] rounds to 0.3 on the display, while [↱] [SHOW] exposes the full 53-bit significand (15 decimal digits) for numerical analysis.

Releasing or tapping any key restores normal screen formatting without affecting register contents.

docs.title: 2.10 Configurable Stack Depths: 4-LV, 8-LV, and INF Modes
docs.text:
Unlike historical handhelds that were permanently locked into a 4-level stack, the SC-32 provides configurable stack depths via the [↱] [FLAGS] menu:

Mode ID Architecture Name Accessible Registers Stack Drop Behavior Recommended Application Zone 4-LV Classic 4-Level Stack (Default) \(X, Y, Z, T\) Top-of-stack \(T\)-duplication on drop; full HP-32SII / HP-15C parity Everyday engineering, iterative series, high-speed calculation sprints 8-LV Extended 8-Level Stack \(R_1 \dots R_8\) (with \(R_1\text{--}R_4\) mapped to \(X, Y, Z, T\)) Holds up to 8 nested operands before top-register replication High-order polynomial factoring, multi-stage audio filters INF Unbounded Infinite Stack Dynamic heap allocation (up to 999 levels) True LIFO stack; dyadic drop never duplicates; pulls from history Deep recursive algorithms, large matrix operations

docs.title: 2.10.1 Switching Stack Depth Modes
docs.text:
1. Press Right Shift [↱] followed by [×] ([↱] [FLAGS]).
  2. Select menu item 2: STACK DEPTH.
  3. Choose 4-LV, 8-LV, or INF.
  4. Press [ENTER]. The active mode is saved to non-volatile continuous memory.

docs.title: 2.11 Operator Precedence Parsing vs. Native RPN Efficiency
docs.text: To appreciate the raw speed and architectural purity of RPN, consider how a calculator evaluates a compound algebraic equation: $\(\text{Expression} = \frac{A + (B \times C)}{D - (E^F)}\)$

docs.title: 2.11.1 The Algebraic Infix Bottleneck: Dijkstra's Shunting-Yard Algorithm
docs.text:
When an algebraic calculator evaluates infix text, it must execute Edsger Dijkstra's Shunting-Yard Algorithm: 1. Tokenization: Break input string into tokens (numbers, operators, parentheses). 2. Precedence Comparison: For every operator encountered, look up its precedence weight in an internal table (e.g., ^ has weight 4, ×/÷ weight 3, +/- weight 2). 3. Operator Stack Manipulation: Push operators onto an auxiliary operator stack; if an incoming operator has lower precedence than the stack top, pop operators to an output queue. 4. Parenthesis Matching: Push ( onto the operator stack; on encountering ), pop and discard operators until matching ( is found. If no match, throw syntax error. 5. Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) Traversal: Traverse the generated postfix queue to compute values.

On a microcontroller clocked at 150 MHz, parsing and evaluating this expression algebraically requires over 280 processor clock cycles and consumes dynamic heap memory.

docs.title: 2.11.2 The Native RPN Advantage: Direct Microcode Execution
docs.text:
In native RPN, the user's brain has already performed the parsing intuitively: A [ENTER] B [ENTER] C [×] [+] D [ENTER] E [ENTER] F [yˣ] [-] [÷]

  • Keystrokes: Exactly 13 keystrokes (identical or fewer than infix, with zero parentheses).
  • Execution Clock Cycles: Each RPN operator executes as a direct, in-place binary floating-point instruction taking under 14 clock cycles.
  • Memory Allocation: Zero dynamic heap allocation. Register manipulation occurs strictly within CPU registers and fast on-chip SRAM.

docs.title: 2.12 The Formal Stack Lift State Automaton
docs.text:
To eliminate any ambiguity regarding stack movement, the SC-32 execution engine is modeled as a deterministic finite-state machine.

Trigger Key / Event New stackLiftEnabled State Concrete Stack Effect [ENTER] FALSE \(Y \leftarrow X\); \(X\) remains unchanged; \(Z\) and \(T\) lift upward Numeric Digit (0-9, .) TRUE (while building) If Lift=TRUE: \(T \leftarrow Z, Z \leftarrow Y, Y \leftarrow X, X \leftarrow \text{digit}\)If Lift=FALSE: \(X \leftarrow \text{digit}\) (overwrites \(X\) directly) Arithmetic (+, -, ×, ÷) TRUE \(T \leftarrow T, Z \leftarrow T, Y \leftarrow Z, X \leftarrow Y \text{ op } X\) (Dyadic drop) Monadic (√x, 1/x, LN) TRUE \(T, Z, Y\) unchanged; \(X \leftarrow f(X)\) [x⇄y] PRESERVED \(X \leftrightarrow Y\); \(Z\) and \(T\) completely undisturbed [R↓] PRESERVED \(X \leftarrow Y, Y \leftarrow Z, Z \leftarrow T, T \leftarrow X\) (Cyclic roll down) [↱] [R↑] PRESERVED \(X \leftarrow T, T \leftarrow Z, Z \leftarrow Y, Y \leftarrow X\) (Cyclic roll up) [LASTX] TRUE \(T \leftarrow Z, Z \leftarrow Y, Y \leftarrow X, X \leftarrow \text{LASTX}\) (Lifts stack) [C] (Clear Active Entry) FALSE \(X \leftarrow 0\); \(Y, Z, T\) completely unchanged [C] (Clear Whole Stack) FALSE \(X \leftarrow 0, Y \leftarrow 0, Z \leftarrow 0, T \leftarrow 0\)

docs.title: 2.12.1 The Invariant Principles of Stack Conservation
docs.text:
1. The Invariable Dyadic Drop: Every two-operand operator pulls one value from the stack. Registers \(Z\) and \(T\) drop downward.
  2. The Constant \(T\)-Replication: Because \(T\) copies itself into \(Z\) while retaining its own value, any calculation with fewer than 4 active terms never encounters undefined or garbage registers.
  3. The Unbroken Lift Chain: After any calculation, you do not need to press [ENTER] before typing the next number. The act of typing a digit automatically preserves the result.

docs.title: 2.13 The Golden Rules of Stack Conservation
docs.text:
When evaluating complex mathematical or engineering formulas, follow these four strategic rules to optimize register usage:

  1. Evaluate the Heaviest Sub-Expression First: If an equation has a complicated term and a simple term, evaluate the complicated term first. It collapses into a single register, leaving the rest of the stack free for the remaining terms.
  2. Work From the Innermost Parentheses Outward: In rational fractions, always evaluate the lowest denominator or deepest radical first, then invert ([1/x]) or divide.
  3. Exploit [↰] [LASTX] to Avoid Storing Common Terms: In symmetric equations like \(\frac{x^2 - 1}{x^2 + 1}\) or \(\frac{\sin x}{x}\), evaluate the first term and recall \(x\) via [↰] [LASTX] rather than dedicating a lettered register.
  4. Use [x⇄y] to Adjust Dyadic Direction: When calculating \(B - A\) or \(B / A\), if \(A\) is in \(Y\) and \(B\) is in \(X\), a single touch of [x⇄y] restores proper algebraic order.

docs.title: 2.14 Engineering Design Briefing: The Apollo Guidance Computer & Real-Time Hardware Pipelines (Problems 2.1 through 2.30)
docs.text:
In this engineering expedition, you step into the role of a flight guidance officer and hardware systems architect. When mission-critical algorithms execute in real time, there is zero tolerance for syntax errors, stack overflow crashes, or missing parentheses. The following 30 problems provide exhaustive practice in 4-stack dynamics, register conservation, \(T\)-duplication, and [↰] [LASTX] recovery across collegiate engineering disciplines.

Inside-Out Stack Architecture: Algebraic Trap vs. RPN Shortcut — Invariant Stack Pipelines vs. Parenthesis Nesting

The Algebraic Parenthesis Trap: Consider evaluating the chained heat transfer equation governing a shell-and-tube exchanger *([Dijkstra, 1961](appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-dijkstra1961))*:

U = ( ( 18.5 * 4.2 ) + ( 7.1 * 9.6 ) ) / ( 14.3 - 5.8 )

An algebraic interface forces the user to construct an artificial syntax tree with three nested levels of parentheses. The user cannot see intermediate quantities—such as the first tube-wall product ($77.7$) or the total convective numerator ($145.86$)—until the final closing parenthesis and = key are pressed. If the answer diverges, the engineer has zero visibility into which term failed *([Strogatz, 2012](appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-strogatz2012); [Ellenberg, 2014](appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-ellenberg2014))*.

The RPN Stack Shortcut: The SC-32 evaluates expressions from the deepest sub-term outward, matching the physical flow of energy *([Łukasiewicz, 1924](appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-lukasiewicz1924); [Burks et al., 1954](appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-burks1954))*. The first numerator product ($77.70$) is formed in place; entering the second product auto-lifts the first into Register $Z$; pressing [+] collapses them into the total numerator ($145.86$). Evaluating the denominator ($14.3 - 5.8 = 8.50$) automatically positions numerator and denominator in Registers $Y$ and $X$. A single tap of [÷] yields $U = 17.16\text{ W/m}^2\text{K}$. Every intermediate physical quantity is inspected live, with zero syntax overhead.

docs.title: 2.14.8 Problem 2.8: 3D Vector Norm without Variable Registers

docs.title: 2.15.1 Cognitive Load & Syntax Elimination in Multi-Step Formulations
docs.text:
In collegiate engineering mathematics, evaluating complex multi-step rational expressions often introduces significant cognitive friction. In standard algebraic notation, calculators function as opaque intermediate buffers: expressions such as \(\frac{(14 + 6)(9 - 4)}{3 \times 5}\) bury intermediate subtotals beneath nested parentheses, withholding numerical feedback until the terminal evaluation key is pressed. A syntax error or typing misstep leaves the practitioner with no diagnostic visibility into where the evaluation failed.

Reverse Polish Notation eliminates this syntax barrier by aligning arithmetic entry directly with the underlying mathematical parse tree. Operands are placed into the operational stack before operators execute, ensuring intermediate results are immediately displayed and available for inspection. By making the calculation transparent at every step, cognitive overhead shifts from managing syntax rules to understanding the physical and mathematical behavior of the problem.

docs.title: 2.15.2 Non-Commutative Operational Recovery via Coordinate Exchange
docs.text:
A frequent operational hurdle in postfix calculation is operand ordering during non-commutative operations—specifically subtraction (\(Y - X\)) and division (\(Y / X\)). In an algebraic calculator, reversing the order of operands demands clearing the expression buffer or retyping prior terms.

On the SC-32, operand inversion is corrected in a single operation without disturbing the upper stack. Pressing [x⇄y] swaps the contents of Registers \(X\) and \(Y\) instantly. If a division yields the reciprocal of the desired quotient, the user can either apply [1/x] directly or execute [x⇄y] [÷] to complete the evaluation with zero syntax overhead. Intermediate values remain intact in hardware registers, eliminating recalculation and scratchpad re-entry.

docs.title: 2.15.3 Constant Replication and Stack Mechanics in Register \(T\)
docs.text:
The four-register operational stack (\(X, Y, Z, T\)) operates with deterministic push-and-drop mechanics. During any dyadic operation (\(X \circ Y\)), the values in \(X\) and \(Y\) combine into the new result in \(X\), Register \(Z\) descends to \(Y\), and Register \(T\) descends to \(Z\) while simultaneously replicating its own value in \(T\).

This automatic replication of the top register provides an efficient mechanism for repetitive evaluations, geometric series (\(a r^n\)), and scaling operations. Loading a common ratio or conversion factor into Register \(T\) allows successive powers or scaled quantities to be generated simply by keying successive values and pressing the operator, without requiring explicit memory recall keystrokes.

docs.title: 2.16 Summary & Looking Ahead
docs.text:
Chapter 2 unlocked the spatial logic of Reverse Polish Notation. By deconstructing mathematical parse trees from the inside out, you mastered stack lift upon entry, dyadic stack drop, the non-commutative coordinate exchange ([x⇄y]), continuous cyclic rolling ([R↓], [↱] [R↑]), error recovery via [↰] [LASTX], and constant replication in Register \(T\). Calculations that previously required unwieldy parentheses and scratchpad memory now flow naturally through four visible registers, providing continuous numerical feedback at every keystroke.

With this structural fluency in hand, you are ready to expand from elementary arithmetic into advanced scientific analysis. In Chapter 3: Algebra, Logarithms & Transcendental Functions, you will apply the stack to exponential growth, logarithmic scales (decibels, pH, and radioactive half-lives), arbitrary powers and roots, numerical part extraction (IP, FP, ABS, SGN), and dynamic display formatting across FIX, SCI, ENG, and ALL.

docs.title: 3.1 John Napier's 20-Year Labor (1614): How Logarithms Doubled the Lifespan of Astronomers, and Cody & Waite's Range Reduction
docs.text:
In the damp stone halls of Merchiston Castle near Edinburgh, Scotland, in the early decades of the seventeenth century, Scottish mathematician and baron John Napier (1550–1617) sat watching the intellectual crisis of his era unfold. Across Europe, the scientific revolution was stalling—not for lack of astronomical genius, but under the sheer, crushing burden of arithmetic.

Johannes Kepler, Tycho Brahe, and contemporary naval navigators were going blind by candlelight, spending months manually multiplying eight-digit sines and chords to determine planetary orbits and guide merchant fleets across uncharted oceans. A single calculation error on the four-hundredth page of an orbital ephemeris could invalidate a year of painstaking sky observations.

Napier dedicated twenty grueling years of his life to a singular obsession: could the brutal labor of multiplication be transformed into simple addition?

In 1614, Napier published his masterpiece, Mirifici Logarithmorum Canonis Descriptio ("Description of the Wonderful Rule of Logarithms") (Napier, 1614). By mapping numbers into geometric ratios and continuous flow distances, Napier discovered that: $\(\log(a \cdot b) = \log a + \log b \qquad \text{and} \qquad \log\left(\frac{a}{b}\right) = \log a - \log b\)$

The effect on science was explosive. Calculations that previously took astronomers four exhausting weeks could now be executed in an afternoon. Decades later, the great French mathematician Pierre-Simon Laplace observed that Napier's logarithms, "by shortening the labors, doubled the life of the astronomer."

Figure 3.1: The physical distributive area model: geometric decomposition of multi-digit polynomial multiplication into visual sub-rectangles.

Three and a half centuries later, the battle for logarithmic precision moved from quill and paper into silicon microcode. When evaluating exponential (\(e^x\)), logarithmic (\(\ln x\)), and power (\(y^x\)) functions on digital computers, naive textbook Taylor series suffer from catastrophic cancellation—the complete annihilation of significant digits when subtracting nearly equal floating-point numbers.

In 1980, William J. Cody and William Waite published their landmark treatise, Software Manual for the Elementary Functions (Cody & Waite, 1980), solving the range reduction problem. They demonstrated that before evaluating transcendentals, the argument \(x\) must be rigorously reduced to a primary kernel \([-\ln 2 / 2, +\ln 2 / 2]\) using extended-precision constants, preserving all 53 bits of IEEE-754 mantissa. The StackCalc SC-32 builds directly upon this intellectual lineage, providing transcendentals and powers that guarantee 12 visible decimal digits of monotonic precision across all engineering domains.

CHAPTER BASELINE MODE: [ALL] (Full 12-digit scientific mantissa; Standard Base-10 Arithmetic; Degrees angular mode default).
