docs.title: C.4 Authoritative HP32SII Deviations Master Index
docs.text:
The SC-32 intentionally deviates from the 1988 vintage HP-32SII in exact alignment with the project button rubric:

  1. [↱] + +/- = |x| (Absolute Value):
  2. HP32SII Original: ( (open parenthesis for algebraic equation editor).
  3. SC-32 Rationale: Parentheses are redundant in direct RPN mode; direct absolute value is far more useful in applied engineering.
  4. [↱] + E = ÷R (Integer Division & Remainder):
  5. HP32SII Original: ) (close parenthesis for algebraic equation editor).
  6. SC-32 Rationale: Returns integer quotient in \(Y\) and remainder in \(X\) in a single keystroke.
  7. [↱] + <- = Unassigned:
  8. HP32SII Original: = (equals for algebraic equation editor).
  9. SC-32 Rationale: Equality comparison belongs in the x?y and x?0 menus; left unassigned.
  10. [↰] + 0 = REGS (Register Viewer):
  11. HP32SII Original: INPUT (program input prompt).
  12. SC-32 Rationale: Programming prompts are replaced by dynamic equation parameters; REGS allows instant inspection of all variables.
  13. Key Row 7, Col 3 (Multi-Action Key):
  14. HP32SII Original: R/S (Run/Stop program execution).
  15. SC-32 Assignment: Primary: x∥y, Left Shift [↰]: TVM, Right Shift [↱]: PLOT, Alpha: (i).
  16. SC-32 Rationale: Traditional line programming is replaced by RPN step equations, numerical quadrature, root finding, and financial solvers.
  17. [↰] + + = LBL:
  18. Restored equation safety key ensuring equations retain explicit labels.
  19. [↱] + XEQ = POLY:
  20. Cubic polynomial solver workspace (A B C D EXEC CLR on LFU softkeys).
  21. Top 6 LFU Dynamic Softkeys:
  22. Context-aware softkey strip permanently positioned above the primary math rows.

SC-32 APPENDIX D // MATHEMATICAL CONSTANTS, SI UNITS & MASTER STEM EQUATION DIRECTORY ● IMMUTABLE MATHEMATICAL CONSTANTS • 58 STEM EQUATIONS • PARENTHESIS-FREE RPN SEQUENCING

Figure D.1: The StackCalc SC-32 technical reference bench instrument: rapid parenthesis-free evaluation of fundamental engineering and mathematical equations.

DIRECTORY BASELINE: Immutable mathematical constants; Complete BIPM SI prefixes (10³⁰ to 10⁻³⁰); Exact international unit conversions; Scientific notation entry syntax via [E]; Full 12-digit mantissa stack precision.

docs.title: D.1 The Architecture of Precision: Constants and Equations in RPN
docs.text:
A scientific calculator is not merely a tool for performing isolated arithmetic operations; it is a computational laboratory for modeling the physical universe. On the StackCalc SC-32, the synergy of Reverse Polish Notation (RPN), continuous four-register stack visibility (\(X, Y, Z, T\)), and dedicated scientific functions provides an unparalleled environment for STEM calculations.

SC-32 Scientific Register Hierarchy & Data Flow

> [ REGISTER T ] Top / Constant Buffer <-- Retains constant factor during drop > │ > [ REGISTER Z ] Third Stack Level <-- Holds intermediate vector/matrix term > │ > [ REGISTER Y ] Second Stack Level <-- Stores dyadic base, dividend, angle > │ > [ REGISTER X ] Active / Display <-- Direct keyboard entry & live readout > > [ LASTX REG ] Recovery Buffer <-- Automatically captures previous X > [ STATS BANK ] 6 Accumulators <-- Σx, Σy, Σx², Σy², Σxy, n > [ MEMORY A-Z ] 26 Global Registers <-- Persistent storage via [STO] / [RCL]

docs.title: D.1.1 The Concrete-Representational-Abstract (CRA) Framework
docs.text:
1. Concrete (Key Entry & Hardware Tactility): Scientific magnitudes are keyed using the tactile 400g snap-dome keys. Entering a power-of-ten scale factor such as \(6.62607015 \times 10^{-34}\) is accomplished cleanly via 6.62607015 [E] 34 [+/-].
  2. Representational (Four-Register Visual Feedback): As operations execute, intermediate physical quantities (such as angular frequency \(\omega\) in \(Y\) and capacitance \(C\) in \(X\)) remain continuously visible on the transflective \(132 \times 65\) LCD, eliminating memory ambiguity.
  3. Abstract (Parenthesis-Free Formula Decomposition): Equations with complex nesting (such as blackbody radiation laws or relativistic Lorentz transformations) are evaluated inside-out or bottom-up, completely avoiding algebraic parentheses.

docs.text:

docs.title: D.5 Specialized RPN Idioms & Stack Optimization Patterns
docs.text: Mastery of the SC-32 involves recognizing recurring computational structures and leveraging dedicated hardware keys to minimize button presses and eliminate redundant variable stores.

docs.title: D.5.1 The Harmonic Mean Idiom ([x∥y])
docs.text: The SC-32 provides a dedicated primary key [x∥y] which calculates: $\(X = \frac{X \cdot Y}{X + Y} = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{X} + \frac{1}{Y}}\)$ In algebraic calculators, entering a reciprocal sum requires 12 to 16 keystrokes with fractions and parentheses. On the SC-32, it takes exactly one keystroke: * Parallel Resistors: \(R_{\text{eq}} = R_1 \parallel R_2 \parallel R_3\) \(\rightarrow\) R1 [ENTER] R2 [x∥y] R3 [x∥y]. * Series Capacitors: \(C_{\text{eq}} = C_1 \parallel C_2\) \(\rightarrow\) C1 [ENTER] C2 [x∥y]. * Thin Lens Optics: Focal length \(f = d_o \parallel d_i\) \(\rightarrow\) do [ENTER] di [x∥y]. * Spring Series Compliance: \(k_{\text{eq}} = k_1 \parallel k_2\) \(\rightarrow\) k1 [ENTER] k2 [x∥y]. * Reduced Mass in Two-Body Problem: \(\mu = m_1 \parallel m_2\) \(\rightarrow\) m1 [ENTER] m2 [x∥y].

docs.title: D.5.2 The Difference-of-Squares Idiom
docs.text: When evaluating expressions of the form \(a^2 - b^2\) (such as Pythagorean legs \(b = \sqrt{c^2 - a^2}\) or numerical aperture \(NA = \sqrt{n_1^2 - n_2^2}\)): * Traditional RPN: c [↰] [x²] a [↰] [x²] [-] [√x] (6 keystrokes). * Stack Factoring Alternative: c [ENTER] a [ENTER] [+] [↰] [LASTX] c [x⇄y] [-] [×] [√x]. When numbers are large multi-digit values, entering them once and using [x⇄y] and [↰] [LASTX] avoids re-typing.

docs.title: D.5.3 Constant Factor Replication in Register T
docs.text: When evaluating a formula with a repeated scalar factor \(K\) across multiple variables (e.g. converting several values from feet to meters using \(0.3048\), or multiplying items by sales tax \(1.0825\)): 1. Load the constant into the stack: 1.0825 [ENTER] [ENTER] [ENTER] (fills \(X, Y, Z, T\)). 2. Enter Price 1: 10 [×] \(\rightarrow\) Displays result \(10.825\). Register \(T\) drops to \(Z\) and replicates \(1.0825\) in \(T\)! 3. Enter Price 2: [CLx] 25 [×] \(\rightarrow\) Displays \(27.0625\). Register \(T\) continues to supply \(1.0825\) indefinitely without ever touching memory registers!

docs.title: D.6 Equation Bank Programming & Automatic Variable Prompting
docs.text:
The StackCalc SC-32 provides a non-volatile Equation Bank accessed via [↱] [EQN]. Any standard formula can be stored as a symbolic expression and evaluated repeatedly, solved numerically via Brent's root finder, or integrated via Romberg quadrature.

Equation Bank Workflow: Entry, Solving & Integration

  1. Create Equation: [↱] [EQN] → Type formula using named variables $A$–$Z$. Example: Y = A × X² + B × X + C
  2. Evaluate (Prompt): [XEQ] → SC-32 sequentially prompts: A? → enter value → [R/S], X? → enter value → [R/S], B? → enter value → [R/S], C? → enter value → [R/S]. Result displays in Register $X$.
  3. Numerical Root: [↱] [SOLVE] X → Solves for $X$ when $Y = 0$ using Richard Brent's hybrid algorithm.
  4. Numerical Integral: [↱] [∫] → Prompts for variable, lower, upper. Evaluates Romberg adaptive quadrature.

docs.title: D.6.1 Benchmark Example: Parabolic Motion Integration
docs.text: Evaluate \(\int_0^4 3 X^2 \, dX = [X^3]_0^4 = 64.0\): 1. Enter Equation mode: [↱] [EQN] 2. Enter keystrokes: 3 [ENTER] X [↰] [x²] [×] 3. Assign label: PARABOLA 4. Set integration bounds: Lower bound \(0.0\), Upper bound \(4.0\). 5. Press [↱] [∫] X 6. The transflective screen indicates active Romberg convergence steps and halts with 64.0000 in Register \(X\).

docs.title: D.7.1 Dimensional Dependency Tracking & Conceptual Grounding
docs.text: In collegiate engineering and physics education, learners often struggle with algebraic syntax friction, losing sight of physical scaling relationships while navigating nested parentheses. Formulating standard reference equations—from relativistic dynamics to thermodynamic cycles—into step-by-step RPN pipelines reveals physical dimensional dependencies directly. Intermediate operands in Registers \(Y\) and \(Z\) anchor dimensional analysis, allowing students to inspect intermediate physical products (such as momentum, kinetic energy, or pressure heads) before collapsing terms into final units.

docs.title: D.7.2 2022 CODATA Physical Constants & Verification Precision
docs.text: The SC-32 hardcodes fundamental physical constants according to the latest 2022 CODATA recommendations (including the Planck constant \(h\), speed of light \(c\), elementary charge \(e\), and Avogadro constant \(N_A\)). Because these values are defined with exact SI definitions or high-precision mantissas, computing physical benchmarks with 4-level stack traces ensures that experimental calculations and textbook derivations match standard reference tables to full floating-point precision without compounding rounding errors.

docs.title: D.7.3 Hardware Stack Persistence & Register Flow Control
docs.text: Translating multidisciplinary equations into pure postfix execution highlights the architectural efficiency of the 4-register operational stack (\(X, Y, Z, T\)). In operations requiring constant reuse, filling Register \(T\) provides perpetual constant replication, while the single-cycle parallel harmonic key ([x∥y]) and one-touch recovery via [↰] [LASTX] eliminate scratchpad register allocation. The deterministic behavior of the stack ensures rapid, error-free execution across all 58 core scientific formulas.

docs.title: D.8 Diagnostic Checkpoints & Singularity Handling
docs.text:
Diagnostic Checkpoint D.1: Scientific Exponent Entry Syntax

Never press `[×] 10 [yˣ]` to enter scientific notation! Doing so pushes an extra operator onto the stack, consuming two stack levels.

Always use the dedicated [E] (Exponent) key: * Correct: 1.602176634 [E] 19 [+/-] (Single atomic number entered into Register \(X\)). * Incorrect: 1.602176634 [ENTER] 10 [ENTER] 19 [+/-] [yˣ] [×] (Consumes 4 stack registers and risks stack overflow).

Diagnostic Checkpoint D.2: Trigonometric Angular Modes in Physical Laws

Physical formulas involving wave motion, optics, and projectile trajectories demand careful attention to the active angular mode:

  • Geometric & Surveying Formulas (Snell's Law, Law of Cosines, Great Circle): Require Degrees mode ([↰] [MODES] [DEG]).
  • Analytical Calculus & Fourier Syntheses (Pendulum period, Harmonic oscillations): Require Radians mode ([↰] [MODES] [RAD]). Verify the LCD annunciator at the top of the display before running chained trigonometric sequences.

Diagnostic Checkpoint D.3: Mathematical Singularity and Boundary Handling

* **Division by Zero ($x / 0$):** The SC-32 halts chained execution and displays `DIV BY ZERO`. Press `[<-]` to recover prior stack state.

  • Square Root of Negative Real (\(\sqrt{-x}\)): In Real mode, displays INVALID ARG. In Complex mode ([↰] [CMPLX]), returns pure imaginary result \(i\sqrt{x}\) into \((x, y)\) coordinate representation.
  • Logarithm of Non-Positive Real (\(\ln(0)\) or \(\ln(-x)\)): Displays DOMAIN ERROR.

docs.title: Appendix E: Primary Sources & Annotated Further Reading Guide
docs.text:
SC-32 SCHOLARSHIP // ANNOTATED FURTHER READING & PRIMARY SOURCES ● 1914–2026 CHRONOLOGY • THEMATIC PATHWAYS • BIBTEX CATALOG

The architecture of the StackCalc SC-32 does not exist in isolation. It represents the conscious convergence of more than a century of research across mathematical logic, stack-oriented computer organization, numerical error analysis, cognitive science, and scientific instrument craftsmanship.

While the detailed historical narratives of William Hewlett's 1972 Corvallis genesis, John Napier's 1614 logarithms, Cody & Waite's range reduction, Eratosthenes' geodesy, Carl Friedrich Gauss's 1801 orbital recovery of Ceres, and Claude Shannon's 1937 boolean algebra have been woven directly into the opening chapters of this manual, this appendix provides an authoritative, automatically indexed guide to the primary literature, complete with chapter cross-references and verified BibTeX citations.

docs.title: 1. Welcome, Explorer! (Wait—Did Your Parents Buy You This Book?)
docs.text:
If an adult handed you this book and said, "Here, read this math manual," you probably wanted to groan and hide it under your bed. We get it! Most school math books are torture: pages of boring drills, confusing rules like "borrow from the neighbor," and giant tangles of parentheses ( ( 15 - 3 ) × ( 4 + 2 ) ) ÷ 6 = ? where one tiny mistake ruins your whole page.

Here is the secret: this is not a normal school math book, and the calculator in your hands is not a normal calculator.

Look closely at the bottom-right corner of the StackCalc SC-6. Notice anything missing? There is no equals (=) button.

Why? Because on a normal calculator, the = button is a trap. You type a long chain of numbers and parentheses, cross your fingers, hit =, and hope it doesn't flash SYNTAX ERROR. On the SC-6, you use Reverse Polish Notation (RPN)—the exact same "inside-out" secret code used by rocket engineers, tournament math champions, and computer scientists.

Want to beat every grown-up in your house at a 5th-grade math challenge right now? Hand a parent their phone calculator, pick up your SC-6, and race them on: $\((15 - 3) \times (4 + 2) \div 6\)$

While they are still hunting for the ( and ) brackets on their glass screen, you tap: 15 [ENTER] 3 [-] 4 [ENTER] 2 [+] [×] 6 [÷] \(\longrightarrow\) 12!

Zero parentheses. Zero scrap paper. Done in five seconds flat. Flip to Chapter 2 to see how Stack Math and your 4-level number stack work, or jump straight to Chapter 8 to test your reflexes against the built-in Arithmetic Sprint Game ([f] [?])!

Unlocked Keycaps Ribbon — Master Grade Progression

You don't need to learn all 43 keys at once! As you level up from Kindergarten to Grade 6, you unlock new superpowers on your keypad: • Grades K–1: [▦] Ten-Frame, [g] [COUNT] Step Counter / Rack, [f] [LINE] Number Line, [+], [-], [ENTER], [C], [<-], Digits [0]–[9]. • Grade 2: [PV] Place Value Mode, Doubles (N [ENTER] [+]), [g] [REP] Skip-Counting. • Grade 3: [×], [÷], [f] [RECT] Rectangle Area, [🕒] Planetary Clock, Unit Fractions ([.] n [.] d). • Grade 4: [g] [÷R] Quotient & Remainder, [g] [SIMP] Factor Reduction, Mixed Numbers [a ᵇ/c], Improper Fractions [f] [d/c], Decimals. • Grade 5: Unlike Fractions, [f] [LCM] Least Common Denominator, [f] [PRISM] Volume, [Σ+] Surface Area Accumulation, Unit Conversions. • Grade 6 (Pre-Algebra & Rapid Math Sprint): [+/-] Signed Numbers, [g] [|x|] Absolute Value, [g] [FACT] Prime Decomposition, [GCF], [f] [LCM], Ratios ([g] [a:b]), Geometric [x²] and [f] [√x] Inverses, Descriptive Statistics ([g] [x̄], [f] [MED], [g] [MODE], [IQR], [g] [MAD]). Strict Gatekeeping Directive: 5th graders and younger NEVER see logarithms (LOG, LN) or abstract powers (yˣ). Advanced functions are segregated exclusively into secondary advanced math extensions.

docs.title: 2. Foreword: The Renaissance of Tactile Mathematics
docs.text:
For Parents & Teachers: The Crisis of Frictionless Computation & The RPN Solution

In an era dominated by glowing glass tablets, cloud-connected mobile applications, and opaque computer algebra engines, children frequently encounter school mathematics as an arbitrary ritual of keystrokes followed by an equal sign (=). A student types 7 + 5 = on a touchscreen; the digits vanish instantly, replaced by 12. What happened between the input and the output? In the traditional algebraic calculator paradigm, the mathematical transformation is completely hidden from view. The physical regrouping of five loose counters with seven counters to form a complete ten and two units never occurs in the child's mind. The intermediate subtotal is swallowed by internal hardware buffers. If the child makes a mistake, the screen flashes SYNTAX ERROR, providing zero spatial evidence of where the reasoning derailed. The StackCalc SC-6 Elementary Calculator & Classroom Companion was engineered to end this era of black-box computation. Drawing inspiration from the mechanical clarity celebrated by David Macaulay *([Macaulay, 2016](appendix-c-formulas-and-conversions.md#cite-macaulay2016))* and the intuitive wonder of mathematics championed by Steven Strogatz *([Strogatz, 2012](appendix-c-formulas-and-conversions.md#cite-strogatz2012))*, it restores physical intuition, spatial clarity, and tactile joy to mathematics from Kindergarten through Grade 6. Designed around a crisp $400\text{g}$ tactile stainless-steel snap-dome matrix, an ambient-light transflective dot-matrix LCD, and dark impact-resistant technical thermoplastics, the SC-6 is not a disposable toy or a passive consumer tablet. It is an authentic, durable scientific instrument built for young hands and curious minds.

| Paradigm | Keystroke Sequence | Cognitive & Pedagogical Reality | |---|---|---| | **Traditional Algebraic (Infix)** | `7` `+` `5` `=` $\longrightarrow 12$ | The `+` key hides `7` in invisible memory while waiting for `5`. The `=` key destroys the problem structure. The learner never sees where intermediate numbers live. | | **Reverse Polish Notation (RPN)** | `7` `[ENTER]` `5` `[+]` $\longrightarrow 12$ | `7` rises visibly to Register $Y$; `5` enters Register $X$; `[+]` fuses them visibly into `12`. Every number is a visible object; zero hidden buffers; zero syntax errors. |

docs.title: 2.1 For the Skeptical Parent: Why Not Just Use a $10 Calculator or Tablet App?
docs.text:
If you are a parent looking at the StackCalc SC-6 and its companion 3D-printed block kits, you should ask a blunt question: "Why shouldn't my child just use a $10 four-function calculator or a free iPad math game?"

Here is the honest answer: 1. Tablet apps hijack attention; tactile instruments build focus. Even the best-intentioned tablet app lives one swipe away from video feeds, pop-up badges, and slot-machine sound effects. The SC-6 has zero Wi-Fi, zero notifications, and zero ads. When your child sits at the kitchen table with physical blocks and the SC-6, their entire attention is on the math in their hands. 2. A $10 calculator hides the work; the 4-level stack shows every step. On a drugstore calculator, typing 7 + 5 = makes the 7 and 5 vanish into 12. When a child makes a mistake on a multi-step word problem, they have no idea what went wrong and have to start over from scratch. On the SC-6, four levels of numbers (\(T, Z, Y, X\)) stay visible on the screen at once, and [f] [LASTX] lets them undo or check their last step immediately. 3. Three 5-Minute Kitchen-Table Lightbulb Moments You Will See in Week One: - The "Make-a-Ten" Snap (Grades K–2): Your child places 8 red counters and 2 gold counters into the physical Ten-Frame tray (10), leaves 3 gold counters beside it (13), and sees the exact same tray light up on the SC-6 screen via [▦]. Finger-counting disappears because they can see \(8 + 5\) as \(10 + 3\). - The Bus Remainder Aha! (Grades 3–4): Instead of getting lost in 3.2222222 when dividing 145 campers into 45-seat buses, your child taps 145 [ENTER] 45 [g] [÷R] and sees 3 full buses on line \(X\) and 10 campers left over on line \(Y\)—matching what happens in real life. - The Fraction Tower Match (Grades 3–6): Before touching a common-denominator rule, your child drops a \(\frac{1}{2}\) block and a \(\frac{1}{3}\) block into the Fraction Studio comparator well, slides five \(\frac{1}{6}\) blocks beside them until the tops are flush, and then verifies \(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3} = \frac{5}{6}\) right on the SC-6.

docs.title: 2.2 The Equals-Sign Trap vs. The Stack Ladder
docs.text:
Decades of educational research in early mathematics education (Jerome Bruner (Bruner, 1966), Zoltan Dienes (Dienes, 1960), and Liping Ma (Ma, 1999)) identify the "equals-sign trap" as the single greatest cognitive stumbling block transitioning from elementary arithmetic to pre-algebra. In typical elementary classrooms, students see = at the end of every line on a worksheet. Consequently, children come to view the equals sign not as a relational statement of balance, but as an urgent command meaning "produce the answer right now!"

When these students later encounter algebraic expressions such as: $\(8 + 4 = \Box + 5\)$ an alarming majority of students write \(12\) in the box (or \(17\)), because their eyes lock onto \(8 + 4\) and treat the equals sign as an immediate trigger to compute (Strogatz, 2012).

The StackCalc SC-6 dismantles this trap by replacing the equals sign with the Stack Ladder. There is no [=] button on the faceplate. Instead, mathematical quantities sit as physical objects on visible shelves: 1. Quantity First: You pick up an object or measure a quantity onto the active shelf (\(X\)). 2. The Elevator Lift: Tapping [ENTER] lifts that object smoothly onto the upper mezzanine shelf (\(Y\)). 3. Second Quantity: You bring another quantity into contact on the ground shelf (\(X\)). 4. Operational Action: Tapping an operator ([+], [-], [×], [÷]) causes the upper shelf to drop down, fusing the objects into a new composite quantity immediately.

On the Stack Ladder, computation is never an opaque command—it is a tangible running balance of physical objects that can be grouped, scaled, and inspected at will.

docs.title: 2.3 Five Stack Math Super-Moves
docs.text:
Throughout this textbook and classroom companion, students and mentors master five foundational Stack Math Super-Moves that bond physical manipulatives to the RPN stack: 1. The Make-a-Ten Snap: Using 3D-printed Ten-Frames ([▦]) to bridge to 10 before chaining addition, turning mental carrying into an intuitive tactile click (Singapore MOE, 2014). 2. The Elevator Stack Drop: Watching intermediate numbers drop floor-by-floor down the 4-register stack (\(T \to Z \to Y \to X\)) as operations execute, eliminating parenthetical clutter entirely (Macaulay, 2016). 3. The Remainder-You-Can-Hold: Using integer division [g] [÷R] to place the whole quotient in \(X\) and the physical leftover remainder in \(Y\) simultaneously—preserving the discrete reality of egg crates, bus seats, and bakery trays (Ma, 1999). 4. The Equal-Fraction Tower Alignment: Testing equivalence and simplifying fractions directly in the 84 mm Fraction Studio comparator well ([g] [SIMP]), where equal fractions physically match in height (Strogatz, 2012). 5. The Skip-Counting Ladder: Locking a constant step increment across registers via [g] [REP] so repeated taps of [+] scale rhythmic times-table ladders without re-entering numbers (Gauss, 1809).

For Parents & Teachers: The Concrete-Representational-Abstract (CRA) Framework

Jerome Bruner's foundational cognitive research established that deep mathematical fluency develops through a three-stage cognitive progression: Concrete → Representational → Abstract (CRA) *([Bruner, 1966](appendix-c-formulas-and-conversions.md#cite-bruner1966))*. The StackCalc SC-6 is the first physical calculating instrument designed specifically to embody and accelerate the CRA sequence within every mathematical domain.

| CRA Stage | Physical / Digital Medium | Classroom & Studio Examples | |---|---|---| | **Stage 1: Concrete (Hands-On Manipulatives)** | 3D-Printed Gridfinity Studio Kits | Ten-Frame Trays, $84\text{ mm}$ Fraction Towers & Comparator Well, 144 Four-Color Counting Tiles, Prime Factor Studio, Planetary Geared Clock. | | **Stage 2: Representational (LCD Sandboxes)** | Transflective Dot-Matrix Visual Modes | Ten-Frame Studio `[▦]`, Step Counter & Bead Rack `[g] [COUNT]`, Number Line Jump Arcs `[LINE]`, Place Value `[PV]`, Geared Clock Dial `[🕒]`. | | **Stage 3: Abstract (RPN Stack Dynamics)** | Multi-Register Stack-Order (RPN) Stack ($X, Y, Z, T$) | Two-Number stack drop, $T$-register constant replication, parenthesis-free order of operations `(15-3)×(4+2)÷6`, multi-face surface area accumulation via `[Σ+]`. |

Stage 1: Concrete (Physical Manipulative Kits): Before you ever press a key on the SC-6, mathematical quantities exist in three dimensions. In Kindergarten and Grade 1, you place solid counters into tactile Ten-Frame trays. In Grade 2 and Grade 3, you dock and stack $19\text{ mm}$ four-color Gridfinity counting tiles to construct physical rectangular arrays for multiplication ($4 \times 6$) and explore planar region coloring without fragile friction snaps. In Grade 4 and Grade 5, you align $84\text{ mm}$ Fraction Towers, physically feeling that two $1/4$ blocks have the exact same height as one $1/2$ block. In Grade 6, you place proportional prime factor blocks into the Prime Factor Studio logarithmic comparator box, physically experiencing Napierian logarithmic addition where stacking a [2] and a [3] block lands exactly on the "6" tick mark of the back-wall slide rule comparator ($h(2) + h(3) = 12.64\text{ mm} + 20.04\text{ mm} = 32.68\text{ mm} = h(6)$). The physical manipulatives share identical geometric dimensions and naming conventions with the SC-6 hardware interface, anchoring subsequent symbolic reasoning. Stage 2: Representational (Visual LCD Sandboxes): The SC-6 graphic LCD features a high-contrast $132 \times 65$ dot-matrix transflective panel. When you enter a visual tool mode, the screen shifts seamlessly from raw numerals into high-resolution vector diagrams that mirror your physical manipulatives (Ten-Frames via [▦], dynamic jumping number line via [f] [LINE], bead rack via [g] [COUNT], and dual geared analog clocks via [🕒]). In this representational stage, numbers are visible, countable objects living directly within the dual-stack columns of the calculator. Stage 3: Abstract (RPN Operational Stack Dynamics): Once you understand the underlying physical and visual behavior, you transition effortlessly to the abstract stage. The visual frames give way to standard numerical registers ($T, Z, Y, X$). Now you harness the true power of Reverse Polish Notation: chaining multi-step problems without intermediate scratch paper, utilizing two-number stack drops to carry intermediate answers automatically into the next operation, replicating constants through the top register ($T$) for rhythmic skip-counting ladders, and accumulating multi-face geometric surface areas directly into hardware statistical memory ([Σ+]).

docs.title: 4. Three Foundational RPN Breakthroughs for Your Math Journey
docs.text:
Three core operational capabilities illustrate why a dedicated tactile RPN instrument and physical manipulative studio transform elementary mathematics:

  1. Parenthesis-Free Multi-Step Evaluation: In standard curriculum problems such as \(((18 + 6) \times (15 - 7)) \div 8\), algebraic calculators require balancing nested parentheses, where a single missing bracket produces a syntax error. On the SC-6, you evaluate the expression from the inside out: 18 [ENTER] 6 [+] 15 [ENTER] 7 [-] [×] 8 [÷] \(\longrightarrow\) 24! The first sub-expression \((18 + 6 = 24)\) lifts cleanly into Register \(Y\); the second sub-expression \((15 - 7 = 8)\) forms in Register \(X\). Tapping [×] multiplies them into \(192\), and tapping 8 followed by [÷] produces \(24\). The calculation requires zero parentheses, zero scratch paper, and zero memory register overhead.

  2. Visible Unreduced Fractions and Deliberate Simplification ([g] [SIMP]): When exploring fraction equivalence, you place a \(1/2\) block (\(42.0\text{ mm}\)) beside three \(1/6\) blocks (\(3 \times 14.0\text{ mm} = 42.0\text{ mm}\)) in the Fraction Studio comparator well. On traditional calculators, typing 3/6 immediately forces an automatic reduction to 0.5 or 1/2, erasing the unreduced state. The SC-6 preserves the unreduced fraction on screen when entering . 3 . 6 [ENTER]. You deliberately press [g] [SIMP] to divide out common factors step-by-step, observing how both numerator and denominator scale down until the annunciator confirms LOWEST TERMS.

  3. Discrete Integer Division with Remainders ([g] [÷R]): In real-world sharing—such as distributing 17 counting tiles equally among 5 friends—a decimal quotient (\(3.4\)) obscures the concrete outcome. Tapping 17 [ENTER] 5 [g] [÷R] displays the whole quotient 3 in Register \(X\) and the exact remainder 2 in Register \(Y\) simultaneously. Pressing [x⇄y] swaps the two values on the screen, allowing you to verify both the grouped units and the leftover items in a single keystroke.

docs.title: 5. The Four SC-6 RPN Superpowers
docs.text:
The StackCalc SC-6 equips you with four unique operational tools—referred to throughout this manual as the Four RPN Superpowers. These capabilities are completely absent from traditional consumer calculators, transforming difficult elementary math concepts into effortless, rhythmic operations.

THE FOUR SC-6 RPN SUPERPOWERS

SUPERPOWER 1: [g] [REP] / [REP] Rhythmic Skip-Counting & Times Tables Replicates X into all registers; rhythmic [+] builds times tables (7, 14, 21, 28...). SUPERPOWER 2: [g] [÷R] / [÷R] Simultaneous Whole Quotient & Remainder Divides in 1 stroke: Quotient in X, Remainder in Y. [x⇄y] swaps to inspect. SUPERPOWER 3: [SIMP] Step-by-Step Fraction Factor Reduction Divides out prime factors one at a time; announces "LOWEST TERMS" when irreducible. SUPERPOWER 4: [f] [LASTX] Self-Checking Inverse Arithmetic Recalls the prior number into X to verify operations via inverse math (add -> sub).

docs.title: 5.1 Superpower 1: Rhythmic Skip-Counting Ladders ([g] [REP])
docs.text:
• Keycap: Row 3, Col 5 ([g] [REP], mapped to executeRep())
  • The Challenge in Early Math: Memorizing multiplication tables through rote chanting often fails because you do not experience the steady, rhythmic accumulation of equal groups.
  • The RPN Solution: When you enter a number (e.g. 7) and press [g] [REP], the value 7 is instantly replicated across all four stack registers: $\(X = 7, \quad Y = 7, \quad Z = 7, \quad T = 7\)$
  • Now, every tap of the [+] key adds another group of 7. As you tap [+] rhythmically, the screen climbs: $\(7 \xrightarrow{[+]} 14 \xrightarrow{[+]} 21 \xrightarrow{[+]} 28 \xrightarrow{[+]} 35 \xrightarrow{[+]} 42 \xrightarrow{[+]} 49 \xrightarrow{[+]} 56 \dots\)$
  • Because the top register (\(T\)) automatically duplicates upon every two-number drop, you can skip-count indefinitely! Multiplication is no longer an abstract flashcard; it is an active, rhythmic ladder.

docs.title: 5.2 Superpower 2: Simultaneous Whole Quotient and Remainder ([g] [÷R])
docs.text:
• Keycap: Row 4, Col 6 ([g] [÷R], mapped to intDiv)
  • The Challenge in Early Math: When you learn division, standard calculators produce confusing decimals. Dividing \(17 \div 5\) produces 3.4. But what does 0.4 mean when you are packing 17 eggs into 5-egg cartons, or sharing 17 cookies among 5 friends? It means 3 cookies each and 2 cookies left over! Decimal calculators force you to perform messy scratch-paper long division just to find the remainder.
  • The RPN Solution: Entering 17 [ENTER] 5 [g] [÷R] executes integer division in a single stroke:
  • Register \(X\): Displays the whole quotient \(Q = 3\) (each friend gets 3 cookies).
  • Register \(Y\): Holds the exact remainder \(R = 2\) (2 cookies left over in the jar).
  • Tapping [x⇄y] (Row 3, Col 3) instantly swaps registers, allowing you to inspect the remainder and swap back. Sharing and packaging problems are solved in seconds with absolute conceptual clarity.

docs.title: 5.3 Superpower 3: Step-by-Step Fraction Factor Reduction ([g] [SIMP])
docs.text:
• Keycap: Row 1, Col 2 ([g] [SIMP])
  • The Challenge in Early Math: Traditional fraction calculators automatically reduce every fraction to lowest terms immediately upon entry. If you key \(4/8\), the calculator instantly displays \(1/2\). While convenient for an engineer, you never see that \(4/8\) has a common factor of 2 or 4, missing the entire conceptual bridge of equivalent fractions.
  • The RPN Solution: StackCalc SC-6 enforces unreduced fraction arithmetic by default. When you key . 12 . 18 [ENTER], the screen displays 12/18. The fraction remains unreduced through additions and multiplications until you deliberately press [g] [SIMP]:
  • First press of [g] [SIMP]: Divides numerator and denominator by their greatest common factor, displaying 2/3.
  • Second press of [g] [SIMP]: Detects that \(\gcd(2, 3) = 1\), leaves 2/3 intact, and momentarily flashes LOWEST TERMS across the screen.
  • You retain complete ownership over the simplification process.

docs.title: 5.4 Superpower 4: Self-Checking Inverse Arithmetic ([f] [LASTX])
docs.text:
• Keycap: Row 3, Col 1 ([f] [LASTX])
  • The Challenge in Early Math: Teachers constantly urge students to "check your work." But checking addition via subtraction or checking multiplication via division requires re-typing numbers, creating new opportunities for typing errors and cognitive fatigue.
  • The RPN Solution: The SC-6 hardware automatically preserves the value that was in Register \(X\) immediately prior to any arithmetic operation inside a dedicated hardware register called LAST x.
  • Suppose you calculate \(47 + 36 = 83\): 47 [ENTER] 36 [+] \(\implies \mathbf{83}\)
  • To verify the calculation, you simply press [f] [LASTX]:
  • The previous number (\(36\)) is recalled into Register \(X\), automatically pushing the result (\(83\)) into Register \(Y\).
  • You press [-]: $\(83 - 36 = 47\)$
  • The original starting number (\(47\)) reappears! You have independently verified your work in two keystrokes without writing down a single intermediate digit.

docs.title: 6. Visual Manipulative Sandboxes Overview
docs.text:
The SC-6 integrates five dedicated visual manipulative sandboxes directly into the dual-stack calculation engine. Unlike educational apps that isolate visual models in separate mini-games, the SC-6 renders manipulatives in-place within the \(Y \mid X\) stack registers, allowing live RPN arithmetic directly with concrete visual objects!

SC-6 VISUAL MANIPULATIVE SANDBOXES

  1. TEN-FRAME STUDIO [▦] • Dual 2x5 dot-matrix frames in Y and X columns. • Solid circular counters (●) and open cells (○). • Number bond complement readout: e.g. "7 (10-3)" and "3 (10-7)". • Tap [.] to add counters one-by-one; tap digits (7) to set directly. • Press [+] to combine frames: 7 + 3 fills a complete 10-frame!
  2. NUMBER LINE JUMPING TOOL [LINE] • Horizontal integer axis with dynamic tick window and numeral labels. • Start point dot at Y; forward hop arcs for [+], backward arcs for [-]. • Full support for negative numbers: hops left of zero naturally. • Multi-jump arcs for skip-counting and array multiplication.
  3. NUMBER RACK / REKENREK [g] [COUNT] • Dual horizontal wires with 10 beads each (5 solid ●, 5 hollow ○). • Rest position on right; active counted position on left. • Seeing groups of 5 and 10 at a glance with tactile slide transitions.
  4. PLANETARY ANALOG CLOCK [🕒] & DIGITAL TIME [🕒] • Dual 12-hour analog clock dials with vector-rendered hands. • Continuous hour hand angles: at 3:30, hour hand is at 105°, not 90°! • Modulo-60 elapsed time arithmetic via native HP-32SII H.MMSS format. • Instant conversion to pure decimal hours via [f] [▸HR] (strictly no units).
  5. CLASSROOM DICE [🎲] & RPN EQUATION QUIZ ENGINE [?] • 32x32 pixel die face with authentic pip patterns (1 to 6). • Discrete PRNG tools for probability labs: [f] [1…x] and [g] [t…x]. • Gamified Math Quiz Engine: 6 levels of rapid arithmetic sprints with streak scoring.

docs.title: 6.1 Mode Annunciator Badges & Non-Destructive Switching
docs.text:
Whenever a visual sandbox is active, the top LCD status bar displays a high-contrast 1-bit mode annunciator badge:

Active Display Mode Header Badge Visual LCD Representation Regular Number Mode (Default) (None) Standard 41+ px digits (\(Y \mid X\) dual or \(X\) single) Ten-Frame Mode [▦] \(2 \times 5\) concrete grid frames with nearest-10 overflow Number Line Mode [LINE] Horizontal axis with jumping parabolic arcs Number Rack / Rekenrek [g] [COUNT] 10 beads along wires (5 solid, 5 hollow) Analog Clock Face Mode [🕒] 12-hour analog clock dials with hour/minute hands Digital Time Mode [🕒] Colon-separated digital time (H:MM:SS) Quiz / Equation Mode [f] [?] Gamified arithmetic sprints across Levels 1–6 with streak scoring

docs.title: 6.2 Three Foolproof Ways to Return to Regular Number Mode
docs.text:
Students and teachers never get "trapped" inside a visual mode. The SC-6 provides three foolproof, frictionless pathways to return immediately to standard numbers: 1. Universal [C] (Clear / Cancel) Key: Pressing [C] (Row 7, Col 1) when no digits are actively being typed instantly dismisses any active visual mode and restores Regular Number Mode ([NUM]). 2. Mode Key Toggle: Tapping the active mode key a second time acts as an immediate toggle back to Regular Number Mode (e.g. in [▦], pressing [▦] returns to numbers). 3. Number Display Keys ([g] [FIX], [f] [ALL], [FDISP]): Pressing any standard numerical formatting key immediately exits visual graphics and renders the active stack in that numerical format.

Strict Data Preservation Guarantee: Switching between visual modes and number mode is 100% non-destructive. The stack registers (\(X, Y, Z, T\)), LAST x, and continuous memory are never altered. Visual modes are simply alternative optical lenses for viewing the exact same underlying RPN stack values.

docs.title: 8. Quick-Start Adventure Showcase: 30 Things You Will Master Across K–6
docs.text:
To show you the fun, speed, and superpower clarity of Stack Math across your entire elementary math journey, here are 30 exciting hands-on adventures! Each adventure features an authentic mission, step-by-step keystrokes, a full 4-register stack trace table (\(T, Z, Y, X\)), and a pointer to the chapter where you can explore the topic in depth.

QUICK-START ADVENTURE SHOWCASE DIRECTORY

Adventures 01–05 : Grades K–1 Counting, Number Bonds & Single-Digit Addition (Explore in Chapter 03) Adventures 06–10 : Grade 2 Place Value Bundling, Doubling & Subtraction (Explore in Chapters 03 & 04) Adventures 11–15 : Grade 3 Array Multiplication & Rhythmic Skip-Counting (Explore in Chapter 04) Adventures 16–20 : Grade 4 Division with Remainder & Sharing Scenarios (Explore in Chapters 04 & 05) Adventures 21–25 : Grade 5 Fraction Arithmetic, Towers & Reduction (Explore in Chapters 05 & 06) Adventures 26–30 : Grade 6 Mixed Operations, Time & Surface Area Memory (Explore in Chapters 06, 07 & 09)

docs.title: 8.1 Adventure 01: The Ten-Frame Number Bond (Making 10)
docs.text:

  • Visual Sandbox Keystrokes: Press [▦], then enter 7.

Keystroke Register T Register Z Register Y Register X Operational Commentary [C] 0 0 0 0 Clean baseline stack in [NUM] mode. 10 0 0 0 10 Key target capacity (\(10\)) into Ground Floor \(X\). [ENTER] 0 0 10 10 Target capacity lifts smoothly into Mezzanine Floor \(Y\). 7 0 0 10 7 Enter red counters into Ground Floor \(X\). [-] 0 0 0 3 Subtraction combines \(Y - X = 3\). Result in \(X\)!

For Parents & Teachers: The Diagnostic Misconception Playbook

When children first encounter a calculator, they bring intuitive habits formed from pencil-and-paper worksheets and consumer touchscreen apps. The following diagnostic playbook equips classroom teachers and homeschooling parents with instant detection clues, root cause explanations, and exact remediation keystrokes:

**SC-6 DIAGNOSTIC MISCONCEPTION & REMEDIATION MATRIX** | Observable Screen State | Probable Misconception | Exact Remediation Steps | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Register $X$ shows `0` after entering numbers | Student pressed `[C]` expecting "Confirm" instead of `[ENTER]`. | Explain that `[C]` clears active input. Use `[ENTER]` to commit! | | Register $X$ shows `16` instead of `8` on $12 - 4$ problem | Pressed `[+]` instead of `[-]` on minuend/subtrahend. | Press `[f] [LASTX]` to restore subtrahend ($4$), then press `[-]` twice! | | Screen displays `3.4` instead of `Q: 3, R: 2` on $17 \div 5$ | Student used regular division `[÷]` instead of integer `[g] [÷R]`. | Remind student to use `[g] [÷R]` for whole division with remainder. | | Fraction displays unreduced `12/18` after addition | Wondering why $12/18$ did not simplify automatically. | Explain SC-6 unreduced default: student deliberately presses `[g] [SIMP]`. | | Transient display flashes `LOWEST TERMS` | Student pressed `[g] [SIMP]` on an irreducible fraction (e.g. $2/3$). | Celebrate! Fraction is in irreducible form ($\gcd(\text{num}, \text{den}) = 1$). | | Display shows `3:50` instead of `3:30` in `[🕒]` | Student entered `3.5` expecting 3 hours and 30 minutes (half hour). | Explain clock format: 30 minutes is `.30`, not `.5`! Key `3.30` for 3:30. | | Transient display flashes `INVALID DATA` in Ten-Frame mode | Attempted negative number in `[▦]` or non-power-of-10 in `[PV]`. | Explain ten-frame rules: a physical frame cannot hold negative dots. | #### Misconception 1: The "Confirm with Clear" Reflex - **Student Behavior:** The child keys `12`, then habitually taps `[C]` because on a smartphone or cash register, `C` is sometimes confused with "Continue" or "Confirm." Register $X$ resets to `0`, and the child complains that the calculator "lost" their number. - **Root Cause:** Conflation of Clear with Enter. - **Teacher Script:** *"Remember, on StackCalc, the big [ENTER] key is like the elevator doors closing. It locks your number into the elevator so it can ride upstairs to Floor Y. The [C] key is the red emergency button that sends everyone out of the building. Use [ENTER] when you want to keep your number!"* #### Misconception 2: Decimal Hours vs. Clock Minutes - **Student Behavior:** When trying to enter 2 hours and 30 minutes, a Grade 4 student types `2.5` because they know that 30 minutes is "half an hour." When they switch to `[🕒]`, the screen displays `2:50:00` (2 hours and 50 minutes). - **Root Cause:** Conflating decimal fraction of an hour ($0.5\text{ hr}$) with clock hours, minutes, and seconds notation (`H.MMSS`). - **Remediation:** 1. Have the student observe the difference: in `[🕒]` mode, `2.30` translates directly to `2:30:00`. 2. If they have `2.50` decimal hours and want colon time, press `[f] [▸HR]` to convert between decimal hours and `H.MMSS` automatically! #### Misconception 3: The Order of Subtraction & Division - **Student Behavior:** In evaluating $15 - 8$, the student keys `8 [ENTER] 15 [-]` and gets `-7`. - **Root Cause:** In traditional reading, they saw "subtract 8 from 15" and typed 8 first. - **Teacher Script:** *"Look at the horizontal screen. The left column (Y) is what you have in your basket first. The right column (X) is what you take away. If you have 15 apples and take away 8, the 15 must go into the left column first: 15 [ENTER] 8 [-]!"* - **Quick Fix Keystroke:** If the student enters them backward (`8 [ENTER] 15`), tell them: *"Do not re-type! Just tap [x⇄y] to swap their columns, then press [-]!"*

For Parents & Teachers: Infix Parenthesis Clutter vs. RPN Keystroke Efficiency Audit

To see how Reverse Polish Notation eliminates clutter and speeds up calculation, compare these classic elementary problems solved on a standard algebraic (infix) calculator versus the StackCalc SC-6:

| Problem & Curriculum Context | Algebraic Infix Keystrokes | SC-6 RPN Keystrokes | Stroke Economy | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **1. Inverse Check** $(47 + 36) - 36 = 47$ | `47 + 36 = - 36 =` (re-types number) | `47` `[ENTER]` `36` `[+]` `[f] [LASTX]` `[-]` | **6 strokes** vs. 9 | | **2. Order of Operations** $(15 - 3) \times (4 + 2) \div 6$ | `( 15 - 3 ) × ( 4 + 2 ) ÷ 6 =` | `15 [ENTER] 3 [-] 4 [ENTER] 2 [+] [×] 6 [÷]` $\to$ **`12`** | **11 strokes** vs. 18 (zero parens) | | **3. Division with Remainder** $125 \div 8 = 15\text{ R }5$ | `125 ÷ 8 =` ($15.625$), then `15 × 8 = 120`, `125 - 120 =` | `125` `[ENTER]` `8` `[g] [÷R]` $\to$ `15` ($Y$) & `5` ($X$) | **5 strokes** vs. 21 + paper | | **4. Adding Unlike Fractions** $\frac{3}{8} + \frac{5}{12} = \frac{19}{24}$ | `( 3 ÷ 8 ) + ( 5 ÷ 12 ) =` (yields decimal `0.79167`) | `. 3 . 8` `[ENTER]` `. 5 . 12` `[+]` $\to$ **`19/24`** | **8 strokes** vs. 17 | | **5. Surface Area of $5 \times 4 \times 3$ Prism** | `2 × 5 × 4 + 2 × 5 × 3 + 2 × 4 × 3 =` | Accumulate face pairs with `[Σ+]`, then `[f] [Σx]` $\to$ **`94`** | Zero scratch paper |

Why RPN Eliminates Cognitive Overload: 1. Zero Parentheses: On algebraic calculators, students must hold the entire mathematical expression in working memory while managing open and close parentheses ( and ). A missing parenthesis causes a syntax error that wipes out entry. On the SC-6, students evaluate sub-expressions as they go. Working memory is freed to focus on mathematical concepts rather than punctuation syntax. 2. Zero Scratch Paper: Notice Problem 3 (Division with Remainder). On an infix calculator, finding the remainder requires three separate calculations and intermediate notes on scratch paper. On the SC-6, pressing [g] [÷R] provides both quotient and remainder simultaneously in 5 keystrokes. 3. Frictionless Error Recovery: In Problem 1, pressing [f] [LASTX] recalls the previous number from hardware memory, enabling instant inverse verification in 2 keystrokes.

docs.title: 9. How to Use This Textbook & Learning Pathways
9.1 Reading Pathways
docs.text: This manual is structured to support multiple learning environments: - Classroom Teachers: Begin with Chapter 01 for instrument ergonomics and setup, followed by Appendix B for turnkey 45-minute station plans. Use the Unlocked Keycaps Ribbon at the top of each chapter to enforce developmental grade boundaries. - Homeschooling Families: Progress sequentially through Chapters 02 through 07. Focus on the diagnostic checkpoints at the end of each worked problem to ensure your child experiences steady, confident progress without frustration. - STEM Specialists & Makers: Dive directly into Chapter 08, Chapter 09, and Appendix A to fabricate physical manipulatives on 3D printers and lead hands-on maker labs. - Calculator Connoisseurs: Explore Chapter 02 for stack dynamics comparisons against the HP-32SII, Chapter 06 for the Master Surface Area via Stats Mode technique, and Chapter 07 for number-theoretic dualities.

docs.title: 9.2 Automated Engine Reliability Guarantee
docs.text:
To maintain the highest standard of educational trust and publishing integrity, every mathematical equation, keystroke sequence, and diagnostic readout documented across all chapters of this manual is continuously verified against the underlying StackCalc calculation engine.

Our automated verification suite runs hundreds of algorithmic checks covering: - Two-Stack & Whole Number Arithmetic: Proving non-destructive place value extraction, quotient and remainder precision, and exact register conservation. - Visual Manipulative Synchronizations: Guaranteeing 100% data preservation when toggling between visual sandboxes (Ten-Frames, Number Line, Dice) and standard numerical mode. - Timed Mental Math Sprints: Verifying millisecond response timers, streak scoring algorithms, and spaced retrieval queues in the hardware quiz engine.

Every single calculation presented in this volume executes with zero errors, ensuring that what you read in print corresponds exactly to what your fingers experience on the physical instrument. Welcome to the joy of tactile mathematics and Reverse Polish Notation!

docs.title: 10. Safety, Regulatory, Trademark & Parent/Educator Notices
docs.text:
[!WARNING] CHOKING HAZARD — SMALL PARTS (16 CFR § 1501 / ASTM F963): The physical StackCalc manipulative kits (Counting & Array Tiles, Ten-Frame Flip Counters, Fraction Studio 1/12 Blocks, Prime Factor Studio Blocks, Math Dominoes, and Polyhedral Dice) contain small modular parts (\(7.0\,\text{mm}\) minimum thickness). Not for children under 3 years of age. Use only under adult or educator supervision for learners in Grades K–6 (ages 5+). - 3D-Printed Part Inspection: When fabricating manipulative kits on classroom or home Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) 3D printers, adults must use non-toxic PLA or PETG filament and inspect every finished piece prior to student handling—removing any loose filament strings, sharp seam burrs, or delaminated layers.

A swallowed button or coin cell battery can cause Internal Chemical Burns in as little as 2 hours. - KEEP new and used batteries OUT OF REACH of children. docs.title: 1.1 Why Real Buttons and Blocks Beat a Glowing Tablet Screen
docs.text:
Picture an eight-year-old sitting at a wooden kitchen table on a rainy Tuesday afternoon. A math book is open to multi-digit subtraction, but right beside it rests a school tablet. Within ninety seconds of starting homework, a red notification badge slides across the glass: a message chime, a game update, a colorful video banner. Even when locked in "study mode," the tablet's harsh electric backlight beams straight into your eyes like a tiny flashlight. Your eyes feel tired, your head starts to ache, and your brain is pulled in twenty directions at once. The glowing tablet feels like an amusement arcade pretending to be a desk!

Now look at the other side of your desk: the StackCalc SC-6. Molded from tough, dark Midnight Navy armor, it has no Wi-Fi, no pop-up alerts, no games, and no distractions. Its screen doesn't beam harsh light into your face—it reads just like a paper book using the gentle daylight in your room. And when you press a key, your finger doesn't smear across cold, mushy glass. Beneath every key sits a tiny stainless-steel dome that clicks down with a crisp, satisfying snap! Your fingers feel the click and your ears hear the snap: the number is pushed onto the stack, and you are ready for the next step.

Figure 1.1: The StackCalc SC-6 Elementary Handheld in Midnight Navy with sliding 15° easel desk cowl. A dedicated tactile tool for deep mathematical focus.

The SC-6 is built like an astronaut's pocket instrument. Nothing on it is flimsy or disposable. Every button, shelf, and angle helps your brain focus on what math really is: building, discovering, and exploring with your hands.

For Parents & Teachers: Cognitive Load & Working Memory Limits

In John Sweller’s Cognitive Load Theory *([Sweller, 1988](appendix-c-formulas-and-conversions.md#cite-sweller1988))*, extraneous mental load from glowing tablets and split attention destroys mathematical understanding. George A. Miller’s foundational research on working memory limits ($7 \pm 2$ items) *([Miller, 1956](appendix-c-formulas-and-conversions.md#cite-miller1956))* explains why young minds drown under notification-heavy operating systems. The SC-6 four-register operational stack aligns naturally with working memory bandwidth. Following David Macaulay’s cutaway architecture of physical machines *([Macaulay, 2016](appendix-c-formulas-and-conversions.md#cite-macaulay2016))*, every radius, wall thickness, and micro-foamed snap-dome was engineered to anchor the child’s wandering attention in the tactile reality of mathematical thought.

CHAPTER BASELINE MODE: [NUM] Standard Base-10 Arithmetic • 4-Stack XYZT • Clean Display

Unlocked Keycaps Ribbon — Hardware & Instrument Control

• Instrument Controls: [C] Clear / Reset, [<-] Destructive Backspace, [g] [OFF] Low-Power Deep Standby, [g] [FLAGS] Hardware System Flags. • Hardware Status Display: Four-register active stack (T, Z, Y, X), Battery Reserve Indicator, Active Visual Sandbox Header Badge ([▦], [f] [LINE], [PV], [🕒], [🎲], [f] [?]). • Classroom Safety Envelope: Recessed display window with 1.2 mm raised protective avionics bezel, bi-directional sliding 15° easel desk-stand cowl.

[!NOTE] Faceplate Themes & Shift Legend Conventions: Because the StackCalc SC-6 hardware faceplates and companion app support multiple visual themes (Pure Black, Retro Futurism, Pioneer, Stealth, Supernova, Voyager, and Arcade), keycap and shift accent colors vary by faceplate. Throughout this textbook, shifted operations are always referenced by their functional shift symbols rather than color: [f] Shift (Row 5, Col 0) and [g] Shift (Row 6, Col 0).

docs.title: 1.2 Meet Your Stack Calculator: The Screen, The Number Stack & Your Secret Shift Keys
docs.text: Before we build block towers and solve puzzles, let's take a quick tour of your calculator: its daylight screen, the 4-level number stack, the big ENTER button, and the secret shift keys.

docs.title: 1.2.1 The Daylight Screen & The 4-Level Number Stack (\(T, Z, Y, X\))
docs.text:
Unlike phones or tablets that shine bright electric light straight into your eyes, the SC-6 features a Daylight Screen. It reads just like paper in a book, catching the natural light in your room!

On the screen, numbers don't vanish into hidden memory. Instead, they stack up on four visible shelves—the 4-Level Number Stack (\(T, Z, Y, X\)), just like stacking physical blocks, pancakes, or books on your desk: - Level \(X\) (The Ground Shelf / Active Entry): This is the bottom shelf of the screen where numbers appear as you type them, and where the immediate results of every calculation appear. - Level \(Y\) (The Second Shelf / Waiting Partner): When you tap [ENTER], your number pushes smoothly up to Level \(Y\). Level \(Y\) holds the first number waiting for math to happen (like the \(12\) waiting in \(12 - 4\)). - Levels \(Z\) and \(T\) (The Mezzanine and Top Shelves): Above \(Y\) sit two more shelves. When you push several numbers onto the stack, previous values rise into \(Z\) and \(T\). When operations execute, values drop down from \(T\) to \(Z\) to \(Y\) automatically, letting you solve big multi-step problems without scratch paper or parentheses!

docs.title: 1.2.2 The Big ENTER Button: Pushing Numbers Onto the Stack
docs.text:
Look at the big, friendly black [ENTER] button in the lower-right area of the keypad. It is the heart of Stack Math!

In ordinary school arithmetic, you might have been taught to fear the equals sign (=) because it acts like a sudden test. On the SC-6: 1. There is no = button: In Stack Math, combining two numbers is the answer! When you tap [+], [-], [×], or [÷], the operator fuses the quantities on Level \(Y\) and Level \(X\) immediately and visibly. 2. [ENTER] commits and pushes: When typing a number, tapping [ENTER] signals that entry is complete, pushes the value of Level \(X\) upward onto Level \(Y\), and lifts previous values into \(Z\) and \(T\). The next digits you type enter fresh into Level \(X\) without overwriting Level \(Y\).

docs.title: 1.2.3 One Button, Three Superpowers: How the [f] and [g] Keys Work
docs.text: Instead of hiding cool math tools inside confusing computer menus, each button on the SC-6 has up to three superpowers: - Primary White Keycap (Direct Press): Tapping any key directly executes its primary action printed in crisp white on the keycap face (numeric digits 0–9, [ENTER], [+], [-], [×], [÷], clear [C], and backspace [<-]). - [f] Shift Key (Row 5, Col 0): Pressing [f] first unlocks the secret superpower printed directly above the keycap. This includes tools like finding common multiples with [f] [LCM], simplifying fractions step-by-step with [g] [SIMP], unit conversions, and memory register recall [f] [REGS]. - [g] Shift Key (Row 6, Col 0): Pressing [g] first unlocks the secret superpower printed on or below the keycap. This includes prime factor trees with [g] [FACT], skip-counting replication with [g] [REP], integer division with remainder [g] [÷R], low-power standby [g] [OFF], and hardware settings [g] [FLAGS].

docs.title: 1.2.4 Setting Up Your 15° Classroom Desk Stand
docs.text: Your SC-6 includes a rugged, bi-directional sliding protective cowl. At the start of math time: 1. Slide the protective cover downward off the front of the calculator. 2. Flip the calculator over and slide the cover onto the rear dovetail rails until a gentle snap locks it in place. 3. Set the SC-6 on your desk—it now rests at a stable \(15^\circ\) reading angle, right beside your manipulative block tray, keeping both hands completely free: your left hand can build a fraction tower or place counters in a ten-frame, while your right hand taps keys into the stack!

Screen washes out in classroom daylight (\(1,000\text{ lux}\)). SC-6 + Base-10 Blocks: Slide cowl to 15° easel \(\to\) lay 3 hundreds flats, 4 ten-rods, 7 unit cubes \(\to\) tap 347 [ENTER] on 400g snap-domes. Sunlight transflective LCD has infinite contrast. 4 strokes vs. 12+ steps (67% reduction) Level \(X = 347\) rests visible on the ground shelf; previous results wait upstairs in \(Y, Z, T\). Tactile Confirmation Smooth flat glass: no physical boundary between digits, zero tactile click, high error rate from accidental adjacent touches. 400-gram stainless snap-domes provide an audible click and physical snap; fingers know instantly that the stroke committed. 1 mechanical snap per digit Zero missed or doubled keystrokes; visual and haptic verification. Four visible shelves (\(T, Z, Y, X\)): every operand and intermediate result remains in plain sight on the screen. docs.title: 1.3 Why the Calculator Is Dark and the Blocks Are Bright
docs.text:
Why is your calculator molded in dark Midnight Navy or Slate Gray, while your math blocks are bright white, radiant gold, and electric blue?

Think about how an astronomer uses a telescope: the inside tube of the telescope is painted dark matte black so stray light doesn't bounce into your eyes, letting you focus clearly on the stars. The dark shell of your SC-6 creates a quiet, restful frame of deep focus around the display with zero glare.

Your math blocks, on the other hand, are the stars! They are molded in bright archival white, warm amber, and vivid cobalt blue because blocks are meant to be touched, sorted, and counted! Your hands instinctively reach for the bright physical objects to build arrays, trains, and towers, while your eyes rest comfortably on the dark, glare-free calculator that records the results. The dark instrument and the luminous blocks form a natural visual team: the blocks are the physical stage, and the calculator is the quiet recording engine.

For Parents & Teachers: Color Discipline & Physical Manipulatives

To prevent cognitive confusion in young learners, the SC-6 establishes a strict material separation: all exterior handheld calculator chassis, bezels, and battery covers are molded exclusively from dark, impact-modified technical thermoplastics (Midnight Navy, Space Gray, and Technical Matte Black). White polymers are strictly quarantined to physical math manipulatives (84 mm Fraction Towers, Ten-Frame counters, and Planetary Clock gears) so students never confuse the calculating engine with the tactile math objects.

docs.title: 1.4 Built Like a Tank: How Your Calculator Survives the Classroom
docs.text:
Classroom tools must endure energetic daily life: slipping off 30-inch classroom desks onto hard floors, tumbling in backpacks packed with heavy metal binders, and surviving custodial wipe-downs.

The SC-6 is built around four physical principles of durability:

docs.title: 1.4.1 What Hides Inside a Clicking Button?
docs.text:
Beneath every keycap rests a tiny arch of spring-tempered stainless steel, shaped like a microscopic umbrella. When your finger pushes down on the dished keycap, the metal arch resists until you reach exactly 400 grams of downward force. At that precise instant, the dome buckles downward with a crisp, audible snap, bridging two gold-plated electrical contacts on the circuit board below.

You feel that snap instantly in your fingertip and hear a gentle click. You never have to wonder, Did the calculator hear me? Your finger felt the number commit. As soon as you lift your finger, the steel arch springs back to its resting shape in less than two milliseconds, ready for your next number. This mechanical feedback completely eliminates the double-taps and skipped strokes common to flimsy rubber calculators.

docs.title: 1.4.2 Why Your Screen Works Like Paper Instead of a Flashlight
docs.text:
Most phone and tablet screens are like tiny lightbulbs: they shine bright electric light directly into your eyes, causing pupils to constrict and delicate eye muscles to tire after twenty minutes of homework.

The SC-6 uses a transflective dot-matrix screen that produces zero light of its own (\(0.00\text{ mW/sr}\cdot\text{m}^2\)). Instead, it operates just like the printed paper page of this book. Ambient daylight enters through the protective front glass, passes through the liquid crystal numerals, strikes a mirror-like reflector on the back wall of the screen, and bounces straight back out to your eyes. The brighter the classroom or the sunshine on the patio, the crisper and blacker the numbers appear! You can explore math for hours without a hint of optical strain.

docs.title: 1.4.3 The Sliding 15° Desk Stand: Built-in Easel
docs.text:
Slide the protective cover downward off the front face of the calculator. Turn the calculator over and examine the back: two precision dovetail guide rails run along the outer edges of the chassis. Slide the cowl upward along those rails until a gentle snap locks it firmly in place.

Set the instrument down on your desk. The SC-6 now tilts toward your eyes at an exact \(15^\circ\) reading angle—just like a miniature drafting easel! Both of your hands remain completely free: your left hand can build a fraction tower or arrange counters in a ten-frame, while your right hand taps numbers into the stack. When math time concludes, slide the cowl off the back, slide it over the front glass display, and place the calculator into your backpack. The screen is armor-plated against metal binder rings, rulers, and compass points.

docs.title: 1.4.4 Secret White Bubbles: Why the Letters Never Rub Off
docs.text:
Traditional school calculators print their numbers and symbols with surface ink. Within a few months of daily math practice, your fingers wear off the numbers—leaving blank keys right when you need them most.

The SC-6 completely eliminates surface ink. Instead, every number and symbol is permanently created inside the keycap using 1064nm Infrared Laser Micro-Foaming:

How Laser Micro-Foaming Works Inside the Keycap

• Invisible Light, Below the Surface: A focused infrared laser passes harmlessly through the top protective skin of the keycap without burning or scratching the surface. • Microscopic White Bubbles: Tiny mineral particles blended inside the polymer absorb that brief flash of warmth and expand into millions of microscopic, light-scattering gas bubbles sealed safely beneath the outer skin. • Lifetime Classroom Legibility: Just as white seafoam looks bright white because tiny bubbles scatter light in every direction, those sealed micro-bubbles create a crisp chalk-white symbol (15.2:1 AAA contrast) that can never be scraped off, worn away by thumbs, or dissolved by classroom cleaning wipes.

Each keycap features a gentle \(0.8\text{ mm}\) spherical concave dish in SpaceMono-Bold typography that naturally guides your fingertip toward the center of the key, tested to over 1,000,000 presses with zero fading.

docs.title: 1.5 Instant-On Readiness & Continuous Backpack Memory
docs.text:
Beneath the tough thermoplastic shell, the SC-6 is engineered so you never wait for a booting screen and never lose your work:

Instrument Feature Classroom & Backpack Advantage Instant-On Readiness Wakes from sleep in under \(5\text{ milliseconds}\) the moment you press [C] Continuous Memory Automatically preserves all stack numbers, registers, and quiz streaks when powered off Year-Long Power Reserve A single CR2032 coin cell provides over \(350\text{ hours}\) of active classroom discovery

When the SC-6 turns off—either by pressing [g] [OFF] or after 3 minutes of quiet desk time—it saves every number on your stack (\(X, Y, Z, T\)), your LASTX history, your statistical sums, and your math quiz streak into non-volatile memory. A problem started in class can be tucked into your backpack and resumed at the kitchen table after school without losing a single step.

docs.title: 1.6 Meet Your Math Blocks: Building Numbers with Your Hands
docs.text: To make sure every number on the screen connects directly to something you can hold and explore, your StackCalc SC-6 comes with eight physical 3D-printed math block sets. Each set is molded in bright, durable colors that match the calculator's screen modes and number stack:

docs.title: 1.6.1 The Ten-Frame Trays & Flip Counters
docs.text:
• The Physical Tool: Two 5-pocket trays with ten two-color disc counters (coral red on one side, radiant gold on the other). Built-in scoops make it easy for your fingers to slide and flip counters.
  • How It Works with the SC-6: Tap [▦] to mirror your trays right on the screen! Register \(Y\) shows the top tray, and Register \(X\) shows the bottom tray. Flip counters to find friend pairs that make 10 (\(7 \text{ red} + 3 \text{ gold} = 10\)). Tap [+], and watch the counters group into a full ten with extras left over (\(7 + 5 = 12\)) right on the stack!

docs.title: 1.6.2 The Four-Color Counting & Array Studio
docs.text:
• The Physical Tool: 144 smooth-docking counting tiles in four colors: clean white, cobalt blue, radiant gold, and slate gray. Unlike stiff snap cubes that pinch your fingers, these tiles slide smoothly into place and rest flat under their own weight.
  • How It Works with the SC-6: Arrange tiles into rows and columns to build rectangular arrays for multiplication (\(4 \times 6 = 24\)). Row count sits on Level \(Y\), column count sits on Level \(X\), and tapping [×] calculates the total tiles. Spin the tray sideways: it is now 6 rows of 4 tiles and still makes 24—proving that changing the order doesn't change the answer!

docs.title: 1.6.3 The 84 mm Fraction Towers & Comparator Tray
docs.text:
• The Physical Tool: A precision \(84.0\text{ mm}\) master tower for the whole (\(1\)), along with matching fraction pieces (\(1/2\), \(1/3\), \(1/4\), \(1/6\), \(1/8\), \(1/12\)) and a side-by-side comparison tray.
  • Why Exactly 84 mm? Because 84 is a magical number for fractions: it divides cleanly by \(1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 12, 14, 21, 28, \text{ and } 42\)! That means every single fraction piece has an exact, clean height in millimeters (\(1/1 = 84\text{ mm}\), \(1/2 = 42\text{ mm}\), \(1/3 = 28\text{ mm}\), \(1/4 = 21\text{ mm}\), \(1/6 = 14\text{ mm}\), \(1/12 = 7\text{ mm}\)) with zero uneven edges!
  • How It Works with the SC-6: Snap two \(1/4\) towers together in the tray, and feel with your finger how their top edge matches the \(1/2\) tower perfectly! On the calculator, type . 2 . 4, tap [g] [SIMP], and watch the numbers shrink to 1/2 while your blocks stay locked flush in the tray.

docs.title: 1.6.4 The Prime Factor Studio & Number Block Scale
docs.text:
• The Physical Tool: Secret puzzle blocks for prime numbers (\(2, 3, 5, 7, \dots\)) whose heights scale so that stacking blocks multiplies their numbers together!
  • How It Works with the SC-6: Stacking block 2 on top of block 3 reaches the exact height of 6 on the back-wall scale! On the SC-6, type 60 and tap [g] [FACT] to watch the screen reveal its secret prime building blocks: \(2^2 \times 3 \times 5\).

docs.title: 1.6.5 The Planetary Geared Clock
docs.text:
• The Physical Tool: A real working clock with interlocking planetary gear teeth. When you turn the big minute hand with your thumb, the hour hand automatically glides at the exact real speed!
  • How It Works with the SC-6: Tap [🕒] to open the clock screen. Enter a start time and elapsed minutes, then tap [+]. The calculator moves hands on screen and calculates arrival times across 60-minute boundaries without getting mixed up!

docs.title: 1.6.6 The Polyhedral Dice & Spinner Studio
docs.text:
• The Physical Tool: Precision gaming dice (\(d4, d6, d8, d10, d12, d20\)) and a balanced spinning dial for classroom probability games.
  • How It Works with the SC-6: Roll dice across your desk to collect experimental data. Tap [🎲] to roll matching digital dice into Level \(X\), saving your rolls on levels \(Y, Z, T\) to create live dot plots and frequency tables.

docs.title: 1.6.7 The Place Value Studio
docs.text:
• The Physical Tool: Proportional base-10 unit blocks (\(1\)), ten-sticks (\(10\)), hundred-flats (\(100\)), and thousand-cubes (\(1000\)).
  • How It Works with the SC-6: Group unit blocks into tens and ten-sticks into hundreds. Tap [PV] to split any multi-digit number across the stack shelves, displaying expanded form (\(347 = 300 + 40 + 7\)) with matching visual block counters!

docs.title: 1.6.8 The Number Rack (Rekenrek)
docs.text:
• The Physical Tool: Two sturdy metal rails with ten sliding beads each, split into five red beads and five white beads.
  • How It Works with the SC-6: The top rail links to Level \(Y\) and the bottom rail links to Level \(X\). Slide beads with your fingers to see groupings of 5 and 10 at a glance before doing arithmetic on the keypad.

docs.title: 1.7 Taking Care of Your Stack Calculator
1.7.1 Adjusting Screen Contrast
docs.text:
If your daylight screen appears too faint in a cozy room or too dark under bright sunshine, you can tune it in seconds: 1. Press [g] [FLAGS]. 2. Press [7] for Display Contrast. 3. Tap [+] to make numbers darker, or [-] to make the background lighter. 4. Press [ENTER] to save your favorite setting!

For Parents & Teachers: Instrument Maintenance & Diagnostic Checkpoints

**1. Battery Voltage & Replacement:** When battery voltage drops below 2.65V, a low-battery outline flashes in the upper-right corner of the LCD. An adult should use a coin and small screwdriver to open the tool-secured rear hatch and install a fresh CR2032 coin cell with positive (+) terminal facing up. Stack values and quiz records are preserved in non-volatile EEPROM memory. **2. Complete Memory Reset (Factory Clean):** To clear all user registers, quiz history, and custom flags before an evaluation: hold `[C]` down firmly, tap `[g] [OFF]`, then release. The display flashes `"ALL REGISTERS RESET - FACTORY CLEAN"`. **3. Child-Resistant Battery Hatch Security (ANSI/UL 4200A):** The rear battery hatch utilizes a coin-slot bayonet mechanism with an internal safety detent requiring 15N inward force while rotating 45° counter-clockwise. Inspect annually to ensure the silicone O-ring seal is seated.

COIN CELL BATTERY INGESTION HAZARD (REESE'S LAW / 16 CFR PART 1263)

This instrument operates on a CR2032 3.0V lithium coin cell battery. DEATH or serious injury can occur if ingested. A swallowed button or coin cell battery can cause Internal Chemical Burns in as little as 2 hours. KEEP new and used batteries OUT OF REACH of children. Battery replacement must be performed exclusively by an adult, ensuring the retention fastener is securely tightened. Seek immediate medical attention if a battery is suspected to be swallowed or inserted inside any part of the body (U.S. National Battery Ingestion Hotline: 1-800-498-8666).

docs.title: 1.8 What to Do If You Get Stuck (Troubleshooting Pathways)
1.8.1 Screen Is Dark or Blank
docs.text:
• Check 1 (Sleep Mode): The SC-6 automatically goes to sleep after 3 minutes to save power. Tap [C] once—the screen wakes instantly in under 5 milliseconds!
  • Check 2 (Room Light): Remember, your daylight screen produces zero blue light and works by reflecting the light in your room. If the room is dark, turn on a lamp or move near a window.
  • Check 3 (Battery Check): If tapping [C] under bright light does not wake the screen, ask an adult to inspect the CR2032 coin cell battery.

docs.title: 1.8.2 Returning to Normal Numbers from a Sandbox Mode
docs.text: If your screen is showing clock dials ([🕒]), ten-frames ([▦]), or number lines ([f] [LINE]), and you want standard numbers back, choose any of these three easy pathways: 1. The Universal Clear Key: Tap [C] once or twice. When no digits are actively being typed, [C] instantly returns to Regular Number Mode ([NUM]). 2. The Mode Toggle: Tap the active mode button again (if in [▦], tap [▦] again). 3. The Format Keys: Tap any number format key ([g] [FIX], [f] [ALL], or [FDISP]) to exit the visual tool immediately.

docs.title: 1.9 Hands-On Studio Proof: Your First Math Discovery
docs.text:
Hands-On Studio Proof: The Tactile Instrument & The Manipulative Dock

Step 1 (Physical Concrete Intuition): Take your 3D-printed Ten-Frame tray and counting tiles from your manipulative studio. Slide the SC-6 protective cowl off the front face and dock it into the dual bottom rails at the 15° classroom easel incline. Step 2 (The Representational Bridge): Press [C] to wake the instrument. Feel the authoritative 400g snap-dome click under your thumb. The transflective screen instantly illuminates with zero blue light, displaying the clean horizontal Y | X operational baseline. Step 3 (Scaling on the Calculator): Lay 5 counting tiles into the physical ten-frame tray. On the calculator keypad, type 5 [ENTER]. Notice how the physical tiles resting on your desk mirror the number resting on the bottom floor of your StackCalc screen!

docs.title: 1.10 Story-Driven Problem Expeditions (The Calculator Workshop & Maker Bench)
1.10.1 Expedition 1: The Calculator Workshop & Maker Bench (Problems 1.1–1.6)
docs.text: Mission Briefing: Before heading out into the field with your manipulative studio, you step into the Maker Bench workshop. Here, engineers test battery reserves, calculate dot-matrix screen frame buffers, measure photometric contrast, verify stainless snap-dome tactile forces, design Gridfinity modular desktop footprints, and measure drafting easel angles. Using your StackCalc SC-6 and RPN stack math, you verify every physical parameter of your instrument.

docs.title: Problem 1.1: Battery Reserve Life on the Kitchen Table
docs.text:
• Workshop Mission: The SC-6 operates on a single CR2032 lithium coin cell with a nominal reserve capacity of \(225\text{ mAh}\). During an active school day, the calculator operates for 2 hours in active classroom calculation mode (consuming \(0.65\text{ mA}\)) and spends 22 hours in low-power sleep mode (consuming \(0.0025\text{ mA}\)). Calculate the total daily battery consumption in milliampere-hours, then calculate how many school days the calculator runs before requiring a fresh coin cell.
  • Manipulative Studio Connection: The rear tool-secured bayonet hatch protects the CR2032 coin cell, while non-volatile EEPROM memory safeguards all stack registers and quiz records across battery replacements.
  • Keystrokes: 0.65 [ENTER] 2 [×] 0.0025 [ENTER] 22 [×] [+] 225 [x⇄y] [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 166.051660517
  • Step-by-Step RPN Reasoning & Stack Logic:
  • 0.65 [ENTER] 2 [×] — Active daily power consumption: \(0.65\text{ mA} \times 2\text{ h} = 1.30\text{ mAh}\).
  • 0.0025 [ENTER] 22 [×] — Sleep standby power consumption: \(0.0025\text{ mA} \times 22\text{ h} = 0.055\text{ mAh}\).
  • [+] — Combine active and standby draw: \(1.30 + 0.055 = 1.355\text{ mAh/day}\) daily consumption.
  • 225 [x⇄y] [÷] — Load the \(225\text{ mAh}\) battery capacity and divide by daily consumption: \(225 \div 1.355 \approx 166.05\text{ school days}\) (well over a full academic year!).
  • 4-Register Stack Trace Table (\(T, Z, Y, X\)):

docs.title: Problem 1.2: Screen Memory (Dot-Matrix Frame Buffer)
docs.text:
• Workshop Mission: The transflective daylight LCD features a graphic dot-matrix resolution of 132 columns by 65 rows. Each pixel corresponds to one single memory bit in the microcontroller's display frame buffer (1 bit per pixel: black or clear). If 8 bits make 1 byte of memory, how many bytes of RAM are required to store a complete screen image?
  • Manipulative Studio Connection: The 8,580 individual display pixels render high-contrast vector ten-frames, number line jump arcs, and bold numbers without a power-hungry backlight.
  • Keystrokes: 132 [ENTER] 65 [×] 8 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 1072.5
  • Narrative Stack Analysis: Key 132 [ENTER] 65 [×] to calculate the total pixel count: the stack multiplies the horizontal columns by vertical rows, placing \(8,580\text{ pixels}\) in Register \(X\). Now key 8 [÷] to pack bits into bytes: the display drops the stack, revealing exactly 1072.5 bytes (allocated as \(1,073\text{ bytes}\) of continuous frame buffer memory) with \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 1072.5)\).

docs.title: Problem 1.3: Daylight Transflective Screen Contrast
docs.text:
• Workshop Mission: In optoelectronics quality assurance, screen readability is measured by the photometric contrast ratio: the luminance of the reflective background compared to the luminance of the black active liquid crystal segments. Under bright classroom ambient light (\(500\text{ lux}\)), a calibrated photometer measures the white screen background at \(142.0\text{ cd/m}^2\) and the activated black pixels at \(9.35\text{ cd/m}^2\). Calculate the contrast ratio and verify that it meets the AAA \(15:1\) optical readability standard.
  • Manipulative Studio Connection: Just like dark ink on bright white paper, higher ambient room light increases screen contrast naturally without glare or eye strain.
  • Keystrokes: 142 [ENTER] 9.35 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 15.187165775
  • Narrative Stack Analysis: Key 142 [ENTER] 9.35 [÷]: the stack lifts the white background luminance \(142.0\text{ cd/m}^2\) to Register \(Y\), inputs the black segment luminance \(9.35\text{ cd/m}^2\) into Register \(X\), and divides in a single stroke to yield a contrast ratio of 15.19:1 \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 15.1872)\), successfully surpassing the rigorous 15:1 AAA standard!

docs.title: Problem 1.4: Clicking Button Snap-Dome Spring Rate
docs.text:
• Workshop Mission: The tactile snap-dome switches under every SC-6 keycap are engineered from spring-tempered stainless steel. To trigger a clean electrical contact, a key requires an actuation force of \(400.0\text{ grams}\) over a tactile key travel distance of \(1.6\text{ mm}\). Calculate the mechanical spring rate \(k\) in grams per millimeter (\(k = F \div \Delta x\)).
  • Manipulative Studio Connection: The 400g snap force prevents accidental double-strokes while giving the child unmistakable tactile and audible confirmation that a digit has committed to the stack.
  • Keystrokes: 400 [ENTER] 1.6 [÷] \(\rightarrow\) 250

Register \(Y\) holds the \(400.0\text{ g}\) downward load while Register \(X\) takes the \(1.6\text{ mm}\) travel. Tapping [÷] divides the quantities, leaving a spring rate of exactly 250.0 \(\text{g/mm}\) \((T: 0, Z: 0, Y: 0, X: 250)\).
